instead, we need to target  herbicides and measures for control against  weeds, where
they belong. Again, it is a collaboration. We have wildings, which, as many of you may
well know, are plants that are in the wrong place and that have spread to areas where
they must not spread. The estimates s ay that in about 20 years’ time  around about a
quarter of our entire land scape could be taken up with the se wildings, these plants that
have invaded good pastoral land, and we need to hold them in check. The longer that we
do not actually spend money and  the longer that we hold back, the more expensive and
difficult the process is going to be. I envisage of doing more detailed work on this
programme of high -priority weed work. We are going to target the dirty dozen of
weeds. Department of Conservation officials and I are having a very good time looking
around at the various places around the country —[Interruption]—do not tempt me; it is
low-hanging f ruit over there, is it not ? It is too low hanging. The dirty dozen in the
Opposition members can look after themselves.
When it comes to weed control we do really need to get specific. I want to engage
the hearts and minds of New Zealanders to join with us in this fight because the
suffocation of our New Zealand forests and  the seedlings that are not making it through
to the stage that they need to are the sorts of reasons why we need to try to combat the
weed probl em. I intend to work with Weedb usters and a lot of other very strong
community groups to ensure that we can win this war on weeds.
The New Zealand flag conside ration is, of course, going on at the moment.
Ultimately the law will come through the Ministry for  Culture and Heritage. We do
indeed have many opportunities to look at flags. I will be hosting an exhibition here in
Parliament. There is just not enough ti me in this call to do justice to all I intend to do,
but thank you for your time today.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: It is always good to follow Poison Ivy.
Expectations were very high in th e Budget that the Government would finally —finally,
4042 Budget Debate 27 May 2015
after years of being in denial, years of Nick Smith’s photo opportunities and political
stunts—do something about the housing crisis. First -home buyers were watching with
horror as the average Auckland ho use price cracked over $800,000 in the month before
the Budget. House prices in Auckland went up on average by $100,000 in the last 12
months. Renters watched as their rents in Auckland went up by 10 percent over the
year, because landlords were seeking a return on the investment that they had made in
skyrocketing house prices. There is a housing crisis and people desperately want action.
The Reserve Bank Deputy Governor, Grant Spencer, publicly embarrassed the
Government by coming to this Parliament and saying that the Government needed to do
more, that they were not doing enough, and that they needed to something about
speculators. So the stage was set for this National Government to finally do something
meaningful about the housing crisis. What we heard  about was a speculators’ tax. John
Key announced at the National Party conference that he was going to change the rules
for tax  property speculators, and he announced a so -called—and not very bright —
brightline test that would tax speculators who buy a house and flick it on within 2 years.
At first glance it was remarkable that the Government, which has been denying for
the last 2 years that speculators are a problem in Auckland, at last announced some
policy that was supposedly targeting speculators.  But it did not take very long for the
commentators, the analysts, and the general public to realise that this was a Clayton’s
tax response to rampant property speculation  in Auckland. The so -called 2-year test is
simply an invitation to speculators  to buy a property, hold it for 2 years, and flick it on.
Treasury analysis from 2010 indicates that the tax will be lucky if it nets as many as
1,000 speculators every year, when there are 80,000 property sales every year. It will be
lucky if it nets $18 million a ye ar, when there are hundreds of millions —in fact,
billions—of dollars in turnover every year from property speculation.
John Shewan, probably the most influential of the Government’s tax advisers,
commented that this measure will not curb skyrocketing hous e prices and that it
certainly will not do anything to deter property speculators. This knowledge seemed to
finally catch up with Bill English, the finance Minister, on Q+A last weekend when he
was asked whether he thought this tax measure would have any e ffect. He said: “I don’t
know. I have no idea if it will have any effect.”
What a damning statement because what that means is that the National Party used
Budget tax policy as a political stunt to announce policy where they have no idea
whether it will have any impact at all, and on an issue that is probably the most pressing
public policy of the day, and that is the urgent need to rein in the Auckland housing
crisis, which is making an entire generation of young New Zealanders Generation Rent.
Young people in Auckland—good hard-working New Zealanders—have no prospect of
ever owning their own home in Auckland unless mum and dad are wealthy enough to
write them a very big cheque.
The second announcement on housing policy that we heard as part of the Budget  was
Nick Smith last week announcing that he had found 500 hectares of vacant
Government-owned land, zoned residential, that he was going to make available to
property developers to put houses on. On the face of it, it was a perfectly sound idea —
in fact, so sound that the former Labour Government, 7 years ago, did exactly the same
thing. It did an inventory of available Government land, and what did the National Party
of the day do? It derided it, it ridiculed it, it thought it was the funniest thing it had  ever
heard, and as soon as National got into office it shut down that work and did nothing at
all.
Nick Smith, in his mad, poll -driven panic to try to come up with something to
announce on housing before the Budget, got his officials to go back to the shelf and dust
off the work that Labour did 7 years ago. In the meantime, the National Government
27 May 2015 Budget Debate 4043
had done nothing, zilch, nada about the idea of developing vacant Government land in
Auckland.
On the surface, what seems to have been a perfectly simple idea has been completely
stuffed up by Nick Smith, the Minister for Building and Housing. He rushed out the
announcement so fast that he did not give his officials the time to even go and look at
the parcels of land that were on his list —the list of parcels of land that added up to the
500 hectares that he announced. He is the harum -scarum Minister for Building and
Housing. If you want a good idea stuffed up give it to Nick Smith, because that is what
he did. He rushed it out. The officials did not have time to go and look at the sites of
land. They did not even have time to pick up the phone and talk to the Government
agencies that own this land, to ask them what they were doing with it and what they
intended do with it.
The 500 hectares of land  that Nick Smith announced last week includes electricity
substations, the Māngere Lawn Cemetery, the SAS training base in Papakura, and the
Ōtāhuhu fire station, just to name a few examples. Nick Smith in the House today
denied that any of those things wer e on his land, but I guarantee this: those public
facilities were on lists that his officials prepared that led to him announcing 500
hectares of vacant Government land.
Nick Smith has been extremely evasive and economical with the truth. On Monday
he denied categorically to the news media that the Hepburn Road electricity substation
was on the list. Yesterday he was in this House in question time promoting it as a site.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: And he tabled some lists.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: And he tabled the land title for the substation. I want to quote
Nathaniel O’Connor, who was interviewed a year and half ago concerning the Hepburn
Road substation, where Nick Smith wants to build houses. When that substation blew
up and caused a fir e a year and half ago, Nathaniel O’Connor, whose house is located
150 metres from the substation, was reported as saying: “Our lights flickered, then there
was a really loud arcing sound, and a second after that there was a huge explosion. You
could feel i t inside your chest.” Well, I think that probably Nick Smith could feel a
tightening in his chest as we have discussed this over the last couple of days in the
House. Bill English told the media in very reassuring terms: “I presume the substation is
not always exploding.” So Bill English is very relaxed about it.
Nick Smith thinks that building houses on an electricity substation is the answer to
Auckland’s housing crisis. If that is true, we are in a lot more trouble that we thought
previously. Things are a lot worse than we imagined. We have three housing Ministers
in this Government —three housing Ministers: Nick Smith, Bill English, and Paula
Bennett. I think that John Key should appoint three more, because since he announced
those three housing Ministers Auckland housing prices have gone up by $60,000.
What have we got? We have got a weak, half -hearted tax change to try to catch
speculators. We have got a bizarre Nick Smith special —overcooked, under -prepared,
and he has not done his homework. Both of these announcements were rushed out. They
are half-baked, and were scrambled together at the last minute, in a panic. Their only
objective is to make it look as if the Government is doing something —anything—about
the housing crisis in Auckland.
But what we know is that these measures will have minimal impact. They will not
make any difference to the generation of young New Zealanders who are locked out of
the housing market. They are first -home buyers who simply want the dream that their
parents and grandparents had in this country and that is to own a home of their own. It
will not help the kids in my electorate in west Auckland who are living in uninsulated
garages because mum and dad cannot afford to pay the rent and cannot find a house
anywhere.
4044 Budget Debate 27 May 2015
These measures will not be effective. What we need is a comprehensive crackdown
on speculators. We need thousands of new affordable homes to be sold to first -home
buyers. This Government is a crushing, crushing disappointment.

items.speaker: ALASTAIR SCOTT
items.text: Talofa lava, Mr Speaker. Over the
last week or so Opposition members have criticised us for our projected surplus
forecasts. They say that they are not big enough. Well, the question is:  what would they
do differently? We know that a surplus comes from two parts: the income side and the
expenditure side. We know that the revenue side has taken a hit because of lower dairy
payouts and the lower interest -rate environment that we find oursel ves in —all these
things affect the revenue side and are out of our control. So to increase our surplus, we
have to look at the cost side: the expense side. We have to spend less. So the question to
the Opposition members is: what would they have done? What  would they have cut to
get a larger surplus today, tomorrow, and in the future?
Would they have cancelled free GP visits for under -13-year-olds? I do not think so. I
do not think they could. Would they have cancelled the increase in paid parental leave
that we put in place? Would they have cancelled the $11 million of funding available
for the kiwi breeding programme, I ask the Minister of Conservation? Would they have
cut the funding for kauri dieback? Would they have reduced expenditure in health,
which would have seen waiting lists grow, cancer treatment patients go back to
Australia, and queues for elective surgery? These are the consequences of cutting
expenditure, which is the only thing you can do if you want to increase your surpluses.
Would they ha ve cut the rheumatic fever investment that this Government has made?
Would they have taken away the $359 million that we are investing in schoolteachers,
to encourage and incentivise teachers to do better for our kids? Maybe they would claw
back the $790 m illion that we have just announced for the most needy —that is, the
children in beneficiary households.
These are the sorts of things that you have to do if the surplus is the only thing that
you are concerned about. But we are not because we know that it i s much more
important to continue the spending and the investment in those things that I have just
mentioned. You know where Labour is going to get the money from? It is going to go
for the superannuitants. It is going for the superannuitants. There are tw o or three things
that it could do. It could raise the age of entitlement, which we have said we would not
do. Maybe it could means test superannuation, which we have said we would not do. Or
maybe it can simply reduce the amount, which we have said we would not do.
This Budget focuses on those who are in need the most: the children of beneficiary
families. This Budget is a good Budget. This Budget is fiscally responsible. This Budget
has cut the kick -start programme, which is a programme that is not about focusing on
the most needy. We know that the $1,000 per person was going only to middle and
higher-income families. It was not targeted at beneficiaries and it was not targeted at
lower-income families, which is why we are cutting that back. There are 2.5 million
people involved in that programme. It is working. I support this Budget. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr PARMJEET PARMAR
items.text: All businesses, farmers, and households are
so pleased with this Budget. Again, this National Government, under the leadership of
the Rt Hon John Key, has proved that we are working hard for all. We are working hard
for all New Zealand families and children. We are working hard for all —from the
young ones to the old ones. National Government members are doing what we promised
to do. We promised to work hard for our families and children. We promised to work
hard to get families ahead. We promised to work hard for mums and dads and children
to get a better start in life and for young ones to get better opportunities to succeed.
This National Government is continuously implementing plans to support a stronger
economy, to support more jobs, and to support higher incomes to help New Zealand
27 May 2015 Budget Debate 4045
families and children. Since 2011,  194,000 jobs have been created under this National
Government—194,000 new jobs. This equates to 120 new jobs a day. Budget 2015
shows our commitment to address the drivers of hardship. Under this National
Government there are 42,000 fewer children in bene fit-dependent families than 3 years
ago. This shows that our spending is working. This shows that our spending is helping
those who need it. At the same time, we respect the taxpayers who pay for it.
Budget 2015 provides $790 million to help children in h ardship, to help children in
New Zealand’s poorest families. This National Government is continuously working
hard to deliver better public services. We are always seeking new and better ideas to
deliver better public services because we are focused on get ting results for our New
Zealand families and children. At the same time, we are working hard to reduce cost.
Yes, we are working hard to reduce cost. We are not like the previous Labour
Government whose spending increased by 50 percent, even when it becam e clear that
the global financial crisis was coming our way. That is why, when we came in in 2008,
Treasury projections were of doom and gloom and endless debt for New Zealand.
Yes, our focus is on children in hardship, and along with that we have a big b oost for
health and education. Health spending is going to be a record $15.9 billion next year.
This includes $98 million to help New Zealand families get timely elective surgeries
and for prevention and treatment of orthopaedic conditions. In education, e arly
childhood, primary, and secondary education spending will be a record $10.8 billion
next year. In tertiary education it will be $3.1 billion. We are investing in more things —
things that matter to our families and children. We are able to do this becau se we know
how to carefully manage the Government’s books. That is why we are able to invest in
things that matter to New Zealand families and children.
A strong economy is important if families are to flourish. Economic growth is
forecast to average 2.8 p ercent over the next 4 years. Average wages are forecast to
increase by $7,000, to $63,000 per annum by mid -2019. The unemployment rate is
forecast to drop below 5 percent by 2016, and there will be ACC levy cuts of $500
million in 2016 and 2017. This is o n top of the $1.5 billion that we have already put in
New Zealanders’ pockets, and at the same time our focus is to get our net debt below 20
percent by 2020.
We are also working hard to make houses affordable. This Budget provides $52
million for facilit ating housing development on Crown -owned land in Auckland. We
are also helping more young New Zealanders into their first homes through our
KiwiSaver HomeStart programme. This programme is aimed at helping 90,000 families
to buy their first home. This prov es how responsible this National Government is. This
National Government has just delivered a great Budget, a Budget that will keep New
Zealand on the right track. Thank you.
DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First): New Zealand has developed a housing crisis since
the National Government took office in 2008. It has developed it since then. It has been
like the frog in the saucepan, waiting for the heat to increase without noticing it until the
pot boils over. The crisis during that time has become chronic and this Government has
done little or nothing about it. In fact, this Government has had a worse record in
meeting housing demand than any other Government in living history. In the last 6
years house prices have gone through the roof in Auckland, and nobody over there
could deny it. Houses are now unaffordable to most homebuyers, and very little is being
done to help. We have had some action taken on access to KiwiSaver, at the price,
though, of compromising retirement savings. Too many people do not have access to
enough money in a KiwiSaver account to make any difference. The causes of the crisis
have not been addressed. Few Kiwis have left for Australia, that is true, and that has led
4046 Budget Debate 27 May 2015
to an increase in demand, but so has relatively uncontrolled immigration —56,000 in the
last year. That has led to a very significant increase in demand for housing, and the
Government has done nothing at all about that. According to the Bank of New Zealand,
11 percent of homes are sold to foreign buyers in Auckland —11 percent —and the
Government has done virtually nothing about that.
Even this Government cannot deny the problem now. It is belatedly bolstering tax
rules on residential property, which is something that should have  been done years and
year ago. There is no need at all for a capital gains tax if income tax is broad enough.
No action has been taken on that either. The Government is not doing enough about
foreign buyers. Requiring overseas buyers to have a New Zealand tax number is not
nearly enough. Determined buyers from overseas will not be deterred by that at all. The
brightline test for all buyers selling within 2 years is much too easily avoided and will
have little effect. Two years is too short. Although special  housing areas and accords
with councils will help, the real issue has been the Government’s unwillingness to
invest directly in housing itself. New Zealand First’s policy is for the Government to
buy and develop land for housing, and to use existing Crown  land for the same purpose,
and for the Government to sell directly smaller sections, thereby making modest homes
more available to more people, with easy repayments over 25 years at a low interest
rate.
The Government has taken a leaf out of New Zealand First’s book with its use of
Crown land, but only 400 hectares of it —a very small portion. It is only 400 hectares
and only as a last -minute effort in the Budget to try to look a little bit better. It is very
cosmetic. Even that land is ill -defined. We do not really know exactly what land the
Government has got in mind, and not all of it, of course, will be suitable. Only $52
million has been allowed for in the Budget to develop that land, and that seems very
light. There is also very little information about how all that will work. The Government
should take another leaf out of New Zealand First’s policy, which requires a permanent
special agency to buy and develop land for residential housing.
The Government has had an even worse record in social housing.  The average rental
is now $379 a week. Since 2008 the increase under National has been $65 a week or 20
percent, and 11.7 percent above the Consumers Price Index. That is huge. People cannot
avoid that. In Auckland people typically have to pay 50 percent of their take -home
income in rent, and that is crippling. In Christchurch people often have to pay
something like $1,000 a week or more for an ordinary three -bedroom house. It is a very
significant problem in the major cities. The Government’s social housi ng measures will
not help to increase rental housing stock. Those measures are designed to minimise the
role of the State and to emasculate Housing New Zealand. This Government is actually
abdicating its responsibility for social housing by contracting it out to non-governmental
organisations and private providers. Government members say there will be flexible
purchasing, as described in the Government’s recent legislation, allowing what they call
tailored agreements, dictated in detail by Ministers, who wi ll be biased, of course. That
is to try to give certainty to providers so that they can go out and borrow money and
build homes. But are they really capable of doing this job? We really will not know
until it happens —until the worst happens, perhaps. But H ousing New Zealand, of
course, could do all that, and used to do all that much faster and much better. So what is
the point of this exercise of farming it out to non-governmental organisations?
The whole thrust of the Government’s housing programme is to suppress demand for
State rentals, to do little for first -home buyers, and it simply does not adequately
address the housing crisis at all.

items.speaker: KELVIN DAVIS
items.text: The membe r for Wairarapa,
Alastair Scott, spoke earlier and said that the Labour Opposition is criticising the
27 May 2015 Budget Debate 4047
Government’s Budget trajectory. We are not criticising the trajectory; we are criticising
the deficit. Over the last 3 or 4 years all we have heard is tha t this Budget is going to
deliver a surplus, and it has failed to do that. All we have heard are broken promises and
squandered opportunities. This Budget has done nothing, nothing whatsoever, to
address the real issues that are going on in New Zealand.
We also criticise the fact that the Government has borrowed $84 billion over the last
7 years. The last Labour Government left the new National Government in a great
position and with great opportunity. We had zero Government debt, and now we have
got $84 b illion worth of debt. Government members do not say a lot about that. They
keep talking themselves up, but all we can see is $84 billion worth of debt. I do not
criticise $790 million going towards the families that need it the most, but $790 million
or $25 per family per week is not enough even to keep up with the cost of living. They
seem to forget that in 2006 Working for Families delivered a $60 tax credit for families
on the benefit as well. We hear a lot of talk from Government members. They are
talking themselves up, but the reality is they are not delivering. This Government has
lost its way. It is failing to meet the needs of New Zealand families, and it has no long -
term plan to address the challenges ahead. The Government is robbing from our
children’s future, just to scrape by today. This is a Government of broken promises.
We have a beautiful creature in Māoridom. It is called the kēwai. A kēwai is a
freshwater crayfish. A freshwater crayfish moves by flapping its legs and moving
backwards, and t his is what I would say is a “kēwai Budget”, where the Government
members are backtracking and back -pedalling as fast as they can flap themselves. They
promised a surplus and all we have got is another deficit. There were nine surpluses
from this side of the House and seven deficits from over there.
What would a responsible Government do? It would grow incomes. This
Government has failed on that. It promised that incomes would grow by $7,000 and it
has failed to meet that by some $3,000. It has not fixed t he housing crisis. Phil Twyford
was very eloquent in describing the issues around the housing crisis in Auckland. The
Government has not hit the speculators, and when it started to hit the speculators it was
just a Clayton’s attack. We are not going to see much difference in what has happened. I
think of my nephew. He is very lucky that he bought a house some 5 years ago in
Auckland for $400,000. He sold it at the end of last year for $790,000. He is one of the
lucky ones. But people coming into the housing  market now are the ones who are going
to miss out. A real Government would invest in a productive and diverse economy. All
this Government is doing is relying on dairy and disaster. If it was not for the
Christchurch earthquake, the growth in our economy would be about 25 percent less
than what it is now.
This Government needs to prepare New Zealand for the next generation of wealth
creation. It is not doing that. It has not transformed tertiary education to match skills
with future jobs. By the way, some thing that we need to keep harping on about is the
previous Labour Government’s record when it comes to unemployment. We got it down
to 3.4 percent—3.4 percent—and what has this Government done? Well, it has doubled
that now. Not only that, in Whangarei in  2007 there were 58 people on the
unemployment benefit. You could just about name them if you sat down and tried to
memorise their names. You could basically do that. I do not know how many hundreds,
if not thousands, are on the unemployment benefit now in Whangarei.
Let us have a listen to some of these broken promises. Well, there is the surplus. We
have already covered that. We have had seven deficits. We are promised now that next
year there will be a surplus. Actually, let us remember the Minister of Finance’s
analogy. He said: “Oh, well, if you’re trying to lose 10 kilogrammes to fit a suit for your
brother’s wedding and you lose only 9.8 kilogrammes, well, what does it matter?”. I
4048 Budget Debate 27 May 2015
prefer this analogy. When the All Blacks go to the Rugby World Cup thi s year in order
to bring home that William Webb Ellis Cup, they need a surplus of points —more
points—than the other team. If they end up with a deficit of points, they are losers; they
have lost. That is why the people of New Zealand are losing because of this Budget.
What else? Jobs and wages —this is in John Key’s open letter to New Zealanders
after the election. He promised that “Over the next 2 years we expect to see about
150,000 jobs created.” National will fall short on that promise by 60,000. Then t here is
the KiwiSaver kick -start contribution of $1,000. The Government is robbing our
children’s future to scrape by today. That is unacceptable. Then we have new taxes. Of
course, we were told there would be no new taxes. That was an election promise —no
new taxes. Well, we have got a new capital gains tax that is not really a capital gains
tax. We have got an airport tax that we are told is not really a tax; it is a levy. We have
got a broadband tax. What is the next one? National promised to increase exp orts to 40
percent of GDP. Well, that is heading south as well. Then there are the regions. Well,
the regions spoke —Northland spoke. It has been forgotten. The Minister of Transport,
Simon Bridges, said: “We’ll promise 10 bridges.” Thank God his name is no t “Simon
Tunnels”, or else we would have 10 tunnels going through Northland. This is a reckless
Budget.
I just want to touch on the police estimates, because the poor police are doing a great
job out there but they are just getting no Budget increases. In  fact, they have had $15
million in cuts this year. I know that the Minister is going to get up here and say: “Oh
no, that is not true. We’re implementing $160 million in new initiatives.” Well, really,
what the Minister has done is taken a pack of cards, shuffled it, allowed a few cards to
fall out on to the floor, and then re -dealt them and said that it is all new money. Well, I
can tell everyone that it is not new money; it is $15 million less. Let us just have a look
and let us just use the estimates th at came out last week. If we look at the columns in
Budget 2014 -15, the final budgeted amount was $1.624 billion, and in the estimated
actual it was $1.624 billion. What is the budget for 2015 -16? It is $1.609 billion. That is
a Budget cut, and no Minister  can walk in here and say that they have increased the
funding for police. It is here in black and white that the Government has cut the police
Budget, and that is unacceptable.
But when you look through the police Budget, what do you see? You see that th e
Government’s targets are more on revenue collecting. For example, it has got greater
targets in chasing up people using cellphones while driving. I think it is trying to double
the number of people who are using cellphones whom it wants to catch. There i s
funding for incorrect lane changing and warrants of fitness, and yet there are people like
our colleague the Hon Phil Goff who had his motorbike pinched. He ain’t going to see
that again, because the high-volume crimes—those really irritating crimes such as theft,
burglary, assault, shoplifting—are not having as much money put into them.
In fact, many of the cuts are coming from catching drivers speeding. The
Government wants to catch more people but it is actually giving the police less money
in order to catch speeders. Heavy vehicle fleet—I take it that that is catching trucks that
are overloaded. Fatigue and distraction—the Government is taking away $133,000 from
that. Traffic management—it is taking away $408,000 from that. Alcohol and impaired
drivers—now, you would think that that would be a massive priority, but it is taking
away $2.815 million from there. High -risk drivers—it is removing $5.128 million from
there. So the Government is asking the police to do more, to catch more people, but it is
giving them less money, and these are all high revenue collecting crimes —rather than
going out and catching those criminals who are breaking into homes and, like I say,
stealing the Hon Phil Goff’s motorcycle. This Budget does not deliver.
27 May 2015 Budget Debate 4049
I would really li ke to carry on about the Department of Corrections. There is a big
mess there and it all comes around the prison privately run by Serco, which is a direct
transfer of jobs from the public sector through to the private sector. Unfortunately, my
time has expired. Kia ora.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call Nuk Korako —5
minutes.

items.speaker: NUK KORAKO
items.text: Kia ora, e te Mana Whakawā . Talofa lava. Kia ora. E
mihi atu ana ki te whanaukatanga ki Te Moana -nui-a-Kiwa, ā, huri noa te Whare, kia
ora.
[Thank you.  I acknowledge the relationship with the Great Sea of Kiwa . And,
throughout the House, hello there.]
First of all, this is a split call. Obviously, it is my first time  standing and speaking as
a member of the House in a Budget debate. The last speech, by Mr Davis, epitomises
for me what has actually happened since the announcement of the Budget last week,
called “ A plan that’s working ”. I have listened very carefully to the debate, which
started last week, and I understand now that that people across the other side of  the
House have selective memories and that in some ways they have selective hearing as
well. I just remind Mr Davis of the fact that when Bill English took over as Minister of
Finance in 2008, what he accepted was possibly one of the biggest hospital passes that
was ever given to a Minister of Finance. What happened there was that the Labour
Government had squandered 9 yea rs—9 years—of good economic conditions, and over
the last week we have had constant reminders from the other side of the House that
Labour ran surpluses for 9 years.
But at least let me ask those members opposite what they have to show for it. What
do they have to show for it?
It is all very well boasting about making surpluses, but you did absolutely nothing for
children living in hardship, nothing for Māori, and nothing to support our most
vulnerable people. Labour had 9 years of spending up large, yet it  did not increase
benefits one bit,  in real terms. It took a National Government, with the support of the
Māori Party, to give our most vulnerable whānau a $25-per-week increase as part of a
$790 million package of support for children and whānau living in  hardship. There is
also some targeted support, and that is what I want to concentrate on —two major ones,
particularly for Māori. The first one is the Te Ture Whenua Māori network, where we
are investing almost $13 million in supporting Māori landowners im prove the
productivity of their land, along with a timely review of the Māori Land Act —under the
Māori Land Act, if you take into account that 11 percent of land in the North Island is
under that legislation, 80 percent of that land is underdeveloped. We c ould see $8
billion injected into the Māori economy, along with 5,000 jobs created over the next 10
years. That is part of this innovative situation that we have actually put into this Budget,
about starting to review all of that legislation.
Today the New  Zealand economy continues to grow, and so does the Māori tribal
economy. This Budget also appropriates $1.4 billion over the next 5 years for the
settlement of historic Treaty claims —and I want to talk about Treaty settlements. The
Government’s commitment  to its programme of Treaty settlements is more about
pumping money into the Māori economy if we look at that and think about those Treaty
settlements and if you look at the work of Minister Finlayson and what he has done over
the last two terms —over 40 Tr eaty settlements. In doing that, that is actually linked to
regional economy. When we look at the largest iwi, Ngāpuhi, it has just begun
negotiations with the Crown. But all we have heard on that side of the House is
negativity—a lot of negativity. We heard it last night, about whether a settlement would
really change things up there. I say to my Māori colleagues on the other side of the
4050 Budget Debate 27 May 2015
House, just look at Waikato-Tainui, just look at Ngāi Tahu. All of that, the references to
the scourge of property devel opers and all of that that we have heard from that side of
the House —Ngāi Tahu are the largest property developers in the South Island, and
those properties are being invested in the future of our people.

items.speaker: MATT DOOCEY
items.text: Talofa lava. It is great to be a New
Zealander. It is great to live in New Zealand. I know that many other people who live in
this fine country know it is great to be a Kiwi and great to live in New Zealan d. The
reason I know this is because of the recently released New Zealand General Social
Survey, the biggest social survey outside the 5 -year census. It shows that 83 percent of
people are highly satisfied with their lives. That is between eight and nine p eople out of
10 who are highly satisfied with their lives. And 87 percent of people have a high sense
of purpose in their lives. That is fantastic news, but there is a lot more to be done, and
that is what this National Government is doing.
It is also great to be a Canterbury National MP, and it is great to be part of a team of
Canterbury National MPs. We have increased the Budget for the Canterbury rebuild
from $15.5 billion to $16.5 billion. That is an extra $1 billion for the Canterbury
recovery, and that shows the faith that the voters put in us in the last election because, of
course, this National Government won the party vote in every electorate in Canterbury.
A lot of the credit for that needs to go to our Minister for Canterbury Earthquake
Recovery, the Hon Gerry Brownlee. It was great to see the opening of the bus exchange
in Christchurch on Monday morning, another great anchor project opening in the
recovery. We are committed to the recovery and this Budget proves that. It is one of our
top four priorities.
I remember campaigning in the last election, when I met many voters who were
voting National for the first time. They had voted Labour all their lives, but they were
voting for National because National was working hard for New Zealand, listeni ng to
New Zealand, and working for the working people of New Zealand. I come from a
background in mental health, which is about making a difference in people’s lives, and
this Budget is making a difference in people’s lives. I am proud to be part of a
Government that, at the first opportunity for this term, stood up in this Budget debate
and supported children and families. This will make a big difference in people’s lives.
The $790 million child hardship package will give working families up to $25 a
week. That is over 50,000 families who will get up to $25 a week. People also said to us
that they wanted us to support the vulnerable, and that is why we are increasing the
benefit by up to $25 a week. That is the first uplift since 1972. I was born in 1972, so
beneficiaries have not had an uplift like this in my whole lifetime. It took a National
Government to deliver that. It is about making a difference in people’s lives, and  this
National Government is delivering.
This National Government cares. We care about New Zealand and in New Zealand
we have a mixed economy of care. We have State provision, we have private provision,
and we have community provision. It is not about a s mall State; it is about big
communities and it is about this Government backing communities. To all those
creative, community -sector organisations, we believe in you —we believe in you to
make a difference. This mixed economy of care is about flexibility and choice. This was
demonstrated in our social housing reform, where our legislation will allow an extra
3,000 people to access housing support.
To those 3,000 people, tell them that the Labour Party said no, the New Zealand First
Party said no, and the Green Party said no, but that it was this National Government that
said yes to them. And to all of those tenants with high, complex needs —like mental
health and drug addiction —the Labour Party said no to extra support, the New Zealand
First Party said no to that legislation for extra support, and the “Red Green Party” said
27 May 2015 Budget Debate 4051
no, but this National Government said yes, because at the end of the day this party is
working hard for New Zealanders. We are listening to New Zealanders, because the
National Government is the working people’s party. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: Mr Assistant Speaker, a split call?

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: A 5-minute call.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: Yes. As a number of my colleagues have already noted,
the 2015 Budget statement said virtually nothing about the biggest economic issue
facing this country—that is, climate change. The Budget revealed new policy, of course,
on a variety of household issues. They are important issues, especially to those directly
affected, but they are not the overarching macroeconomic issues that will at the global
level—and, therefore, at the national level —overwhelm e verybody if they are not
properly addressed.
The Minister of Finance is tinkering at the margin with his seventh Budget. It is like
the captain of a ship transferring his passengers into a dingy with an outboard motor.
Both are heading into the hurricane ahead. The captain is saying: “Not to worry, we
have just enough freeboard to stay afloat.” He is saying this even as the sea is getting
bigger. That hurricane is climate change —literally hurricanes, storms, and floods that
are already occurring.
Why is e xtreme weather relevant to New Zealand’s Budget? It is because the stress
on the planet’s resources through global population increase and burgeoning economic
activity per person is unsustainable. We are incurring today a global ecological
overshoot of 50 percent. Although New Zealand is rare in having a national ecological
surplus, we are negatively affected, including our fiscal outlook, by the unsustainable
and worsening global economy. That is the reason the Minister is failing, even though
he is widely seen as a successful economic steward.
The most important global meeting to date occurs in December. It is the 21 st annual
United Nations Climate Change Conference in Paris. It is the equivalent of the failed
conference in Copenhagen in 2009, but it is m ore important because we have lost 6
critical years, yet there is not a word on this in the Budget.
The world has lost ground. No longer are the negotiators engaged in global planning.
Top-down is out; bottom -up is in. Binding commitments are out; volunta ry
contributions are in. We going to tame dangerous climate change, you understand,
through voluntary contributions by 194 competing States jealous of their national
sovereignty. God help us, for we know not what we do.
That voluntary contribution is labe lled in the latest jargon “INDC”, or intended
nationally determined contribution. It is “nationally determined”, not “globally
determined”; it is “intended”, not “committed”, and the jargon is sanitised to the point
of stupefaction. Global warming above 4 degrees, which is labelled by international
organisations as catastrophic, is described by this Government as having “substantial
environmental, economic and human impacts”. God help us.
New Zealand is lumbering its way towards its intended nationally det ermined
contribution. It has held public consultations throughout the country. The Minister for
Climate Change Issues is conspicuously absent. He does not care; his mind has moved
on. He will, none the less, announce the intended nationally determined cont ribution
within a few months. It will be insufficient —probably between 10 and 20 percent. He
will pepper it with conditions and irrelevancies. He will imply that he is in possession of
complex and arcane knowledge that accords superior insight.
The Green Party has already said that the intended nationally determined
contribution must be 40 -plus percent. That would bring New Zealand’s net emissions
down from 67 megatonnes today to 40 megatonnes in 2030. That is consistent with the
Green Party policy of achieving climate neutrality by 2050. Is getting to 40 megatonnes
4052 Budget Debate 27 May 2015
feasible? Yes, it is. As far as can be determined, we could do at least that, and we are
talking about domestic abatement alone. In fact, it is possible that we could go further.
What might be N ew Zealand’s maximum abatement potential, assuming all policy
signals are optimal and there is sufficient political will? The experts will differ, but the
range could be anything from 40 megatonnes down to perhaps 20. So let us have the
debate over what ca n be done —a genuine public debate, not a trite, ministerial
sermon—and let us then have a genuine, cross-party political debate.
My final point is that that is simply our domestic abatement. If we are talking about
doing our fair share in the global effor t to ensure a 2 degrees Celsius outcome, New
Zealand’s national responsibility target goes far, far beyond that.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Gareth Hughes—a 5-minute
call.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Assistant Speaker. Ngā mihi nui ki a
koutou. Kia ora. According to the Bible, it took only 7 days to form the earth and all the
plants and animals on it, yet Bill English, managing a so-called rock star economy, has
not been able to achieve this over 7 years. Of course, this was National’s seventh
Budget. It continues 7 years of deficits, debt, dairy dependence, and declining
homeownership. It seems the only indicator that i s not going backwards for National is
our greenhouse gas emissions, which we know are just going up and up.
The Budget did nothing for a whole generation of young Kiwis who are swimming in
student debt and cannot get into their first home, or for Kiwi wor kers, half of whom
have seen their wages stagnate under National. After 7 years our economy is more
dependent on a few raw commodities. It is a simpler economy than when we started.
Just this week we saw a massive $2.6 billion trade deficit, the largest in  the 6 years
since the middle of the worst global recession we have seen in decades. What we are
seeing now are the impacts of falling dairy prices and also the dependence our country
has on exporting this raw milk powder around the world.
Likewise, you can see it with the data that we saw in the Budget. The horses that the
National Government has picked are not working. We have seen oil royalty income go
down 38 percent, minerals income go down 34 percent. We have seen coal royalty
income go down 33 perce nt. On the other side of the ledger though, we have also seen
flat to declining science funding. Tertiary education has seen $1 billion stripped out of it
over the last 7 years. We have seen New Zealand continue to languish in the bottom half
of the OECD. We are going backwards on the important things like science and
innovation, yet we are increasing our dependence on things like dairy and oil, which are
not paying off. You can see it in the perilous state of the country’s books that Bill
English showed us, but you can also see it in the experience of the majority of Kiwis.

items.speaker: Hon Anne Tolley
items.text: Perilous?

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Well, Ms Tolley, in this country Kiwis are working some of
the longest hours for some of the lowest wages, an d we are paying some of the highest
costs of living in the entire developed world. The whole country is sprinting just to keep
where we are. We are not actually getting ahead as a country. The fact is we have got
290,000 Kiwi kids in poverty, yet for a cou ntry—[Interruption] I hear the National
backbench interjecting. For a country that is feeding 20 million people around the world
in our agricultural exports, it is a travesty that we have got hungry kids going to school
without food, but your party voted against supplying them food in schools.
Under National’s New Zealand, we see the richest 1 percent controlling 16 percent of
the country’s wealth. And the bottom half, what does it have? It has got only 5 percent.
Every year under National it just gets wor se and worse. But the fact is that it is bad for
our economic performance. The OECD has found that National’s rising inequality has
shaved 10 percent off our GDP over the last decade. Sure, there have been some
27 May 2015 Budget Debate 4053
productivity improvements, but they have not flowed through to the workers. So, sure,
we have got rising inequality, but we are also seeing rising generational inequality.
Previous generations of Kiwis used to have an affordable education and State support
to get into a first home, yet for Kiwis in their 20s or 30s a good job, an affordable
education, and support to get into their first home are considered luxuries. Parents are
struggling to raise their kids, burdened by massive student debt, and the high cost of
living in areas like electricity and food. The majority of young Kiwis are forced to rent.
In fact, we have had to create an entire new name for this new generation, which is
being called Generation Rent. For this generation the dream of homeownership is
slipping further and further out of reach. So we are seeing rising inequality, generational
inequality, but perhaps the biggest inequality is what is happening with the planet,
which the last speaker, Kennedy Graham, just touched on—intergenerational inequality,
in terms of future generations’ security, literally, on the planet.
Over those 7 years under National what we have seen is our emissions increase by 20
percent since National came into power. They are forecast to increase 48 percent by the
end of this decade. Just in the last week, wit hin National’s Budget, guess what there
was? There was $31 million to subsidise polluters. National’s emissions trading scheme
is a complete farce. It is not incentivising the clean -energy economy we should be
developing and those clean -energy jobs; in fac t, it is subsidising polluters, and that is
National’s vision for the future. However, there is a better alternative. That is why the
Greens are putting up so many good ideas to rebalance our economy, reduce inequality,
and give all Kiwis a fair go. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Hon NICKY WAGNER
items.text: Well, Budget 2015 is a great
Budget. It is Minister Bill English’s seventh Budget, and I think he has nailed it. The
Government’s plan is working. We have got a strong, growing economy, and it is
translating into real benefits for Kiwi families, Kiwi hous eholds, and Kiwi businesses. I
think, really, the Budget delivers careful management of public spending, but also
shows investment into better services that Kiwis need. We have prioritised the things
that matter most to most New Zealanders. If you think ab out it, we cannot do anything
in life unless we are healthy, so we have put more money into health: $1.7 billion more
this year. That will mean there is a record spend of $15.9 billion for 2015 -16. And then
there is education. Our Government believes that a good education is the best
foundation for people to live good lives, to be able to have choices in their lives. We
have invested there, again, another $686 million, which means that the suite of early
childhood, primary, and secondary education is gettin g $10.8 billion, and then on top of
that we are spending over $3 billion on tertiary education.
But for me, as the Minister for Disability Issues, I am really interested in what is
being spent for special education. We have increased the amount of spending every year
since we have been in Government. This year we are investing a further $62.9 million
over 4 years. That is more money for the Ongoing Resourcing Scheme (ORS) funding.
What we have got this funding for is for significantly disabled youngsters —people who
have problems with physical or mental issues and learning disabilities. What we are
doing is putting this money in towards giving them a better quality of life and a better
chance of education. We are also going to add $23 million for extra in -class aides for
kids who do not quite meet the Ongoing Resourcing Scheme category. They are the
ones who still need help but are not in the Ongoing Resourcing Scheme. We want to
make sure that our disabled youngsters have the best opportunity to live the lif e of
ordinary kids. We believe that education is the best place to make that happen.
We are also working on housing programmes, obviously. We are particularly
focusing on affordable housing in Auckland and Christchurch, but also for first home
owners. We are investing in ultra -fast broadband, regional highways, KiwiRail, and
4054 Budget Debate 27 May 2015
urban cycleways. They are all things that I think are money well spent. Let us look at
jobs. Our Government believes that work is good for you. We believe in work not just
for getting wages or a salary, but because if you go to work you are part of a team, you
are part of a contribution, you can use your skills, and that is what people do in our
communities. I am delighted that businesses have been able to create 194,000 new jobs
since 2011, but we are backing them to do more. We are backing them to deliver
150,000 jobs over the next 4 years. We also want good wages. Average wages have
increased by 15 percent in the last 5 years. We are expecting that to continue and we are
hoping that the average wage will be able to rise by about $7,000 to get to $63,000 by
mid-2019. The ACC annual levy cuts will also inject $2 billion into the back pockets of
Kiwis between 2012 and 2016, and I think that has been very well received.
But I have to say, the highlight of the Budget has got to be the package for children
from poorer families, which is the $25 a week increase in benefits. We understand that
people on benefits struggle to look after their kids, so $25 will make a difference  for
families with children. As we have already heard, this is the first time in 43 years that
benefits have been lifted. But we are not forgetting the people who are working with
lower incomes either. The Working for Families payments will also increase b y $12.50
a week. That total package is $790 million over 4 years, and that will help about
160,000 low-income families and will touch 300 children. I think that is absolutely a
great effort, it will make a real difference, and it is something that, I think , most Kiwis
support.
Going back to the disabilities sector, I am delighted that Budget 2015 also provides
special money for transition for disabled students. It provides $16.3 million for
participation and inclusion services to help young people who are disabled and who are
leaving school and entering into adult life. We are giving them what we call our very
high-needs support system. I think anyone who has been involved with teenagers
understands how difficult that transition from school to the real worl d is. It is
particularly difficult for disabled people, particularly if they have significant physical,
intellectual, or sensory impairments, or maybe a combination of all these things —
learning, hearing, vision, or mobility impairments. I think this is a particularly important
area, and I am really pleased to see that money has been put there.
Now I want to talk about the Customs Service, because customs and the security and
safety of our border have benefited from Budget 2015. First of all, there is a cap ital sum
of $4.7 million for extra officers to screen departing passengers—that is, screening them
for terrorism and drug threats. That extended risk screening for departures complements
what we already do there in terms of existing automated and face -to-face passport
checks, and also complements the alert system that is already in place. This is an aim to
counter terrorism and to make sure that we can maintain New Zealand’s low -risk status.
It is important that New Zealand is seen as a safe country, and Ne w Zealanders have
told us they want that to remain that way.
It is because they are so keen to see a safe and secure border that we are introducing
the new border processing levy for travellers. It is an important step in managing both
biosecurity and people threats at the border. It brings the screening of travellers and the
cost recovery of processing at the border in line with what we already do with goods.
Since the early 1990s there has been a cost recovery from importers of goods, and now
we are look ing at travellers. The beauty of this levy is that it is flexible because as the
numbers of travellers go across our borders the amount of resource increases. This is
particularly important because we are getting larger numbers every year —about a 3.5
percent increase, and we are expecting that to increase —and more complex passengers,
language issues, and different cultures. It is really important that that resource will be
available where it is needed.
27 May 2015 Budget Debate 4055
The border processing levy is also fairer. At the mome nt taxpayers—that is you, me,
the panel beater from Whangarei, and the solo mum from Christchurch —all pay for
visitors to come across our border. Of those people coming across our border, 58
percent are international visitors. Many of them are on luxury cr uises or golfing trips to
New Zealand, and I do not really think it is right that the New Zealand taxpayer should
pay for them. What is more, it is a lose -lose. We pay for those overseas visitors to come
through our border, but as soon as we go back to the ir country we have to pay again.
This is because most countries have a border levy; it is international best practice. New
Zealand’s border levy will be about $20, give or take, and that is actually very light in
comparison to the countries that we visit —places like Australia, which charges about
NZ$58; the UK, which charges NZ$150; and Canada and the US, which are all very
similar. The majority of the levy will be on the arrival part, simply because that is where
the biosecurity screening happens, but we s till need part of the levy to cover departures
and the face -to-face and screening of passport checks. It will apply to all travellers —
about 95 percent are airline passengers, but also cruise passengers. If you come on your
private yacht or airline, you wil l have to pay as well. We are getting stakeholders a
consultation—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Thank you. The member’s
time has expired.
Su’a WILLIAM SIO (Labour —Māngere): Talofa lava, Mr Assistant Speaker.
Talofa i lau afioga le fofoga fetalai. Talofa fo’i to the members of this House, and I
acknowledge all of those members who have been able to contribute to Sa moan
Language Week. Le vaiaso o le gagana Samoa i lenei vaiaso. Faamalo le tapuaiga a le
tatou Atunu’u, Samoa, i itu e fia o Aotearoa. Fa’amalo foi le tapua’i i le itumalo o
Magele.
The theme of Samoan Language Week this week is “ Tautua nei mo sou manuia a
taeao”, meaning serve now for a better tomorrow. Although “tautua” means serve, it
also means to be a servant to others, but the operative words here are do it now for a
better tomorrow. I think that is quite fitting when we are debating this Budget, beca use
we are talking about what this Government is doing and the ramifications that its
actions will have on the future of this country, on the future of our young people, and on
the future of the next generation of the workforce in Aotearoa New Zealand. Alt hough
the Budget promises so much —and we heard on Thursday, Friday, and Saturday how
this Government just enjoyed crowing and shouting from the rooftops about those
particular promises —I think when we start digging a little bit underneath those
promises and try to identify the detail of those promises, we find that the Government is
woefully short on the things that it needs to do for a better tomorrow.
I want to say that it is woefully short because National ran last year’s election
promising us that ther e would be a surplus this year. National convinced all of us and
convinced the New Zealand public that if National returned to Government, we would
have a $300 million surplus. That was the promise that National made to New
Zealanders at the last election.  Well, what do we get —what do we get? Now
Government members are saying “What’s in a surplus?”. They are trying to blame us
for the Government’s deficit. The reality is that a surplus is important because it is a
sign of an efficient Government. It means t hat the Government can invest in the future.
It means that the Government can pay off debt. Right now we are in hock for $83
billion, paying $10 million in interest. There is no vision for the future because of the
fact that the Government has failed time and time and time again, 7 years in a row, to
achieve that surplus. Every time we try to hold the Government to account, Government
members say “We’ll do it next year.” They promise it for next year. Now I think the
New Zealand public has got wind of this.
4056 Budget Debate 27 May 2015
The Government has now have created a pattern for itself of making promises that it
never intends delivering on—empty promises. Let me just give you an example —when
we talk about the details of this Budget, and the lack of vision for the future. I spoke at a
school assembly in South Auckland on Monday to launch Samoan Language Week this
week. That school belongs to a cluster of schools called the Auckland Samoan Bilingual
Education Cluster. The principal whispered to me that they were really disappointed
that there was nothing in this Budget whatsoever to recognise Pacific bilingual
language, to recognise the value of Pacific bilingual language to students, and the value
of the teachers who work in these units. They said to me that in the last 4 years they  had
been engaging with the Ministry of Education, with this Government, to try to get it to
recognise the value of Pacific bilingual language. What did they get? Zilch —zilch,
nothing.
What this Government has done for Pacific bilingual language education  is cut the
resources that these units required. Remember the Tupu series? Remember the Folauga
journals? The Government cut the development of them. Not only that, it removed
Pacific bilingual education as a goal in the Pasifika Education Plan 2013 -2017. The
Government removed that and there is nothing that is in this Budget today that gives
any hope, any inspiration to the next generation of bilingual students in South
Auckland, that this Government recognises the value of languages. The foundation of
cultural identity, of self -respect, of self -responsibility, and of self -discipline is in the
language, and this Government continues to fail to provide for that.
This Budget continues to fail to eliminate the growing inequalities that we face as a
country. It continues to fail to recognise and address the housing crisis. It continues to
fail to provide any hope whatsoever to hard -working ordinary New Zealanders who are,
day in day out, just doing it tough, and struggling to make ends meet. It fails to provide
any inspiration that someday, if they work harder, they will be able to buy a house of
their own. That dream has become virtually impossible for the low and middle -income
bracket in our communities. It fails to provide any inspiration.
The Budget did pro vide some band -aid fixes. I call them “band -aid fixes” because
they provide no long -term solution to the issues that we face today. For example,
Government members crowed about the $25 that the Government is giving to the
beneficiaries. They crowed on Thur sday, Friday, Saturday —we got sick and tired of
them shouting from the rooftops —but when you look underneath the details, they say
that they are concerned for the poor, but we do not get the $25 now. We have to wait a
whole full year to get it. They have t o wait till next year to get it. What then happens
while we are waiting? Is anything being done for the poor? No. They remain in Struggle
Street. But in the meantime that paltry $25 a week gets swallowed up by the increases in
rent, the increases in petrol  prices, and the increases in power prices. Woe unto those
people during this winter. It is going to be a cold, cold winter.
The other thing is that the Government thinks that people on benefits want to be on
benefits. It thinks that people on benefits lo ve that lifestyle. That is not a lifestyle
choice. The majority of people on benefits find themselves being there through
economic and social conditions out of their control. I have never come across somebody
on a benefit who dreams of remaining on a benef it. Pacific people do not want
handouts. They want a hand up. Sure, the Government said that it was going to try to
get people into jobs. Forcing solo parents, when their child is 3 years old, into a job that
does not exist is not a work plan. The best wel fare support for communities who are
done by is to get them into jobs —high-value jobs, high -paying jobs, jobs that can
enable them to support and sustain their families, jobs that can enable them to contribute
to the community through various activities in schools etc.
27 May 2015 Budget Debate 4057

items.speaker: So let me just make that point
items.text: people do not want your handouts, which are short -
term band-aids. Yes, it has been welcomed by many, but that is because Kiwis generally
have a sense that we have an obligation to look after those who are unab le to help
themselves. To think that the Government is forcing people, solo parents in particular,
to find part -time jobs—show me flexible employers that are willing to work with and
support those young solo parents. Show me them in our community. There ar e some,
but members opposite are expecting every one of those beneficiaries to get into jobs that
will not be there without a comprehensive plan to ensure that they get those jobs.
I have heard speakers here say that the Government is raising incomes. Tha t is a
crock, and that is the softest way I can say that. Flexible industrial laws, fire -at-will
industrial laws, and eliminating good faith bargaining are all the signs of driving wages
down and keeping them low. That is the Government’s mantra.
The hous ing sell -off—Pacific people want to own their own homes. They do not
want to be renting for the rest of their lives, but it is becoming impossible under this
Government. The selling -off of State houses, which we rushed through this House on
Friday and Satu rday, is not a plan to make housing affordable. How on earth does the
Government intend to create more houses if it is selling off State houses? Pushing
people into the lines of social housing is not a plan to ensure that people have some
dignity and are a ble to achieve sustainability and respect for themselves. But that is
what the Government intends to do. Its plan is to keep the money in the hands of the
few and ensure that the rest of the New Zealand population continues to wallow in the
poverty, the in equalities that the Government has created, the mess that it has created
because it has failed, over and over again, to achieve that surplus, which is a sign of
efficient Government. It is not an efficient Government. It does not matter what
Government members say; it is not.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I was not going to reply to the
comments of my dear friend and colleague, as co -chair of the New Zealand - Turkey
Parliamentary Friendship Association—such giddy heights have we risen to!

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: That member will go no further.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Anyway—what was that?

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: He’ll go no further.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I think he will. I think he will one day get his own
chairmanship.
Anyway, I was not actually going to repl y, but I just had to. I actually felt a bit sorry
for the Labour members after that Budget. There they were, listening to Bill English go
on and on during the Budget speech —and that is not a criticism of Bill, because every
Minister of Finance just reads o ut their speech word for word, no problem. They sat
there and they listened to us take a huge chunk out of their territory. I thought: “Gee,
this is going to be interesting. I am going to look forward to Andrew Little’s reply.”,
and then not a lot really h appened, actually. I think he remembered that Bill Clinton
once used to say that “kiss” is the thing to remember —you know, “keep it simple,
stupid”. Then, of course, he got himself all tied up with that other KISS character, Gene
Simmons. I actually felt, almost, a bit sorry for him. I am not going to fib to the House
and say that I did feel sorry for him. I thought: “That has got to be the worst Budget
reply speech that I have ever heard, Andrew Little.” I looked around at his colleagues
on the Labour benc hes and their little heads were down, or they were busy reading
things that they needed to read, or they were looking anywhere except at their leader,
and that said to me everything really. This Budget surprised them. This Budget
delivered on an area where  they had expected absolutely nothing, which is actually
about really giving some people who are at the poorest end of society, in terms of socio -
economic wealth, a little bit more.
4058 Budget Debate 27 May 2015
It was a bit disheartening to hear Su’a William Sio refer to $25 per week  as a paltry
amount. Well, I guess it probably is if you get the sorts of salaries that we get in
Parliament, but, actually, it is not if you are on a benefit. It is actually quite a significant
amount of money. I would say that there would not be too many  people living on
benefits who would say: “Actually, I do not want to have that paltry $25 per week.” I
reckon that they will all want to have it —and, actually, probably they need it —and I
think that is a good thing. This is, of course, the first Governmen t to deliver a real
increase in benefits in 43 years, and that is worth crowing about. In fact, that is actually
a longer time than most of the people here in Parliament, on the other side, have been
alive.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: An entire Matt Doocey.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Yes, it is, in fact, an entire Matt Doocey.
The other thing that I wanted to talk about in this Budget debate, which I am really
excited about, is the extra funding that is going into special education. I am very pleased
to be a member of the Education and Science Committee at Parliament and I would  just
like to say that we have had a wonderful discussion today around special education,
particularly for children who have Asperger’s syndrome and autistic spectrum
disorders—dyspraxia and dyslexia, in particular. We have actually come a long way, I
think, not only as a Government but also generally across parties on this. We are often
in danger in that committee of having peace break out, which I always think, actually,
that the public would rather have.
We talked quite a lot today and learnt quite a lo t about what is actually being done,
and I actually think that over the last few years we have seen some significant
improvement. So when the announcement was made by the Hon Hekia Parata that we
are, in fact, going to be allocating $39.5 million to the On going and Reviewable
Resourcing Scheme, which is also called ORRS, and that is support for an extra 500
students. These are kids who, in fact, do have to learn in a different way, often with
different assistance, but they can often achieve hugely if they a re given the right help
and assistance environment. It also helps to pay for speech language therapists,
psychologists, physiotherapists, and occupational therapists and provides additional
teacher time and teacher aide time.
We are investing an extra $62.9 million of operating funding over the next 4 years to
give kids who have special needs when it comes to learning, or who have different ways
of learning, to be able to learn and to achieve. I am going to speak now to those parents
of children who do not  have these sorts of issues that they need to work around, and
who sometimes say: “Oh, why are you spending all this money and this time on these
kids?”. Well, actually, if you want to just go and have a look at the movie The Imitation
Game, you will see P rofessor Alan Turing. That man clearly had Asperger’s syndrome.
Today he would be diagnosed with Asperger’s syndrome. So much is made of him
being gay and being persecuted for being gay and everything else, but you could also
say that he was persecuted for  being different. He was different because he clearly was
on the autism spectrum and, yet, what did he do with that?

items.speaker: Louisa Wall
items.text: He’s a genius.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Well, apart from being a bit difficult to deal with
sometimes, he was actually, as Louisa Wall has just called out, an absolute genius.
Actually, ordinary people like us here, and I include myself in this —we are pretty
normal, ordinary people; we just get a lot of fun in what we do in our work —are never
going to invent the computer. We are not made like that. We do a lot of talking, we do a
lot listening, and we do all the social stuff, but we are never going to be able to do that.
We need people who are absolutely, completely different from us, who are going t o go
out and think completely differently from the way that we do, and who are going to see
27 May 2015 Budget Debate 4059
things that none of the rest of us would ever be able to see. Sometimes we get to see
their work. That movie, I would say, is an extremely good example for anyone t o see
the behaviours of somebody with the disorder.
Back in the 1940s this was not known as a disorder. He was just really good at
maths. Well, actually, lots of people with autistic spectrum disorder are really good at
maths, because maths is, unlike us —unlike us —completely logical. Also, I always
reckon that maths is a bit magical, really. You can do almost anything with maths. So
sometimes—[Interruption] Yes, you can —absolutely, Mr Assistant Speaker Mallard.
You can do almost anything with maths. It is unbelievably magical, and the more that
we learn about it, the more I find it most interesting. But, do you know what? Instead of
trying to make kids who have different abilities be just like the rest of us, let us
celebrate the fact that they are differen t, because without their differences, we would
still be back in the Stone Age.
Think about Isaac Newton. If you learn anything about Isaac Newton, he was clearly
someone with autistic spectrum disorder. This was a man who lived most of his life in
the Tow er of London —not under guard —but the more I hear about him, the more I
realise that he was absolutely like that. Einstein —clearly. People say that about Bill
Gates—clearly—and Steve Jobs. These are people who often have difficulty talking to
people in the normal social situations that the rest of us thrive in. They do not do
cocktail parties; they actually make a difference. They do not do chatting about nothing;
they actually make a difference. So when I look at this area, I would say to all the
parents who think that it is not money well spent and to all of those teachers who think
“Why do I have to have someone different in my class?”, that thankfully, we do have
people who are different. I hope that now we are getting ourselves intelligent enough —
if I co uld possibly put it in that way —and accepting enough to understand that not all
kids are, thankfully, made the same. If we would only appreciate that, we would get
more from it.
This is the first time that I have seen in one of our Budgets a commitment of  this
order. If I or our committee has done anything to help bring that along, I am very
grateful for it. If we have not, never mind; we will no doubt try better next time. But I
would say that our committee is working very well on this issue and it is a p rivilege to
be part of a team —a cross -party team —that takes this issue seriously. It is an issue
because it behoves us to make the best use we can out of everybody in our society, and
some people are different from most of us. Thank goodness they are; I am  very grateful
for it.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Richard Prosser —a 5 -
minute call.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: Another year has passed and the Minister of
Finance has delivered yet another Budget —another bland helping of not very much.
This Budget will not go down in history as one of the great Budgets. It will not be
remembered in the same way as the Black Budget  or the “mother of all Budgets” are
remembered. In fact, if the Budget is to be remembered for anything, if it is remembered
at all, it will not be for what is in it but for what is not in it. It may go down in the
history books as the “great, dull, beige Budget of 2015”.
In terms of what is not in it, as far as the forestry sector is concerned, there really is
not much at all. Through the last term of Parliament I had a flat down on Thorndon
Quay for when the House was in session. It was just over the roa d from the stadium and
it overlooked the log-loading docks. Every morning on my balcony, over the oatmeal, I
was confronted by the horrible sight of piles and piles of logs —North Island radiata
pine—piling up, ready and waiting for the ships to take them a way to China and Korea,
and other faraway places, where they would be turned into things. Going out with those
4060 Budget Debate 27 May 2015
shipments were shiploads of New Zealand’s forestry and sawmill jobs, and shiploads of
the potential for value-added timber products coming out of New Zealand and adding to
the economy. I am not there anymore. I have moved out to the finance Minister’s home
town of Karori, so I do not get that sight in my face every morning, but that does not
mean the problem has gone away. As far as what this Budge t does not contain for the
forestry sector, it is not going away any time soon.
So the lack of any real commitment to forestry is one of the more disappointing
aspects of this Budget. Expenditure on the management of Crown forestry assets is
expected to fall by about $5 million on the actual, versus the budgeted, expenditure for
2014-15, and the appropriation for 2015 -16 is down by another $15 million on that. At
the same time the value of stumpage per cubic metre is budgeted to fall by about 15
percent over the next year. Indeed, the market report from the May 2015 edition of the
New Zealand Tree Grower magazine, which is the official journal of the New Zealand
Farm Forestry Association, warns that the value of a cubic metre of softwood landed in
China has fallen from US$130 for a JAS, which is an Japanese Agricultural Standard
cubic metre, in October last year to about US$100 in April, and it is forecast to fall to
US$90 or below by the end of this month.
The future for the New Zealand forestry sector and  exports from it is not in the form
of logs. At present there are around 5 million cubic metres of log infantry sitting on the
Chinese wharves, and China has, effectively, stopped buying. Consequently, there are
about a million cubic metres of radiata sitt ing on the docks in New Zealand that,
effectively, have no buyer —there is no market for them. New Zealand has been
supplying around 60 percent to 65 percent of the softwood log imports into China, with
the rest being made up by exports from the United Stat es, Canada, and a few from
Russia. I ask what this Government is doing in this Budget to address this problem and
what incentives and what assistance it is offering the forestry sector and the wood -
processing sector. The answer is between “nothing” and “very little”.
There is the Primary Growth Partnership, of course, and there is a scheme within that
programme that is developing the steep land harvester. That is a great thing, and we are
all in favour of the Primary Growth Partnership. It is a grand schem e, a marvellous
initiative, and New Zealand First fully supports it. We do have one beef and that is that
there is no provision for the retention of rights to a share in the intellectual property that
is generated by the Primary Growth Partnership projects. That intellectual property goes
to a private partner, and all too often that private partner is a foreign partner. But in
other regards the Primary Growth Partnership is pure socialism, and we have every
support for it. It is quite surprising it is being  promoted by a National Government and
