that Labour does not seem to like it, but that is one of the vagaries of politics, I suppose.
My point with the steep land harvester is that although it is going to be a very good
thing, what is the point in it if we  have not got a market for the trees it is going to
harvest and the wood products that can be made out of them, and, more to the point, if
we do not have the capacity to produce those wood products? The magazine New
Zealand Tree Grower  tell us that about 7 0 percent of the logs that China imports are
used for making construction plywood. So the question that comes from that is: why are
they buying logs? Well, they are not building log cabins. If they were building log
cabins you could understand the fact that we are selling them logs. In fact, they are after
plywood, so why are we not selling them plywood? What is it that is in the Budget to
incentivise and to assist the forestry sector and the sawmill sector?

items.speaker: Brett Hudson
items.text: Has the member consi dered that maybe the customers want to buy
logs?
27 May 2015 Budget Debate 4061

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: Well, they do not want the logs for the logs. They want the
logs for the things they can make out of them. The whole point of an intelligent
economic programme is that you sell the product that is worth the most.

items.speaker: Brett Hudson
items.text: They’ll buy the logs from the people—

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: Listen and you may learn. The incentives are not there and
this Government—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Sorry to interrupt the honourable
member. His time has expired. I call Barbara Stewart—5 minutes.

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: In New Ze aland First we have made our
position on the 2015 Budget very clear: we see red, we see red, we see red. But it is not
just the books that are in the red. Basically, the vision of the Government is in the red. It
is not forward-looking in any way.
Basically, the Budget has been a missed opportunity to invest in long -term solutions
and prevention. We need to reduce further demands on our health care system down the
road. We know that New Zealand is on the verge of a great population shift, and that
will mean a change in the demands on our health care system. We know that the over -
65 population is set to double to 1.2 million people over 20 years. Unless this
Government shows that it has a plan for trying to manage this, the whole situation is
going to become totally unmanageable.
Our over -65s deserve to be cared for with dignity, and they need appropriate
conditions in which to live out their lives with some sort of dignity and pride. Without
some sort of action in aged care this sector will become unsustain able. Without
investment there will be staffing shortages. We know that the aged -care workforce is
struggling to try to recruit and retain quality staff, because the work is just too hard, too
heavy, for the miserable pay that they receive.
In Budget 2015  there is absolutely nothing for the aged -care workers. Aged -care
workers will be seeing red, but it is not only them, because every other New Zealander
who is looking ahead to their years aged 65 -plus—people in their 40s and 50s —should
be seeing red as well. What is going to be there for them? And all of this because of the
Government’s inaction today.
The coming crisis will not be just in the aged -care sector; it will also be in the
demand for surgery. Although we appreciate that extra money was made ava ilable for
surgery, the demand is not going to be met by that extra money. There will be longer
waiting lists, and we know that the nurses and doctors are in panic mode because, of
course, there was nothing in the Budget to ensure that more nurses and doct ors are
recruited and retained as well. So we have higher demands on the waiting list and a
shortfall in what can be offered.
Health professionals tell us that the sector is absolutely devastated. It is underfunded,
and they are the ones who see the resul t of underspending. So, of course, they are also
seeing red, seeing red. And, of course, we just have to look to the Southern District
Health Board—it has a deficit of $17.8 million. The funding for Ōāmaru Hospital has
been cut by 5 percent for next year. Dunstan Hospital in Central Otago is set for a $1
million shortfall in funding, with predictions of closed hospital wards, a lack of staff,
and service reductions. So all of those locals are going to face a long trip to
Christchurch to get what they need.
We once ran a health system that was world leading. Today it has been weakened
beyond compare, and everyone is just seeing red. It does not need to be this way. The
answer is simple: invest some money now to save some lives, with further money
further along the road. The extent of missed opportunity within this Budget to do that is
evidenced by the bowel cancer screening programme. We know that bowel cancer is a
terrible disease that kills 1,200 New Zealanders per annum, and, of course, there is
4062 Budget Debate 27 May 2015
nothing in the Budget for this screening programme. We saw an extension of the very
successful Waitematā bowel cancer screening programme, but there was nothing for the
rest of New Zealand. Is this an example of what we are to see —health by postcode? We
really hope not, and we are seeing red over that. Thank you.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: Talofa lava. O manu o le lauamanu e felelei mamao. I
think that the second bit I said was “Birds that fly together go far”, in view of the fact
that this is Samoan Language Week. It is a reflection of the National caucus and how
fantastically we are doing . We actually flock together, we will go very far, and, after
that Budget, we are guaranteed to go very far.
I have to react to the contributions of the members opposite. My dear friend Barbara
Stewart actually tried to quote her leader by saying: “I see red, I see red, I see red.”
Apparently, that is what he said. Darling, you have to have a better memory. He actually
said: “I can see red.”, and I thought he was talking about the fact that he was not colour -
blind, or that he could actually see, rather than about the Budget. He did not actually say
“I see red, I see red, I see red”, as in the lyric. He was trying to connect to the Split Enz
lyric, and he was trying to make fun of the Budget with some sort of rhetoric.
I also have to react to my dear friend Richard Prosser. Sir, you are a great mate, but
with the speed at which you speak, I sometimes lose it. You are like a bullet —so fast. I
am hoping that you actually said “shipload”, rather than something else—I hope.
I remember that people always say that  the grass is greener on the other side, and for
many New Zealanders, for a very long time, Australia was, in fact, the greener pasture. I
will quote from an article: “ The sun seems to shine a bit brighter there,  the pay packets
are a bit fatter, and they have koalas. But times are changing. The decline in long -term
migration figures to Australia is just one example. And the reason is simple: Australia
may have cuddly koalas, but New Zealand has John Key. ” That, apparently, is in
relation to how fantastic our Prime Minister is and how well this Government is doing.
It is about radical incrementalism, which somebody mentioned to me. When people
get sick, do you know how you feed them medicine? We are saying that we are not
trying to force-feed them medicine;  we are convincing them that they are sick and that
they want a certain kind of medicine. This Government is doing exactly that. We are
giving people information about what this country needs and we are showing them the
pathway that we want them to take fo r a better life. Having economic growth is actually
a good thing, and this Budget demonstrates National’s clear commitment to economic
growth and dedication to helping hard -working New Zealanders and their families to
grow. New Zealand is a small economy i n global terms. Our population is a lot smaller
than that of many countries, but our economic performance in recent years has been
very, very strong, and it is ahead of many nations that we could talk about.
Earlier, a member opposite talked about his com munity having been poor for a very
long time. It sort of struck me that the member has been a Labour MP for a very long
time. Before the National Government become the Government in 2008, there was, in
fact, a Labour Government for 9 years, and yet that co mmunity was poor then and it is
still poor now.
You know, sometimes it is about people. This Government is taking action where the
Labour Government did not take action. This Government is increasing benefits and
spending $790 million over the next 4 year s to help children living in some of New
Zealand’s poorest families to be slightly better off. We are not the richest  of nations and
as a nation we cannot actually afford more than that, and we are saying that we are
giving families a helping hand. This is  the first time that a benefit has been raised, in
real terms, in 43 years. The previous Labour Government never actually did that. We
are building a more competitive and productive economy through a number of critical
initiatives.
27 May 2015 Budget Debate 4063
I want to talk a little bit about the way that this National Government has contributed
to education. I know that my learned colleague the Hon Judith Collins talked about the
special education sector, which our Education and Science Committee had a discussion
about. I have to ag ree with Ms Collins that we have a very friendly select committee,
where we actually work together very well indeed. Our discussions on dyslexia,
dyspraxia, and Asperger’s syndrome were really interesting for me because I did not
even know what dyspraxia w as. I knew what dyslexia was, but dyspraxia was
something that was a bit new to me. Apparently, it is about ordering things. For
example—this example is for fun —Superman wears his underwear over his tights. You
could call him dyspraxic because he obviously does not put them on in the right order—
underpants should be underneath the tights, I would have thought. I know I am cracking
jokes about something serious and I should not, but it is a disorder. It is an ability to
learn in a different way.
Our teachers should be better equipped to help children who have disorders in order
to help them learn better, and so that they can cope in our education facilities, like the
new, modern learning environments, which are actually way, way better than they used
to be. When I was child in Korea, there would be 65 children in one class. There would
be two children to each table, in a row, and if you moved, the teacher would throw a
chalk at you, whereas the new, modern learning environment is quite a different thing.
A child who has attention deficit disorder cannot sit in a classroom for 50 or 60 minutes
and they need to move around, but in a modern learning environment the teacher can
cope with teaching the kids who do not have these issues and they can also pay attention
to those who do, in fact, have those issues.
Education is particularly important in many ethnic communities. I know, for
example, that many in the Korean community basically move to a country like New
Zealand because they want a better opportunity for t heir children. What that means is
that when they uproot their family to come to a country like New Zealand, they do not
have the family connections or the social support networks or, potentially, even a job.
Often because they do not have a job, they are e ven poorer than when they were in their
home countries, but they do this because they want a better opportunity for their
children, and education is something that is paramount in their minds.
I am very proud that Budget 2015 invests an extra $686.7 milli on over the next 4
years in education, bringing our total investment in education to $10.8 billion next
year—$10.8 billion, not million. This is a clear indication that reflects National’s
determination and commitment to helping all young New Zealanders fr om all different
ethnic backgrounds to achieve their brightest and fullest potential. That is what we are
focused on when we talk about helping the families who are the poorest and beneficiary
families with children by giving them extra money.
But we also have a commitment for them to be available for jobs, so that instead of
living in a benefit -dependent home, the parents are, in fact, working. Hopefully, it
would be part -time while the children are a lot younger. Personally speaking, I went
back to work when my child was only 5 weeks old and that was because it was my
choice. I had the opportunity to work. If I did not work, my staff could not possibly be
paid. I had more than a dozen staff members whom I had to pay wages to, so I went
back to work when m y son was 5 weeks old. But I was lucky to work in an
environment—the television industry —where people were very forgiving of mothers
who were working and who had children around.
Budget 2015 delivered for New Zealand. I think that Labour and the other
Opposition parties are just sore because they did not think of it first.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labour—West Coast - Tasman): That speech from
Melissa Lee epitomised the attit ude of the National Government to this country and its
4064 Budget Debate 27 May 2015
management of it. Those members think: “Because I did it, everyone else should be able
to do it, too.”, and they overlook the reality for many New Zealanders that many are
born into certain circumstances and are in circumstances beyond their control.
This was a Budget of broken promises and lost opportunities. We have to name the
broken promises because this Government has been given the privilege of being trusted
by the majority of the people of New Z ealand for three elections, and time after time it
has broken the promises. Those people who have enough time to stop and think are
starting to realise that you cannot carry on breaking promises and being trusted by the
people.

items.speaker: John Key said
items.text: “We will be in surplus.” He said: “There will be no new taxes.” He
said: “The $1,000 for KiwiSaver will remain as it is now.” This is quoting word for
word from the Prime Minister. It is an absolute insult to then turn round in a Budget and
to slap on new taxes, to no t get back into surplus for some pathetic reason the
Government members have put up —mainly that they have reduced taxes drastically at
the top end of town —and to then take from young Kiwis the $1,000 incentive. Those
members know full well about financial incentives because, do you know what they
did? They left in the Budget the incentives for their corporate mates. They left the
incentives there through the Primary Growth Partnership to ensure that they would
commit to research and development and to devel oping their businesses, but they were
not prepared to do it for the young New Zealanders who wanted to take up KiwiSaver.
There are two particular areas of my portfolio interest: one is mining, and the other is
dairying. In fact, this Government came into  power saying that those two industries
would take us into a new world. “Mine the national parks and we will all be wealthy.”,
those members said, and they quickly realised that that was a pretty dumb move to
make, not only because New Zealanders want to p rotect their national parks but, in fact,
because if they had looked through the history of mining and looked at what is
happening on the West Coast today, they would have seen that it is a very cyclical
industry. In my region, where I am a staunch advocate for that industry, for us to rely on
that for our future is both naive and stupid —ask the Australians. Mining does have a
future, but we cannot base our economy on that alone.
Dairying, on the other hand, has a more sustainable future, and I have been a
passionate advocate of that as well. But in the absence of an economic plan from the
National Government all of those industries are under threat, and the lost opportunity in
this Budget was to give any indication of where this country is heading. There w as no
indication at all and no idea of where we should be in the future. That was the lost
opportunity. Can I go back to dairying. The reality is that the industry faces not just one
but two or possibly three seasons of low payout, and that leaves our coun try stumbling,
to put it politely, because the National Government has no idea of what else we should
be doing. Even within the primary sector, I ask the Government: “Where is your help
for strategic planning for the meat industry? Where is your help for strategic planning in
the wool sector, or forestry, or indeed fishing?”.
It has taken a hands -off approach —well, not quite. It has got the Primary Growth
Partnership funding, which is corporate welfare —welfare. What those members have
done is committed $300 million of taxpayers’ money and paid it over to their mates —to
their mates —to carry on, for the most part, business as usual for something that the
Office of the Auditor -General could not identify. It could not identify additionality. It
could not identi fy in the six programmes it studied any real additional benefit for the
New Zealand economy, because the National Government just likes paying out to its
mates.
The dairy industry was one of the recipients of that money. The industry is in a bit of
a dilemma at the moment. It does not know whether to keep the cost of production high
27 May 2015 Budget Debate 4065
and hope for a rise in payout, or to wind back production and try to remain sustainable
and viable into the future. The reason is that the dairy industry —our No. 1 industry —
has no strategic plan and no strategic vision.
The big company, the one we still own, is Fonterra —the one that John Key would
like to see floated on the stock market. I am sure that his mate Mark Weldon, when he
tries to slide his way into Parliament, will s it alongside the Prime Minister and ensure
that Fonterra sits on the stock market so that the traders and all the mates over there can
clip the ticket and sell it off—sell it off to foreigners. Take a previous example: the Hon
Ruth Richardson runs around t he country now. She sold off Synlait. She has been a
director on that company for a long time. Now it is completely in the hands of
foreigners.

items.speaker: Hon Jo Goodhew
items.text: All her own work.
Hon DAMIEN O ’CONNOR: Oh, and the member over there says that that is OK.
Read Statistics New Zealand’s report about the growing deficit, the increasing deficit,
because of the leakage from having foreign ownership in our economy. That is a
strategic issue: who should own New Zealand and who shou ld own New Zealand’s
future? Fonterra, our No. 1 company, must be kept in New Zealand hands, but this
Government and the Prime Minister would love to see it sold off.
Can I go back to the primary sector as a whole. We need a primary sector council, a
high-level body that will look at each and every sector and work with them to develop a
strategic plan for the future. The Riddet Institute identified this need years ago. The
National Government continues to ignore the reality that we need strategic planning and
we need leadership to know where we are heading across all the primary sectors. We
need leaders—not just people appointed to bodies, but people who are prepared to show
leadership in the sector. It is not occurring and we are going round in circles wit h our
fingers crossed in the hope that commodity prices will lift.
We need structures that can deliver on those strategic plans. Labour offers an
alternative approach in the primary sector area, one where leadership will be delivered,
where necessary, and  where support will be delivered for those strategic plans and
visions. This Budget ignored that reality and missed the opportunity to show leadership.
I am going to talk about, not a rock star economy, but what is a rock -bottom
economy for too many New Zealanders —not the 250,000 children in poverty, but the
people who run around and care for our elderly in the country. If you are a doctor or a
nurse and you care, you get a reasonable salary. But if you are a support worker in this
country, you get paid $14.75 an hour to go around and look after the parents of the likes
of you, Mr Assistant Speaker, and me, who are living in rural areas. It is an insulting
wage to care for our elderly, which is a measure, in my view, of the failure of the
National Government to do what is right.
Those people who are getting $14.75 an hour get a massive $1.08 per hour for their
travel. I have met one of these support worker s. She is a wonderful woman, who travels
between 600 and 800 kilometres every fortnight, and she gets the grand total of $1.08
times 32 hours. That is the insulting payment she gets for travel.
Up and down this country in rural New Zealand, we have people being paid a
pittance to care for people who, without that care, would be absolutely destitute and
would be incapable of cooking and caring for themselves, and that is the environment
that every one of those MPs over there is overseeing and endorsing. It is an outrage that
must be addressed.
The Government’s policy of caring for people in their homes seems wonderful until
you start to pick it apart. The Minister for the Community and Voluntary S ector, Jo
Goodhew, should be right at the forefront of addressing that issue, which insults those
people and insults the elderly people in our country—
4066 Budget Debate 27 May 2015

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I am sor ry—[Interruption] Order!
The member’s time has expired.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: It is with an enormous degree of
pride and pleasure that I rise in this Budget debate to speak  in support of Bill English’s
seventh Budget. And what a great Budget it is, not just for this John Key - National-led
Government but also for New Zealand and all New Zealanders. It is part of a plan that is
working. It is part of a plan that has been in p lace for 7 years  now—7 years of careful,
prudent, fiscal management—that has enabled Bill English and the National Party team
to negotiate their way, on behalf of all New Zealanders, through some of the most
difficult economic times that our country has se en. It is a Budget that has allowed us as
a Government, now that some light is emerging at the end of the tunnel, to address some
of the real hardship and need that exists in our community.
Before I get into the meat of my presentation to you  today, I jus t want to make
comment on the contribution made earlier this afternoon by my colleague the Hon
Maggie Barry, Minister of Conservation. I was delighted, as the member for
Coromandel, to note that the Budget includes a further spending allowance of $11.2
million to protect further the future of our native bird, the kiwi. People who are familiar
with the Coromandel will know that the Coromandel produces fine kiwi. It is a natural
breeding area, and an awful lot of terrific kiwi preservation work is being done by
worthy organisations such as Moehau Environment Group. I commend to this House the
work that this group and many others do. I was delighted to see this extra spending,
because kiwi are, of course, known around the world as our national symbol and they
are under threat. This is a Government that wants to make sure that that threat is
diminished and that further protection for our kiwi is made available. I am particularly
enthused by the Kōhanga Kiwi project, where kiwi will now be able to be farmed,
essentially. Their longevity and future prosperity as a species will be preserved and
secured.
What I particularly want to talk about, in terms of my Budget contribution today, is
how proud I was when the Prime Minister stood up on election night last year and,  after
acknowledging the comprehensive National Party victory that we were able to secure,
said: “This National -led Government will govern for all people, for all New
Zealanders.” Here in this seventh Budget of Bill English, is the evidence of that
occurring. Yesterday afternoon I listened very closely to my colleague the Hon Paula
Bennett giving her Budget speech. She also spoke of her pride, now being an Associate
Minister of Finance, in the work and preparation that she and the finance team did in the
lead-up to Budget 2015. She reminded us that Bill English and his team have been
working away steadily on this Budget for probably the best part of 12 months. In fact, I
understand that work on Budget 2016 has already commenced.
It is easy to forget that our s is an economy with 2.8 percent economic growth and
that we are projecting a further 150,000 jobs being created. It is easy to remember that
when National first started talking a couple of years ago about creating 170,000 jobs,
members of the Opposition a nd on the left were derisory in their comments about our
ambition and aspiration to create that number of jobs. It would be fair to say that they
took every opportunity to criticise, to discount, and to reject that as any kind of realistic
prospect. Well, here we are now in Budget 2015 saying that no, we did not actually
create 170,000 new jobs. Actually, the economy has produced 194,000 new jobs. Since
2011, 194,000 new jobs have been created in this economy under Bill English’s prudent
and careful management. That is important because it makes an absolutely fundamental
difference to the quality of life and the future prospects of New Zealanders.
Seeing the average wage increase year on year on year is another sign of how strong
our economy is and of what t he tangible, material benefits are for hard -working New
27 May 2015 Budget Debate 4067
Zealanders. That people have more money available in their pockets and are able to get
jobs is a sign of a healthy, growing economy. Seeing us project that unemployment will
continue to drop and that employment will continue to rise is another sign of good
things to come. From the projections, it is easy to see that Budget 2015 indicates well
and truly that we are headed in the right direction. We are projecting a 4.5 percent
unemployment rate, which i s still too high, but it is better than those of almost all
comparable nations around the world.
What we can see is that over the last 6½ years, we have moved resources of the State
to those who fundamentally need them the most. Watching the faces of Oppos ition
members while Bill English was reading his Budget —I was sitting on the cross benches
at the back, as I do as a hard -working backbencher —it was obvious that the blood
literally drained from Grant Robertson’s face. National is unashamed in its approach  of
wanting to target benefits and increases for those who are facing the most difficulties
and who are in the most hardship in our society. Actually, we have done that over a
number of years, as Paula Bennett pointed out in her speech yesterday, by resett ing the
compass, if you like, of welfarism in New Zealand. I remember well when this
Government first came to power in 2008. Paula Bennett was the Minister for Social
Development and Employment. She said in her speech yesterday that she has never
forgotten, as the new Minister for Social Development and Employment, visiting Paris
with a number of social development - type Ministers from around the world and telling
them that we had a social welfare system where there were absolutely no obligations
placed on a person receiving State -funded welfare until their youngest child turned 18.
She said that in other countries, it was unimaginable that a social welfare system could
operate like that, where it was simply a matter of having another child when the
youngest child turned 18 in order to get another 18 years of unquestioned access to State
welfare.
Well, we have fundamentally changed that expectation and the balance of what is
expected of people. Social welfare is part of a social contract. The social contract  is
such that it means that there is support —the benefit of support from the State and other
taxpayers—available to people when they need it most. All of us agree that that is a fine
and wonderful baseline for our social welfare system. But the quid pro qu o is that the
people who are receiving State welfare should not see it as a lifestyle or a permanent
choice; actually, they should be available for work  when they can. Part of the change
that has occurred in the period of time that we have been in Governme nt is that we have
reset this balance. We have made sure that those people have hope and opportunities.
Under the last Labour —Green Government, they did not have hope or opportunities.
We have reset the balance that was lost from our welfare system for so long. Now
people who are receiving welfare can see some bright hope on the horizon and that their
life is not destined to be one of perpetual, unlimited, relentless welfare dependency into
the future. I say that that has got to be a very good thing.
What people sometimes forget is that we could not have made that reset change if it
had not been for the careful, prudent stewardship of the Government’s and the nation’s
financial accounts that Bill English and his team have been able to provide on our
behalf o ver the last 7 years. We could not have done that and reset the welfare
expectation balance if the underlying books had not been sound. I think Paula Bennett
can take huge personal credit for the achievements of the Government in that area and
for the brighter future that so many New Zealanders now have. This is a good Budget. It
is a prudent, careful Budget. It is a Budget that shows that this Government has a great
understanding of what is needed in times of hardship, and it also has a glimmer of hope
for the future for all. I commend it to the House.
4068 Budget Debate 27 May 2015

items.speaker: JAMES SHAW
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker. Budget 2015 contains a
number of “weak tea, might work a little” proposals that the Green Party has been
promoting for years. We were pleased to see that the Greens’ call for additional funding
for things like telecommunications, infrastructure, and biosecurity  are finally being
heeded. [ Interruption] Be careful what you wish for, Brett. Yet this Budget also
demonstrates a remarkable lack of vision on behalf of the Government. Rather than
making a concerted effort towards transitioning to a smart Green economy, the
Government is offering New Zealanders a couple of feel -good policies mixed in with a
myriad of one s that are failing. The end result of this will be the creation of a lost
generation, stuck with an ailing economy and wedded to mid -20th century ideas. We
reject this future. The Green Party is committed to building a smart Green economy that
works for all New Zealanders.
The Budget is not without its merits. From the point of view of economic
development, there are a number of policy initiatives that do align with our call to  move
towards a smart Green economy. A green economy involves more extensive and
intensive use of digital technology and communications. This enables a more
distributed, emergent business -model than the highly centralised, dominant models of
doing business  that we are familiar with today. It enables distributed digital
manufacturing, greater access to better education in our most remote towns and
provincial centres, and weightless exports as a much greater proportion of the overall
economy. In turn, that me ans a much more resilient economy than the highly fragile,
risk-loaded economy that we have today. It means greater distribution of wealth to the
regions and to our small towns and provincial centres. To that end, the Greens support
fully the Government’s move to extend the telecommunications development levy so as
to provide extra funding for the Rural Broadband Initiative. Access to fast, reliable
broadband is an essential and central piece of our economic infrastructure, and it is good
to see the Government taking action on this.
Similarly, we are happy that the Budget provides a $24.9 million boost in funding for
biosecurity in order to make up for the cuts that National made at the beginning of its
tenure. The future of our tourism industry relies on th e protection of our unique flora
and fauna. Biosecurity staff play an essential role in this, and it is good to see the
importance of their work finally being recognised by this Government. However, these
are isolated successes. There does not seem to be a ny overarching strategy to transition
New Zealand to a green economy. In fact, some of the initiatives that are supposed to
protect the environment are doing the exact opposite. In Chris Bishop’s maiden speech,
when he summed up the National Government’s approach to policy making, he invoked
the perennial free-market hero Milton Friedman.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Ha, ha!

items.speaker: JAMES SHAW
items.text: And although you might laugh, Friedman said: “One of the great
mistakes is to judge policies and programs by their intentions rather than their results.”
This is a laudable notion. So let us look at some of what National says its programmes
are intended to do, and then let us take a look at what they actually do.
Although the supposed purpose of the New Zealand emissio ns trading scheme is to
reduce emissions, it is actually doing the precise opposite. The Budget has revealed that
in the 2014 -15 year, the Government handed out almost $114 million worth of free
carbon credits to industries that cause climate change but re ceived only $83 million
through the emissions trading scheme.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Corporate welfare.

items.speaker: JAMES SHAW
items.text: Taxpayers picked up the $31 million difference —and that is
corporate welfare. The consequence is that our emissions have grown b y 13 percent
since the National Government was first elected in 2008. If we are going to judge the
27 May 2015 Budget Debate 4069
emissions trading scheme by its results, as Mr Bishop suggests we do, then it is clear
that the policy is an abject failure. The emissions trading scheme ill ustrates a broader
problem with the Government’s strategy —or lack thereof. Instead of taking decisive
steps towards the creation of a smart Green economy, the Government focuses on
empty gestures and policies that sound positive but that have no impact. Th e effect is
the creation of a lost generation of New Zealanders who will be left with an economy
that is woefully inefficient and that has a heavy carbon footprint. Is that the legacy that
we want to leave the next generation? This is unacceptable.
We need a smart Green economy that works for all New Zealanders, and it is clear
that this Government is not delivering that. The Green Party is proposing meaningful
initiatives to facilitate this transition. Decisive action is needed in order to mitigate
climate change and leave future generations with high levels of natural capital. Instead
of wasting taxpayers’ money on an emissions trading scheme that subsidises polluters,
we need to introduce a proper price on carbon emissions. Pricing carbon properly would
act as a simple but effective incentive to move away from polluting technologies and
industries towards cleaner production and forms of energy. In turn, personal and
company tax rates could be reduced. Under our proposal, polluters would actually bear
the cost of their actions, whilst green businesses and ordinary New Zealand households
would benefit, and that seems fair, reasonable, and equitable to us.
In order to support businesses with the transition from a carbon-intensive economy to
one that is green, we should also set up a green investment fund. The aim of this
Government-owned, for-profit bank would be to provide funds to support green private
investment in the areas of renewable energy and clean technology. Fossil fuel subsidies
would be stopped, raising the overall tax take from oil companies from 46 percent to the
global average of around 70 percent, which would give us more than enough to cover
the $120 million for the first 3 years of the funds’ operation. In time, the bank will see
billions of d ollars going in to things such as renewable energy plants, the development
and production of biofuels, and clean technology products. Investing in a smart Green
economy is essential not only for the environment but also for the future of our
economy.
Alongside these funds for investment, we also need to see greater commitment to
research and development, and the innovation that results. The Greens would allocate an
additional $1 billion over 3 years to research and development, while also collaborating
directly with the private sector by providing tax credits and grants in relation to research
and development. These would provide us with the technology and ideas to drive the
transition to a smart Green economy. These are innovative but sensible policy soluti ons
that are being proposed only by the Green Party. This Government has adopted a “weak
tea, might work a little” version of policies that we have been promoting for years and
years. So, clearly, the Greens have won the policy argument. National has done it
because it has had to, not because it has wanted to. If voters want the real thing, if they
want policies that achieve results rather than just good intentions, then they should
make sure to vote for us at the next election. The Greens are offering long -term
solutions to a sustainable future economy for all New Zealanders, and for that and for
all those reasons, we oppose this Budget.

items.speaker: KELVIN DAVIS
items.text: It gives me great pleasure to resume
my speech on the Organised Crime and Anti -Corruption Legislation Bill. There are two
parts of this bill that I would like to touch on. One is around human trafficking and the
other is around wh at are known as “facilitation payments”. There are two members of

We just need to look at the  news in the last day or so to see the effects of human

they have been murdered, and they have been left buried in the jungle in Malaysia. That
in no way compares to sheep rustling. I am sorry for all the farmers whose sheep do get
stolen—that is unfortunate —but there is no way on earth that we can compare sheep

I do have to say that the picture I just painted around the human trafficking in

makes it a crime to traffick people within a country, not jus t crossing over borders. It is
about the exploitation of people who, for various reasons such as slavery, sexual

The second National MP who should be feeling a little sheepish with himself is none

items.text: Kia ora e te Mana Whakawā. I take this split call on
the Organised Crime and Anti -corruption Legislation Bill. If I could relate a little bit

It was interesting, even when t raveling south. There are interesting stories that I

items.text: Kia ora e te Mana Whakawā. Again, it is a privilege to li ve in

issue. New Zealand is a member of the Financial Action Task Force, which sets

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Following on from that great

look at the bill with regard to money -laundering and international wire transfers and

In my community we have a very big  population from the Middle East,
predominantly a Somali population. A lot of the people who have come from Somalia to
the Hamilton community over the years have been refugees. As refugees, they have

Somali family may well have cousins back in Somalia whom they wish to assist in some

that, and also many previous generations in this House would have done that as well.
The problem that members of the Somali commun ity have got is that there is no
registered bank in Somalia and no ability for them to transfer their money.
The modern money -laundering rules are very strict and very much follow an
international format, and they have been through the Finance and Expendit ure
Committee over the last couple of years. Under those rules, there is not a lot of room for
movement. We need to be very cognisant of those communities when we progress
legislation like this, because—

items.speaker: Phil Twyford

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT

items.text: Mrs Annette King said that it was too much, before the speech
had even started. That was a shame. Before I left the House at dinner time, I was talking
27 May 2015 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 4073
about my Somali community in Hamilton, which is a fine community of people and has

HEALTH (PROTECTION) AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I move, That the Health
(Protection) Amendment Bill be now read a second time . I would like to thank the
Health Committee for its work on this bill. The committee received 71 submissions and
heard 22 oral submissions.
Of course, good health is hugely important to New Zealanders. I think when you
look at it, it would be the No. 1 priority for people across the nation. That is why  I am
very pleased that this bill supports the Government’s unwavering commitment to good
public health, as reflected in the recent Budget whereby health received over $400
million of new funding. Of course, there were a number of excellent new initiatives
there that are supporting working families in New Zealand in terms of their health. But
it was a health Budget for all New Zealanders.
Anyway, this particular bill will amend the Health Act 1956. Back in October 2013
the Government decided to improve the range of measures in the Health Act in two
specific areas: measures to protect the public from the risk of the spread of some
infectious diseases and, in the case of people under 18 years of age, measures to protect
them from the harm associated with artif icial UV tanning. The bill will protect people
from these preventable harms, and it will do so through measures that are proportionate
to the risks that are faced.
Unfortunately, New Zealand has very high levels of sexually transmitted diseases.
This impacts heavily on individuals, families, relationships, and communities. Sexually
transmitted infections have a variety of complications including chronic pain, infertility,
neonatal morbidity, and genital -tract cancer. The bill adds new provisions for the
surveillance and management of infectious diseases. These measures will improve the
availability of information on certain conditions, provide for more effective
management of behaviours that put others at risk of infection, and strengthen legislative
provisions for contact tracing. The bill strengthens the principles applying to medical
officers of health and the courts in exercising disease management powers. People
exercising powers will be required to take into account any known special
4074 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 27 May 2015
circumstances or vu lnerabilities of the individual. These might be due to youth,
disability, incapacity, or other circumstances.
The bill also requires that measures are proportionate to the public health risk that
they pose. The principles also encourage individuals to take  responsibility for their own
health. Currently, sexually transmitted infectious diseases, with the exception of AIDS,
are not notifiable by medical practitioners and laboratories in New Zealand. The bill
makes HIV, gonorrhoea, and syphilis notifiable on a  non-identified basis, along with
AIDS. The notifying information needs to be sufficient to enable different kinds of
public health interventions while complying with privacy safeguards. Submitters said
that clause 5 and clause 6 went too far in restrictin g effective monitoring of serious
sexually transmitted infections in favour of privacy. This is because the list of
identifying information that should not be disclosed with disease notifications included
sex, date of birth, and National Health Index numbe r. The reported -back bill requires
notification of these matters, while protecting the individual’s identity from being
disclosed in the first instance.
Submitters were also concerned about potentially coercive actions by officers, such
as contacting a you ng person’s employer or school and asking for details about friends
and associates. Reluctance to disclose information or to be diagnosed or treated could
arise from fear of the consequences as a result. However, that information may be
absolutely vital in  identifying those who may be at risk, and to prevent the further
spread of disease. The bill says that information requested and provided under new Part
3A will not be used or disclosed for any purpose other than the management of
infectious diseases. Con tact tracing is a valuable public health tool in preventing and
managing infectious disease outbreaks, particularly diseases with a rapid onset such as
meningococcal disease and gonorrhoea. New Subpart 5 extends contact tracing powers
to contacts of people suspected of having an infectious disease, and that is an important
change. That will allow for speedy follow-up, diagnosis, treatment, and containment.
It is important that contact tracers are trained, and are suitably qualified health or
community work practitioners, and the bill has been changed to require that. It clarifies
the interface between appointed formal contact tracers and informal contact tracers. The
latter might be general practitioners, sexual health clinic staff, or organisations like the
New Zealand AIDS Foundation. The bill will not regulate their largely voluntary
contact tracing practices unless they are nominees of district health board employees or
a medical officer of health.
The committee was clear that existing venereal disease le gislation is badly in need of
an update. The current definition of “venereal disease” is not fit for modern conditions.
For example, it does not include HIV, AIDS, or chlamydia. Other outdated provisions
the bill will repeal include section 79 of the Healt h Act. That authorises a medical
officer of health to detain and isolate people likely to cause the spread of infectious
disease. New Part 3A effectively replaces section 79 with graduated powers of
increasing robustness when an individual is not complying  with management aimed at
preventing the spread of further infection.
Part 2 of the bill prohibits the commercial provision of artificial ultraviolet light or
UV tanning services for people under the age of 18. The Health Committee reported
back that it is satisfied that the bill will protect the vulnerable under -18 age group while
allowing adults to make informed decisions. That is comparable to other legislation,
such as legislation on the sale and use of alcohol, which recognises that 18 is an age
where people are capable of making their own choices.
Clause 8 and clause 13 include several new provisions. These provide an
infringement process to deal with breaches of the ban on providing artificial UV tanning
services to people under the age of 18. This process would deal efficiently with offences
27 May 2015 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 4075
and prevent expensive and time -consuming criminal prosecutions. Voluntary standards
and guidelines on the operation of UV tanning beds already exist. However, surveys
have found consistently that there is variable  compliance with those voluntary steps
designed to minimise harm, despite considerable effort to educate operators and to
encourage compliance. I have therefore asked health officials to look into whether the
licensing of premises and operators and the int roduction of mandatory standards are
appropriate.
This bill is going to improve the protections we have for the health of New
Zealanders. It is an important part of our legislative framework for managing and
reducing health risks. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Labour supports this bill, the
Health (Protection) Amendment Bill. We support this bill. The amendments come from
the Public Health Bill, which was introduced by me quite a number of years ago. When
the Minister of Health said that he had an unwavering commitment to good health, well,
I can say that, 7 or 8 years ago, so did we. Unfortunately, we have had to wait some
time for this to  become a big enough priority for the Government to bring into this
House. I am very pleased we are now on the second reading, because there has been
concern that the current legislation does not fully support public health practices. That
has been articulated by those who work in public health and those who have worked in
public health agencies over a very sustained period of time. We realise these concerns.
In fact, there are many more amendments that do need to be made that are in the Public
Health Bill, which still sits on the Order Paper and, perhaps, the Government may like
to lift a few more things out of that bill and proceed with them.
This bill does give effect to the Government’s decision in October 2013 to improve
the range of measures available to protect the public from the harm associated with
infectious diseases and with artificial UV tanning. I think the Minister probably pretty
clearly set out the aim of the bill and, just briefly, it is to increase the range of infectious
diseases that are notifiable to the medical officer of health, without identifying the
information of the patient or the diseased person. As the Minister said, this includes
HIV, gonorrhoea, and syphilis. It also improves the management of persons with
infectious diseases b y providing new management options, including directions issued
by the medical officer of health, court orders, urgent health risk orders, and
interventions. It strengthens legislative provisions for contact tracing of people who
may have an infectious dis ease, and this bill introduces a ban on the provision of
commercial artificial UV tanning services to people under 18 years of age.
I just do want to correct the Minister —maybe he had not been informed —it was not
a unanimous decision of the Health Committe e that we would only ban commercial UV
tanning services for people under 18. In fact, there is a minority report provided from
Labour, the Greens, and New Zealand First, and I will get to that in a moment. I do
want to say, however, that I am really please d at the way the Health Committee is
working under the chairmanship of Mr Simon O’Connor. I thought that we had a very
good chair in Dr Paul Hutchison, and we worked very well together. I have to say that
Mr O’Connor is shaping up to be a very good and open chair.
The work that was done on this bill, I think, is commendable, because when you look
at the number of amendments that have been made, they were made —with the
exception of UV tanning services—through listening to the submissions that came from
the p ublic. Also, I think a very good contribution was made by Kevin Hague, who,
because of his background and the work that he had done in many different spheres but,
particularly, working for the AIDS Foundation, was very helpful in helping us make
some of these amendments.
4076 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 27 May 2015
I do not want to go through all the amendments we made. Anyone reading the bill
would see that the select committee improved the bill by the amendments we made. But
I do want to look at the amendment relating to privacy and identifications of persons.
We have recommended that the changes here will ensure that the information collected
by the new Part 3A, “Management of infectious diseases”, is to be used or disclosed
only under the provision of the Health Act. This is to encourage individual s to provide
private information without fear of inappropriate disclosure. I think it is really important
that the fear that something about a person could somehow be made public is
recognised. I think that we have amended that so we make that a lot stronger. Also, with
regard to identifying information, it does allow the sex, date of birth, and the National
Health Index number of a person with a notifiable disease to be disclosed. That will
assist medical officers of health with disease surveillance.
The only other point I want to mention is in the whole area of appeals. I want to pay
credit to Kevin Hague for raising this issue and getting an amendment up, which would
never have happened in the way it did if we had the previous Minister of Health, Tony
Ryall. Although Dr Coleman is not here to hear this little bit of praise I may give him —
and this will be a very rare occasion —Dr Coleman was sent the suggested amendment
that was made within the committee as we were deliberating. It was an amendment
made by K evin Hague that enabled a person to be able to make an appeal to the High
Court about a District Court’s decision on an order, part of an order, a variation of an
order, or an extension of an order. It gave a proper appeal process, which was not in the
original bill. When we came to an agreement on it, it was sent to the Minister of Health,
and the Minister of Health responded within a very short time and accepted the
amendment. I say sincerely that I do not believe that we would have got the same
response having been through a number of bills under the previous Minister.
However, I do want to express my real disappointment —and I actually even think
that most members on the committee share this disappointment —that we could not get
the Government to agree to ban commercial UV tanning services in New Zealand. You
see, we are a Health Committee, and we do like to base our decisions on good evidence.
That is what we must do. We must look at the evidence, and we must then say: “What is
the best we can do for the p ublic health of New Zealand?”. The Minister said: “These
changes we’re making are proportionate to risk.” Well, that does not apply, I have to
say, to the banning of UV tanning services, which applies only to those under 18.
I would like to say why. The Wo rld Health Organization classified sunbeds as a
carcinogenic in 2009. It estimates that sunbed use before the age of 35 —not 18, but
before the age of 35 —increases the risk of melanoma by 75 percent. Can I repeat that:
sunbed use before the age of 35 increa ses the risk of melanoma by 75 percent. Skin
cancer is one of the most common forms of cancer affecting New Zealanders. Each year
over 2,000 new melanoma cases are identified, and on average 325 New Zealanders die
from melanoma every year.
Sunbed operators  at the Health Committee —and we had  only one submission, I
think, that we heard; only one came along to support it —claimed that artificial UV
tanning beds are an important source of vitamin D. Well, the Ministry of Health, the
National Institute of Water a nd Atmospheric Research, the World Health Organization,
senior dermatologists, and the Commerce Commission argued that short -wave UVB
rays, which are rays that reach the outer layer of your skin, from commercial use, pose a
cancer risk that far outweighs a ny minor vitamin D benefits. The overwhelming
majority of submitters were opposed to the commercial use of these sunbed services.
In fact, Australia, which does not often beat us in terms of public health in many
health measures, has banned them. It can se e that they are of no benefit. We are now
going to rely on some sort of code. Unfortunately, there was very recently, on 8 May, an
27 May 2015 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 4077
undercover surveillance of tanning salons undertaken by Consumer New Zealand, and it
uncovered that more than 40 percent of t he 60 sunbed operators it visited failed to
implement safety checks, such as checking the customer’s age, asking them to sign a
consent form, and providing information on the dangers of UV exposure. One operator
allowed a 14-year-old to use a sunbed.
We do not believe this bill has gone far enough. This was the opportunity for us to
ban the commercial use. We cannot stop what people do in their own homes; that is up
to them. But there is absolutely no benefit from the commercial use of sunbeds. There is
high risk presented to New Zealanders. I just feel that many members on the committee
felt the same way as we did but were unable to do anything about it. So although we
support the bill, we want to strongly stress that during the Committee stage we will be
introducing a Supplementary Order Paper to ban the commercial use of sunbeds.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—Tāmaki): I am very pleased to take a call on this
Health (Protection) Amendment Bill, which is on its second reading here. Can I thank
the Hon Annette King for her generous words. I think such generosity is probably
costing me thousands of votes in my electorate a t the moment —people who are going:
“Oh, what’s he doing?”. But, actually, in all seriousness I do want to acknowledge all
the members of the Health Committee, and in particular Annette King, Kevin Hague
from the Green Party, and Barbara Stewart from the Ne w Zealand First Party, for the
cooperative nature in which the committee is working —Louisa Wall, as well, as a
Labour member, and then my fellow National Party members, Jacqui Dean, Barbara
Kuriger, Scott Simpson, and Dr Shane Reti. It is a fine committee and I think it is one
that is working together because we understand that there is always politics in all things,
but health is one of those matters where we try to work together.
I think we have heard in the speeches tonight, two so far, that by and large  there is a
lot of agreement, but also —and it hints at the political nature or the difference of
views—that you do not agree on everything. I am very pleased to see that members of
the House from all the parties are supporting this, as I understand it. Thi s bill is in two
parts. The substance of the bill is around contact tracing, and the second part of the bill,
not as substantial but of course as important, is around sunbeds.
As the Minister pointed out, we had 71 submissions. I thought that was actually a
really good number in light of the nature of this bill. In fact, I thought there was a very
high quality of submitters who came before us. I cannot remember the exact breakdown
of how many came to talk to us around the contact tracing side of things vers us the UV
tanning, but I am sure other members will echo —well, I hope they will—that it was the
quality of the submissions and the quality of the oral presentations. These were people
who are experts in their field. That is not to take away from the indivi duals who might
come and choose to share their experiences. But I thought there were very high -level
submissions to us. Twenty-two people were heard. It kept the committee busy, but I can
say for myself, and I am sure for the others, that, actually, it was  incredibly fascinating
as we would talk through the different issues.
The first part of this Health (Protection) Amendment Bill is around contact tracing.
For those in the House, and particularly for those at home, this is about how we work
out whom a person with an infectious disease has been in contact with. The intention of
this bill is to enable health authorities to better manage infectious disease outbreaks or
to limit them when they arise. So we are talking infections, and I hope my father,
listening at home, is not going to blush. We are talking about things like syphilis,
gonorrhoea, tuberculosis, HIV, and the like—so some serious diseases that are out there
in the community, or potentially so. With those I note that tuberculosis is currently
under another Act. One of the elements of this bill is to actually take it from being a
4078 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 27 May 2015
distinct Act of Parliament, the Tuberculosis Act, and integrate it into this Health
(Protection) Amendment Bill.
These are serious infectious diseases and when they arise we , as a society, need to
move swiftly and promptly to limit their effect. One only needs to think of the measles
outbreak. That is not —I had better be clear —one of the infectious diseases noted at the
highest end of this bill. There are good reasons for tha t, but I think of the outbreak —I
think it was in Christchurch —and just how swiftly these diseases can spread and
therefore, consequently, the State, the health authorities if you will, need to move
swiftly to manage them.
So we have introduced these extra diseases to be traced. A big part of that is: who are
the people whom those with an infection have been in contact with? Up to now the
provisions have not been sufficient enough or proportionate enough. To put it really
simply, if someone chose not to actu ally enable contact tracing to help with certain
diseases, it would not happen. So we are strengthening the ability of health agents to
encourage and then enforce the information required so that we can make those contacts
and better understand the spread of disease. One of the debates, of course, is around
privacy, and that was discussed at length. There was some concern from some
submitters, particularly around the use of the National Health Index number —that it
could lead to the identification of particu lar people and consequently discourage them
from coming forward.
We heard from a good number of submitters who work within the epidemiological
field, who said that the need for this data is absolutely paramount. Having data such as
the sex, date of birth, and the National Health Index number are very, very important.
One thing the committee did in a few of the changes it looked to bring about was to list
principles, which we are hoping will be clear not only to the public but to the courts if
they need to get involved. The first principle above all others is that the intention of this
bill is to protect public health, not just the person with the infectious disease but all of
us. That is the paramount principle.
But we, as a committee, thought it was also really important to stress that the respect
and dignity of the individual must always be noted and upheld, and, thirdly —although
not in a priority order in this case —that a proportionate response is followed. So,
depending on the nature of the infection, t heir proximity to people, for example, the
length of the infection and so forth —what is the proportionate response? Because, as
indicated implicitly by Annette King in her speech, there is the ability to bring about
court orders to force an individual to r elease the information required. Again, we would
want that to be a proportionate response depending on the infection.
I want to briefly touch on the question of acute hepatitis C. This was something that
members on the committee will know about. We spent a n enormous amount of time
considering whether acute hepatitis C should actually be brought into the same level as
gonorrhoea, syphilis, HIV, and the like. We took a lot of advice and decided it did not
require at this stage to be at that top level, but I think it is really important for the House
to understand, and those submitters, that it does remain on the schedule. It is still part of
the Act. One has to think of this as a graduated bill, a graduated response. Although it is
not at the top level, it is in there. It is a formidable disease and, fortunately, one that
does not occur as frequently as some others, but when it does it needs a lot of treatment.
I am very pleased to see, actually, that there are a number of very good pharmacological
options available now for people there.
Briefly, I want to acknowledge, as the Hon Annette King did, Kevin Hague’s
contribution around appeals. It is really important, and certainly for me, that you always
have consistency in legislation. The ability of a person to be  able to reach through the
respective courts to have their appeal heard around these matters is consistent, so
27 May 2015 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 4079
reaching the High Court makes a lot of sense. I think it is important though that the
orders remain in place. The committee did debate this a bit , that if someone is going to
start going through the legal appeal process, it is not going to stop the ability of the
health organisations to engage. When it comes to infectious diseases we need to move
promptly.
I want to turn to the sunbeds, the UV tann ing beds. The science is very clear on this.
It is unambiguous, and I am more than happy to stand on the Government side and say
this, with the legislation as it is, with a graduated response to UV tanning beds. This bill
seeks to say that under -18s should not use them and that there should be regulation for
those who do. Auckland Council, amongst others, has actually quite a good system in
place already and it was really good that it came in and talked us through how it
regulates sunbeds in Auckland. I think it is a model to follow. I want to be clear that it is
not the model; there are a few we can look at. But we are looking at a regulatory
approach. It is sort of that graduated approach, or one step at a time.
Again, the science is very clear. As many m embers know, I worked at Southern
Cross before coming into Parliament, so although I am not a doctor, I involve myself
with a lot of things medical and particularly in the dermatological and plastics field.
Look, there is no doubt about the issue of skin c ancers in this country and the place that
sunbeds can play in that. I think I heard from one of the experts, one of the doctors I
used to contract with, that something like 7 minutes a day of sunlight is all that we need,
so where is the need for sunbeds in that case?
I think we have come to a proportional response in this regard. We understand the
science; we understand the information put to us by a number of medical experts in the
likes of the Cancer Society. On this side of the House I think we are sayi ng that we
understand that, and we understand the excessive risk for those under 18, but at this
point we feel that an outright ban is probably not the best way forward. We will
introduce a graduated approach to that. We will see that regulations are put in place.
As any responsible group would do —in this case, the Government, the ministry, or
the Minister —we will continue to engage with the information. So I think we have
landed in a good place and, if I might say as I conclude, I think it was good to put a bit
of light on to this bill.

items.speaker: LOUISA WALL
items.text: Kia ora. Lau Afioga le Fofoga Fetalai.
Kia ora. I am a proud member of the Health Committee and I want to echo my
colleague Annette King’s kōrero earlier about how this committee is working. It is a
very productive committee. I think that a lot of the discussions that we have are
incredibly important, because we are talking about a health system that we want to help
design and to ensur e meets the health needs of all New Zealanders. Essentially, the
Health (Protection) Amendment Bill covers two areas. I am going to touch a lot on one
of those areas, but, briefly, the first area is about protecting the public from the risk of
the spread o f some infectious diseases. I think that what we did in the committee was
have quite an interesting discussion about what some of those diseases should be.
Obviously, the bill wanted to introduce tuberculosis to the schedule, but there was much
debate about whether or not hepatitis C should be added. Obviously, because of that, we
had discussions about other diseases that we think should be monitored, because the
spread is actually causing an adverse effect, particularly in some communities. The
second area that the bill covered was really about protection from the harm associated
with artificial UV tanning.
I am going to spend the majority of my contribution talking about the ban on solaria
or UV tanning machines, because I think the evidence was actually incredibly
compelling that 18 is, in fact, not the right age to have set if we were going to protect
the largest number of New Zealanders. I want to agree with my colleague Annette King
4080 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 27 May 2015
when she said that the World Health Organization is categoric in terms  of UV tanning
machines causing cancer. From the evidence that the World Health Organization has
gathered, in fact, 35 years should be the age that we ban the use of UV sunbeds, if we
were going to set an age. That is part of the discussion that I think is  still ongoing.
Essentially, we have set it at 18 years because once you are over 18, you are an adult
and the State ceases to care about you. This is even though we have got overwhelming
evidence that the use of these devices is harmful to you, and in spi te of 2,000 more New
Zealanders getting diagnosed with melanoma every year, and over 326 of us dying
because we get melanoma. So, in spite of all the evidence, we set the age at 18 because
up to the age of 18 you are a child and, as the State, we will prot ect you. But, if you are
over the age of 18, you are on your own and you make your own decisions. So, if you
are not as informed, or if you practise UV sunbed use because you think it makes you
look attractive and you want to be browner, or whatever it mig ht be, we say that that is
your choice.
What we in the Opposition say is that it actually should not be your choice because,
at the end of the day, there are alternatives. If you want to get brown, you can spray
stuff on you these days, right? So if you a re doing it for cosmetic reasons, there are
actually alternatives that are not going to kill you. What we said was that, actually,
given that there is an existing by -law—Auckland Council has one that already bans
under-18-year-olds from using UV tanning ma chines—the effectiveness of this piece of
legislation is essentially going to benefit only 25 percent of the sunbeds that are out
there. Auckland Council made that decision, and the other interesting submission from
my perspective was from Palmerston North  City Council. It made a decision as a
council. It made a decision because it had some evidence from a dermatologist, a
woman called Louise Reiche—I hope I am pronouncing her name correctly—that in the
MidCentral District Health Board region, the rate of m elanoma is 51.55 per 100,000
people. The national average is 39.12.
So, as a council, it got actively involved in this piece of legislation because it was
relevant to the council, and also there was a case of a young 16 -year-old, Jessie Anitoni,
who got c ancer. There was a lot of publicity, I guess, in that community about the
effects of UV tanning machines, so it was very clear that it wanted central government
to ban them. Rather than having every local council in the country going through a
process of b anning these machines, it wanted us to take responsibility as central
government and enact a piece of legislation that was going to benefit the community —
the public good. This is because, when you look at who actually benefits from using UV
sunbeds, there are some cohorts of New Zealanders who do, such as those who suffer
from seasonal depression and are actually prescribed to go and have some UV sunbed
treatments, and also people with psoriasis. So, actually, there is a medical rationale for
using UV sunbeds that we agree with. In fact, it would have been exempted in terms of
a ban because it was to be used in a medical procedure. Those beds are actually in
hospitals and they are available to people who need them.
So I think that the decision that the comm ittee made to set the age at 18 is really not
in the interests of New Zealanders. It is not in the interests of the 326 people who die
from melanoma every year and the over 2,000 New Zealanders who get diagnosed with
melanoma every year. If we had been bra ve—and I do not even think that we would
have been brave. In fact, Australia and Brazil have already banned UV sunbeds because
they realise that it is bad for the community and for the citizens of their countries. Are
their rates higher than ours? Actually, they are not. We have higher rates than Australia.
We have higher rates than Brazil. So this really was, I think, one of the critical decisions
that the committee made —the decision not to ban them —because we think that that
would have somehow sent the message that we were being nanny State, we were telling
27 May 2015 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 4081
people how to live their lives, and we were not allowing them to be adults and make
decisions for themselves. Well, actually, no. Our responsibility as legislators is to
protect the people of New Zealan d, and when we have evidence, which is
overwhelming, that says that the effects of UV sunbed usage is so detrimental and that
there is nothing to be gained from it, then I think it is incumbent on us to act. I have not
given up hope. I want to acknowledge that my colleague Annette King has got an
amendment that wants a progressive system over a period of time that will mean that in
5 years there will be no more UV sunbeds. So we are not going to take them away
immediately, but we want to phase them out prog ressively, and let those people find the
spray-cans if they are doing it because they want to look lovely. They can go to the
chemist and buy those and look all brown, and people will think that they have been in
the sun. They do not need to sit under those sunbeds and actually harm themselves.
The only other thing I wanted to cover was that I was really interested in the
discussion about what is ionising and what is non -ionising. What I want to highlight in
my take -away from the ionising/non -ionising deba te is that I understand that non -
ionising is actually low frequency —it is not as intense. But what I also got from the
discussion we had with the experts was that it is about the compound effect. It is about
the compound effect, so how much is too much? If  you go and have these sunbeds once
a week, once a fortnight, once a month —actually, what is the frequency, when the
compound use of these things actually has the same effect as ionising radiation? That
was not clear. I am clear about what is ionising and non-ionising because associated
with UV radiation are cell phone towers, Wi -Fi, power lines, and all those things. They
are in our environment. I understand that. We live with those. But what we did not get
to do was to consider that if this is non -ionising with a compound effect, then actually
maybe we should limit the frequency. So are we going to say: “OK, you are over 18.
You can make up your own mind, but actually you can use these things only once a
fortnight. If you use them more than that, the compo und effect is like using ionised
radiation.”? So that is my contribution to this debate. I look forward to an ongoing
discussion, because I am hopeful that the Government is going to support Annette
King’s amendment. Nā reira, tēnā koutou katoa. Talofa lava.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: It is a pleasure to stand and take a
call on the second reading of the Health (Protection) Amendment Bill. Just following
from the last speaker, Lo uisa Wall, I think that for many on the Health Committee the
biggest education was actually not about the terms ionising and non -ionising; it was
actually to separate them from iodising. At one stage we had someone who was
convinced that the word was “iodi sed”, as in salt, and, of course, it is a completely
different thing.
I would like to join with other speakers tonight in congratulating the work of the total
committee, actually. When we see a select committee working at its collegial best to
ensure good  outcomes for legislation, I think that that is when we see Parliament
working at its best. I am delighted to report to the House that under the chairmanship of
my colleague Simon O’Connor the committee is functioning very well, very collegially,
and we are getting good results. I think members will have seen something of the tone
of the committee reflected in the speeches that we have heard tonight, and I am sure that
will continue to be the case as this debate continues.
Notwithstanding the minority report of the Labour Party, New Zealand First, and the
Green Party, I am very pleased to learn that I think all those parties are going to support
the progress of this bill through the House. The point of difference between
Government members and Opposition me mbers around the committee stems, as Louisa
Wall has said, from the extension or the potential extension of the commercial UV
tanning clinics, and as the committee chair, Simon O’Connor, made clear during his
4082 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 27 May 2015
contribution—and the Minister—that is at this stage a step too far. I am personally quite
relaxed about that at this stage, but I would like to reserve my personal view on how
that might unfold over the years to come. I think that in many of these matters relating
to health, science, and education we f ind that it is a learning process. Technology and
information change, and we find ourselves in a position to be flexible and nimble of
foot in terms of the legislative response.
This bill seeks to amend the Health Act of 1956, and the fact that we are ame nding
that Act gives some context to the change that has occurred in both medical science and
in human knowledge over the period of time since the principal Act was passed by this
House. So it is very appropriate, given the changes in both medicine and als o in society,
that we update legislation to accommodate changed circumstances.
Back in 1956 I doubt that there could have conceivably been a situation like one that
may exist today where people, for reasons that were probably almost criminally
motivated, would use the fact that they had some kind of communicable disease, some
kind of infectious disease, to actually wreak harm upon other human beings. I think that
would be something that the legislators back in 1956 would have found difficult to
comprehend.
Regrettably, we have had cases in our recent history where, for instance —and this is
very rare, I know, but it is important that as a legislature we accommodate the rare
situations—people infected with AIDS or HIV have gone about actually infecting others
in a way that is, as I say, criminally negligent and culpable if not anything to do with
medical responsibility.
So we need to update our legislation to ensure that as a society we have an
opportunity to protect the greater good of the wider community from what are
essentially rogue individuals. This amendment bill essentially does that. It creates a
progressive stage of restrictions, management, if you like —controls might be another
word we might like to use —in terms of managing people who have a defined range of
infectious diseases. Some of those diseases are quite damaging, and they are highly
infectious, and I think we have an obligation, an absolute obligation, as legislators to put
the protection of the wider community first.
There are times when we have to think about the potential impact on the rights of
individuals versus the rights of the greater, wider comm unity. This bill, I think, seeks to
achieve that through a number of means. One of the, I guess, constitutional issues that
those who are interested in matters relating to civil rights and personal human rights
might have been concerned about —and it was ra ised in the select committee —was the
question of how far these additional management provisions would go in terms of
inhibiting the rights of individuals who may be infected with a particular disease.
So the framework that the committee and this legislati on seek to adopt uses a
principle of risk management and proportionality based on the risk associated with the
individual versus the risk to the wider community. I think the bill places as few
restrictions as are possible while at the same time maintaining  that greater good concept
and principle that is important to protecting the wider public health objectives of the
