original statute and, of course, this amending piece of legislation.
The measures provide, actually, better tools for public health staff to deal with people
who, for one reason or another, do not voluntarily seek treatment or do not voluntarily
modify their behaviour once they have been diagnosed with a communicable and
notifiable disease. So that behaviour, I think, is one that we need to be  able to balance
carefully against the individual’s rights.
So where consent is not given —and I stress that this is a very small minority of
potential cases —the current legislation simply does not allow for an appropriate
response. For instance, the curre nt legislation does not allow for the detention of an
27 May 2015 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 4083
infected person. The provisions in the bill cover the rights, duties, offences, and
penalties, and a range of restrictive powers and procedures for directions and court
orders, and it also creates a reg ime for urgent orders for people whose consistent and
persistent behaviour may place others at risk. I think that is an appropriate, moderate
response given the state of society and science today.
Powers at the lesser end of that regime —for example, the power to give directions—
are able to be exercised by a medical officer of health, and I think that, again, provides
an appropriate response to the lesser communicable and infectious diseases. Directions
are the community-level measures, and they may include , for instance, directing people
to seek testing or treatment, or counselling, or they may involve the direction of people
not to attend public places for a specified period of time. There would be some who
would argue that the restriction on the movement of an individual may be a step too far.
I am not one of those people. I think that this is a balance that is about right. If people
choose not to take their responsibilities to their wider community seriously, then I think
we as a society have an obligation to enforce those responsibilities for them.
The lack of such intermediate powers has been identified as a weakness in the 1956
legislation, so this amending bill we are considering here tonight provides a more
restrictive power—for example, detention in some cases. But that can be exercised only
following a public health order made by a District Court. The select committee
considered appeals and the process all around that sort of thing, and I think we have
landed in a pretty good spot.
I have addressed most of my comments this evening in the second reading to matters
relating to civil rights and the ability of the State and us as a legislature to enforce
powers on individuals in cases when that is required and, I think, balanced and
necessary. This is, I think, a very good piece of legislation. It updates some now quite
old legislation that was well intentioned in 1956 but that is in serious need of an update.
This bill does that and I thoroughly commend it to the House. Once again I thank the
select committee for the collegial and congenial way it has conducted its affairs. Thank
you.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: Talofa lava, Mr Assistant Speaker. I want to begin by
thanking members of the select committee. As o thers have said, the Health Committee
works in a very collaborative way, and I appreciate that from members from all sides. I
also want to pay tribute to the officials who worked with us. This is a fiendishly
complex piece of legislation and the officials did a great job of staying on top of that
work. Thank you to the submitters also, who are no doubt watching this debate tonight.
Some great submissions were heard by the committee. And thanks, in tonight’s debate,
to Annette King and Simon O’Connor for not ing my particular contribution to the
debate in the select committee, and to Jonathan Coleman, in fact, for agreeing to the
changes that I recommended.
As others have noted, this bill has two parts, and both of those parts go to the
limitation of individual liberty. Part 1 limits individual liberty for the sake of the public
good and, therefore, seeks to strike the balance on that issue. Part 2 deals with  another
situation, the restraint of individual liberty, which is where the State intervenes to curtail
the liberty of an individual to take action that would cause harm to themselves. These
are two of the kinds of situations that this House grapples with from time to time.
Picking up on one of Scott Simpson’s comments in the most recent contribution, Part
1, as he said, seeks to amend the Health Act of 1956. I am reminded that a couple of
years ago in this House we passed the marriage equality Act, which was overhauling a
piece of legislation from 1955. That legislation had fossilised in law some attitudes and
mores from our society at that time. I have worked with Nikki Kaye, in fact, to draft a
bill to completely overhaul adoption law because the Adoption Act 1955 fossilises some
4084 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 27 May 2015
mores and attitudes about children that pertained to that time but are no longer relevant
in ours. In 1956 the Health Act was written to deal with some particular issues—chiefly,
tuberculosis, in fact —and it applied attitudes tow ards the restraint of liberty that
prevailed at that time but no longer seem as relevant.
Perhaps unusually in this House, I have had some experience of applying the 1956
Health Act. I used to be the executive director of the New Zealand AIDS Foundation. I
dealt with a situation —in fact, a couple of situations —in a New Zealand city of a
person who had HIV and who had persisted, despite all efforts to change his behaviour,
in having unsafe sex with multiple sexual partners, and I was faced with the dilemma of
what on earth I should do about it. Doing nothing would mean that a number of people
would be needlessly exposed to the risk of HIV infection—something I certainly did not
want on my conscience —so I looked to the law. What did the law allow me to do?
What did the Privacy Act permit me to do? What did the Health Act permit me to do? I
was astonished that, essentially, the only path that the Health Act made available was
for me to notify the medical officer of health, who then would seek a court order to
detain this man indefinitely. That was the only option that the law provided.
So I am relieved that I have played an active part in some of the work that went into
drafting the Public Health Bill, which sits at No. 30 on the Order Paper —it would be
great to move that forward some time —specifically to actually provide medical officers
of health with a wider suite of tools and with the option of action that is proportionate to
the risks that they are trying to mitigate. I am very pleased to see these measures
progress through the House.
I did have some concerns —which I expressed in the first reading debate, and
members of the select committee will know that I raised them repeatedly during our
hearings—about whether or not the existence in the bill of the prov ision that would
enable medical officers of health to obtain identifying information about those who had,
for example, tested positive for HIV would constitute a disincentive for people to test.
Body Positive shared that concern. We heard the Human Rights Commission also
expressing some concern about that point and about whether the contact tracing
provisions would also provide a disincentive for people to test.
At the AIDS Foundation we provided our own testing services. Why did we do that?
We did that be cause we knew that many of those who were at risk feared going to
established health services for testing because, even though those services were offered
anonymously, they did not trust those services to keep their information anonymous.
They feared discr imination. So I am still troubled by that risk —whether the benefit of
better epidemiological data outweighs the risk that some people will no longer present
for testing—but I am reassured by the evidence of the New Zealand AIDS Foundation
and other epidemiologists that my fears are groundless on that point.
I want to just briefly note my approval that we are adding chlamydia to the list of
conditions for which the powers and provisions of this bill can be used by medical
officers of health, because this is our No. 1 sexually transmitted infection. It is the No. 1
infection, which we need to be taking action on. So I am very pleased to see that
development.
I come to Part 2, which is the part of the bill concerned with sunbeds. As the
minority view in the select committee report says, like my Labour colleagues—and I am
sure that Barbara Stewart will mention this in her contribution still to come —I am
disappointed that the Government did not move on this. We have heard, for example,
the evidence of what Austr alia is doing. We have heard the evidence repeatedly from
the cancer organisations and the health experts. In fact, I think that almost all of the
evidence that the select committee heard on Part 2 said: “This does not go far enough.”
27 May 2015 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 4085
There is no benefit t o having these sunbeds, except in the rare cases that Louisa Wall
has mentioned. They should be banned all together. There is no safe level of exposure.
I think it was Scott Simpson, actually, at one point in the select committee —perhaps
after we had just  heard the excellent submission from Consumer New Zealand —who
said that there are still people associated with the sunbed industry who maintain that
there is no link between their industry and cancer. The very next submission we heard
was the one submissio n—the one submission —that we heard from someone who said
that we ought not totally ban these sunbeds. This was someone from the industry who
actually presented us with a couple of reports that she had printed off the internet that,
in fact, claimed that there was no link between sunbeds and cancer.
What that goes to is exactly what Consumer New Zealand had told us, which is that
the industry simply cannot be trusted to act in a responsible way. It has had a voluntary
code for a long period of time and, as Annette King has outlined tonight, the industry
has repeatedly, and in a prolonged way, completely failed to comply with its own
voluntary code. In that time many, many New Zealanders have been exposed to
unnecessary cancer risk. These sunbeds should be ba nned altogether and I encourage
the House to have the courage to do so.

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: I am very pleased to take a call on behalf of
New Zealand First. New Zealand First will defini tely be supporting the Health
(Protection) Amendment Bill.
It is a brilliant committee, the Health Committee. Basically, we work to improve the
health of all New Zealanders, and we all work very constructively towards that end,
which is a really good aim f or a committee. I must say a thankyou to the officials, who
were very patient, and to all of the many submitters who came along to talk to us.
This bill is more and more important —particularly the contact -tracing part —given
the number of people who are now  coming into New Zealand with multidrug -resistant
TB. This type of TB cannot be cured, it can only be managed, so contact tracing of these
people is really, really important. We know that there are many of them in the hospitals,
but we also know that there  are many walking around our streets, our cities, and we
need to ensure that we have notification of them before they contaminate others with the
disease.
We are satisfied with the confidentiality changes made to this bill —thanks to Kevin
Hague from the Gr een Party —regarding the private information of patients. The
information of New Zealanders is not going to be freely available beyond the necessities
of actually managing an infectious disease, so that is an important change that we made
as a Health Committee to the bill.
I was delighted to hear what Dr Coleman said about the inclusion of chlamydia and
other STDs in the list of notifiable diseases. Submitters were absolutely positive that
this was something that had to occur. We need to ensure that there is  some education
around this mandatory notification, especially for younger people, because the last thing
we want is for them to go untreated because they are frightened of some sort of
mandatory notification and not getting themselves checked. So confiden tiality is
important, and we will be very interested to see how this works out.
We in New Zealand First were hoping to see sunbeds banned. We had heard about it
on a previous select committee trip over to Australia, and we do not believe that this bill
actually goes far enough: to ban commercial sunbeds outright. Many of the
submitters—most of the submitters, except one —actually wanted these tanning beds
banned. I would say that damage that is caused to skin by using a sunbed does not just
stop when you turn 18. I know that many years ago I decided that I would like a tan, so
after trying many of the products to paint one on, and getting the racing stripes —not an
even sort of look —I decided that I would go to one of these sunbed clinics. I was
4086 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 27 May 2015
accepted, fair skin and all, and I have never had such a bad burn; it took weeks and
weeks for it to go away, and I did not have any tan whatsoever. As my brother said to
me, I got the vegetable tan: red as a beetroot and peeling like an onion—and it lasted for
months. So I am one of those people who, when I heard the submitters come along and
talk about the evidence of skin cancer before 35 and the increased risk of melanoma,
now know that I have to take some action and, perhaps, look at what I may have done to
myself. We know that 2,000 cases of skin cancer are identified each year, and I am just
hoping that I will not be one of those cases in years to come.
The Ministry of Health recommended banning these sunbeds for commercial use,
and we know that Australia has banne d these beds, as has Brazil. The irony of it is that
our sun over here is just as harsh, and we should be following their lead. We know that
Australia has a higher level of skin cancer than we do, but we have a higher death rate
from skin cancer than Austr alia does. We were quite concerned, too, when Consumer
New Zealand came along and, after doing a check on many of the sunbed operators,
found that the regulations were being regularly flouted: 17 out of 20 operators allowed
type-1 skin mystery shoppers to have a session—I think I must have had a type 1 skin.
Therefore, I think that more needs to be done to ensure compliance with these rules —
perhaps some consent form, perhaps ensuring that people are advised of the dangers —
and, of course, there is the age, but I would have been past that age.
One of the things that really concerns me is that there is no monitoring on the
strength of the light and the intensity of the light that the beds are actually emitting.
Knowing that we are now importing second -hand sunbeds from Australia —and many
people have them privately in their homes —really makes one wonder what can be done
to ensure that the cases of skin cancer that may occur at some later stage are monitored
as much as they possibly can be. So there are quite a few issues there.
I know that we will be speaking on the sunbeds at some later stage, but I would like
to say that this is a good bill. The Health Act 1956 needed updating. Since 1956 a lot
has changed, and we in New Zealand First believe that preventive mea sures are far
better than trying to fix things up once they have actually gone wrong. We need a fence
at the top of the cliff rather than the ambulance at the bottom. So we in New Zealand
First will be supporting this bill, as it is working towards protect ing the health of all
New Zealanders, and for us that is a priority. Thank you.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: I enjoyed Barbara Stewart’s contribution to
this debate, along with other members of the Health Committee. The Health
(Protection) Amendment Bill has been through a good process in the select committee
and the House, and I, along with others, acknowledge the good work that the committee
has done. I felt for the member Barbara Stewart when she described her experience on a
sunbed, receiving what I suspect was quite a bad burn in the process —and have we not
all done that? I too have done that, and I recall g etting bad burns on a number of
occasions. But that was simply being out in the sun as a child, on the shores of Lake
Taupō, back in the day when as children we would be out in the sand digging, catching
tadpoles, swimming, and doing all of the things that kids do.
I vividly remember being badly sunburnt. I come from a medical family —mum was
a nurse and dad was a doctor. The point I am trying to make here is that the perils of
sunbeds are known and are not contested, except by the one proponent of sunbeds w ho
came to the committee. Just as you can receive a bad burn from a sunbed, so you can
from the sunshine. I guess that these days parents and schools —thank goodness—take a
lot of care of kids, so we do not get to see that degree of burning. I highlight the  issue
just to say that we need to be very careful that we do not overly prescribe nanny State
provisions, as somebody today said. Maybe I agree with the position that you cannot
protect New Zealanders from every little bit of harm. I acknowledge that tann ing beds
27 May 2015 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 4087
are dangerous. So is alcohol, but we are not banning that, are we? It is that same
principle of banning versus regulating.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: How about water?

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Good point —a very good point. Do not make m e lose my track.
That is very unfair. The point I was trying to make was that—

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: It’s still a very good story.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Yes, drinking, Ruth. Yes, it is all about the drinking, is it not? The
point I was tryin g to make is that the position we came to in the committee was to
restrict the use of tanning beds to those people aged 18 years and older.
I was walking along Lambton Quay the other day with this in mind. I happened to go
past a sandwich board that was ex tolling the virtues of tanning. As we had just had that
conversation in the select committee, I picked up a brochure, took it back to my office,
and had a look at it. I think what needs to happen in the tanning industry, with solaria
and sunbeds, in the face of the scientific evidence, is for some responsibility to be taken
and for some acknowledgment to be given that there are dangers associated with
sunbeds. In some people’s eyes, there are benefits. That is fine. I acknowledge that there
are benefits, in  some people’s eyes, but there certainly are dangers. I also just want to
make that first point again. The dangers of burning are not just with sunbeds; it can
happen any day of the week outside in the sunshine.
The member is also right in saying that the re was one submitter who had quite a
different view on the scientific evidence, and that was interesting. I thought it was a
brave attempt by that submitter to fight her corner. It was a female submitter. I do not
recall her name. Why not fight her corner in the select committee? The fact is that she
was an importer of sunbeds and, from memory, had franchises for sunbeds. Why not
fight her corner? I know that I have got it all round the wrong way, because the
provisions relating to sunbeds —Part 2, clause 13  of the bill —include the new
provisions that provide for infringement processes to deal with people who do not
comply with the new regulations around sunbeds.
I also thought about the contribution made by a Labour member who said that there
are some health  benefits with solaria, in a very narrow range, and that they relate to
depressive illnesses relating to winter, and also to psoriasis. I do know a couple of
people who suffer from psoriasis, and I do know that occasionally they will take a
course of sunbe d sessions because that provides them with relief. The member Louisa
Wall said that, yes, there are sunbeds available at hospitals. You can go to the
hospital—you can if you can find a car -park—make an appointment, go in, and have
treatment. Or you can go to the solarium during your lunchtime and get your treatment
there. So I do not think that with sunbeds we should necessarily throw the baby out with
the bathwater. There are some beneficial aspects to sunbeds. I will leave that to one
side, but that was t he major cause of disagreement within the committee over this
otherwise accepted bill.
Kevin Hague mentioned in his speech tonight —and he gave some very thoughtful
contributions on this in the select committee —the issue of the need for contact tracing
whilst at the same time protecting the privacy of some vulnerable populations. This was
a point that was also considered very closely by the committee. On the one hand, there
is the need to stop the spread of some pretty infectious diseases such as gonorrhoea and
hepatitis in some populations. STDs are not great diseases to have, and they can hang
around for many years and can cause all sorts of problems later in life —all sorts of
health issues. They are not diseases to be taken lightly. But, as Kevin Hague poi nted out
to the committee—and this was also backed up by submissions —the provisions around
contact tracing need to be very carefully applied so that the rights of individuals are not
4088 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 27 May 2015
necessarily impinged, and so that the rules around contact tracing and th e provision of
information are commensurate with the potential risk that is posed by the disease.
In this bill, contact tracing is designed not to be a mallet, but rather to be a process
that has gradual interventions. The first stage of that is to attempt  to gain voluntary
consent from somebody who has presented at a hospital or a GP’s surgery and is found
to have what is now going to be a notifiable disease. If that consent is not gained
voluntarily, then the bill introduces a duty on a person who may hav e an infectious
disease or who might have been exposed to an infectious disease to provide the
prescribed contact information. That contact information could well be, clearly, people
whom they have had contact with —names, addresses; that sort of thing —obviously so
that the medical officers can trace those people and can confine the outbreak, or
potential outbreak.
The practice of seeking voluntary consent for contact tracing will be the preferred
method and the first option for managing the risk of infectio n. The provisions in the bill
increase the range of infectious diseases that are notifiable, thereby improving the
surveillance of infectious diseases that are of concern, including their long -term impact
on health. The more quality information that is hel d about these things, the more likely
it is that any potential outbreak or spread of an infectious disease or STD can be
contained. There are measures being introduced in the bill to protect the identity of
individuals and to allay concerns that people mig ht not seek treatment if they believe
that their identity will be made public. The issue that Kevin Hague brought very clearly
to the committee is that we do not want populations of people hiding away for fear of
being publicly exposed as having a certain notifiable disease or STD.
The approach taken in the bill, and I congratulate the Minister on this approach, is to
use the principles of risk management and proportionality. Rather than, as I said, using a
mallet to strike a walnut, the principles of risk management and proportionality are
brought into play in this bill. This is a good bill, which is being well supported around
the House. We do have a point of difference, of course, around tanning services —of
course we do—but otherwise I am pleased to see t hat the bill is enjoying good support
and good debate. I commend it to the House.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I call Jan Logie—a 5-minute call.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: Fa‘afetai lava. I rise to take a call on this, the second reading
of the Health (Protection) Amendment Bill. It will be a relatively short call, I think.
Much of the content of the bill has been well covered in the House this evening. The
Greens are supporting this bill, and  also supporting the Labour Supplementary Order
Paper to extend the ban on tanning beds.
This bill does take us forward on both provisions. The bill kind of breaks down into
two halves—one is in relation to contact tracing for infectious diseases. There h as been
an extension and an inclusion of new diseases in that list —which is a good thing —
including chlamydia, which, as my colleague Kevin Hague pointed, is the most
prevalent sexually transmitted infection in this country. So it is very good to have it on
that list.
This legislation was first written in 1956, so it is well overdue to be updated. My
colleague Kevin Hague, in his speech at this stage, told the story of his experience with
the AIDS Foundation—which was quite informative for the House—when he was in the
situation where somebody he knew was, I think, HIV positive and perhaps not engaging
in safe sex. He was concerned about interventions, and contact tracing. The only
possibility at that stage, according to the legislation, was to inform the med ical officer
of health, who would then go to a court, and that person would be detained. So it was a
very, very blunt instrument and not one that balanced people’s rights versus the
outcome in terms of protection. So it is very good that this bill is now i ntroducing
27 May 2015 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 4089
stages, and that first stage, which has already been stated, would be the preferred option
of seeking voluntary consent from people for contact tracing. Then, on a failure of that,
there is to be a duty for that person who may have been exposed to a disease or who
may have the disease to provide the contact information for the tracing to be able to
happen. So that is all very good.
I would just like to note, from that the discussion I have been hearing in the House
this evening from members who sat on the Health Committee, that it sounds as if it was
a very constructive process. It was an interrogation of what this legislation would mean
in practice and in the balancing of it on that basis, and that is a fantastic thing to happen.
That is what we would really love to see happening more often in this House and
through the parliamentary process.
It does seem that the second part of the  bill—which in relation to sunbeds —reached
an ideological divide or a brick wall. It seems that the Opposition side of the House was
primarily weighing on the side of the need to ban the sunbeds because of the extreme
harm that is caused. The fact is that New Zealand has such high levels of melanoma —
2,000 new cases are identified every year and over 300 people die of melanoma in this
country every year—and the information is that, in terms of sunbed exposure for those
under 35, there is, I think, a 73 perce nt increase in the risk of getting melanoma from
using a sunbed. That makes sunbeds, to my mind —not having been through this
process—a dangerous item.
It is disappointing to see that this legislation is banning it only for those under 18,
particularly in light of there having been supposedly voluntary regulations, or a code of
conduct, for the use of sunbeds in place already that have not been abided by. Consumer
New Zealand has been doing surveys and has found that these companies are not
abiding by it. S o how would we expect them to abide by this limit of 18 years? We
know that some pubs do not do it. Are we expecting these people who are already
breaching their own voluntary rules to be consistent just because we pass the law?
I met with Business New Ze aland people the other day to talk about another matter
and they said to me: “Jan, you know, actually, if it comes to what we think is a nanny
State, you pass the law and we’re going to ignore it.” I did not realise business was quite
so anarchic, but appa rently that is how some businesses think. When there is such a
problem with melanoma, I think, actually, we just need to ban sunbeds for safety
purposes. Thank you.

items.speaker: MEKA WHAITIRI
items.text: Talofa, Mr Deputy Speaker.
Talofa e ngā mema o te Whāre nei. It gives me pleasure to take a short call on the
Health (Protection) Amendment Bill. Listening to all the contributions tonight, can I
also acknowledge, obviously, the collegial way in which the Health Committee worked.
In listening attentively to the contributions made tonight, I do want to raise a couple
of facts in relation to them that have come to my attention. Every year 325 New
Zealanders die from melanoma. Sunbed use in creases the risk of melanoma by 75
percent. A Consumer New Zealand survey found that 40 percent of sunbed operators
failed to implement basic safety checks. I understand that the majority of submitters at
the select committee believed that banning sunbeds would result in a decline in skin
cancers.
If I can take us back, Labour supports this bill. It is great to see that the Government
is finally acting on the work started by our colleague the Hon Annette King. The
amendments in this bill are from the Publi c Health Bill introduced by Annette King
some 7 years ago, which was in regard to infectious diseases. That bill stemmed from
the concern that the current legislation does not fully support public health practice as
being articulated by staff in health agencies over a sustained period of time.
4090 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 27 May 2015
The bill gives effect to the Government’s decision in October 2013 to improve the
range of measures available to protect the public from the harm associated with some
infectious diseases and with artificial UV tannin g. The aim of the bill is to increase the
range of infectious diseases that are notifiable to medical officers of health without
identifying the information of patients or diseased persons. This will include HIV
infection, gonorrhoea infection, acquired im mune deficiency syndrome —AIDS—and
syphilis. It also aims to improve and manage persons with infectious diseases by
providing new management options, including directions issued by a medical officer of
health, court orders, urgent health risk orders, and in terventions. It also aims to
strengthen legislative provisions for the contact tracing of people who may have an
infectious disease or who may have been exposed to one. It also aims to introduce a ban
on the provision of commercial artificial UV tanning se rvices to people under 18 years
old.
Tonight we have heard that the tension in the select committee, particularly with the
Opposition members, has been around the full banning of commercial UV operations —
i.e., tanning beds. Of course, Labour will be intro ducing an amendment for the House’s
consideration when we come to the Committee of the whole House, which is around
why we propose an outright ban.
In terms of the select committee, like previous speakers, I too want to acknowledge
the way in which those members have operated and come to the House. I understand
that 71 submissions were received and 22 submissions were heard before the select
committee. I was not a member on that committee, but I do acknowledge the way in
which people have conducted themselves.
I understand too that scientific data was presented to the committee. That scientific
data indicated, coming back to the contentious issues of banning sunbeds, that sunbeds
emit a higher concentration of UV radiation than the sun. Personally, I canno t say that I
have experienced sunbeds. There are probably very few in my family whom I can
actually tap on—

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: Not me.

items.speaker: MEKA WHAITIRI
items.text: Not you either, Mr Kris Faafoi. But there is a serious nature
around the impacts o f UV sunbeds and so, all jests aside, it is important that we do
acknowledge those who lose their lives. A previous speaker, Jacqui Dean, mentioned
something that I do have to differ with her on, in terms of her statement about taking a
mallet to a walnut.  I would hate to be the one who is sitting in front of the families of
the 325 people who do lose their lives every year through these sunbeds.
I look forward to the bill coming back to the House and to its being debated in the
Committee stage. Labour, th erefore, supports it and we look forward to the support of
the Committee in terms of our amendments. Thank you very much.

items.speaker: BARBARA KURIGER
items.text: It is a pleasure to
be here tonight taking a call on the Health (Protection) Amendment Bill. It is
particularly pleasing because this is the first bill that I have actually followed from the
beginning as a new member of Parliament, and I am following i ts way through the
process. So it is always going to be particularly relevant to me.
It is clear that some parts of the legislation from over 50 years ago need updating in
order to improve it for modern times. If I think back to 50 years ago, a lot of infe ctious
diseases and things were actually quite isolated within communities because people
actually did not travel as far as we do now. So when you think about the progress in
travel and the way people shift around communities in the last 50 years, the risk  has
become much, much greater than it ever was in the past. It is also the science that we
have developed over time, and the thought development, and also the tracking systems
27 May 2015 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 4091
that we have. When everything was manual, 50 years ago, there was not the ability to do
some of the things that we do now.
The Health (Protection) Amendment Bill aims to amend and update the Health Act
1956. It also seeks to update the legislation around sunbeds. If I think back, I cannot
remember any of our parents, brothers, sister s, or people back many, many years ago
actually having a fetish for sunbeds. I think people are now starting to learn the lessons
of those sunbeds, and we are starting to become aware of the harm that they are capable
of causing.
Good health is of crucial  importance to New Zealanders, young and old. This
National Government has an unwavering focus over the past 7 years in respect of
maintaining and improving our public health services. New Zealanders are receiving
better and more convenient health care, an d it remains one of the Government’s
priorities.
During this bill’s time in select committee, we heard over 70 submissions that came
in. I was really, really impressed to see the diligence that people applied when they were
presenting their submissions. Th e other thing that I was really impressed with, over the
course of sitting and listening to those submissions, was the way that different groups in
the community that are working together to strive to make things better in the health
sector were actually c oming together and working on joint submissions to make their
cases stronger. I was very, very impressed with that. They did bring a lot of concerns to
us. I would also like to commend the officials who were in the room, because, as you
can imagine, tracki ng a whole range of infectious diseases and contact tracing is
actually quite a large thing to do. So we were always able to test and measure back with
those officials for things, saying: “Is this possible? Can we do it? The things that these
people are asking for—is it possible to do that with your system?”. The reassurance that
they gave us that it was possible certainly helped us to make our decisions.
The provisions in this bill are multiple, and they primarily allow for the tracing of
people who have infectious diseases and the introduction of a ban on the provision of
commercial UV tanning services to those individuals under 18. I have to say that this is
the area where I feel that those people need to be protected more than in other areas.
People who  are under 18 have not actually had the opportunity to read as widely as
older people, and they are still very much minors. They are not old enough to vote, and
they need to be protected in that sense of the word.
But I also want to make a comment. We hea rd before about how we have pubs
letting in people who are 18, and people will not respect the law. Well, to be honest,
pubs will only do that until somebody actually catches up with them and until
somebody actually realises that they are selling alcohol t o a minor. I believe that the
regulations around this are going to ensure that these places are tested, measured, and
audited in order to make sure that they are not breaching the legislation. I also think it is
really important that they do have respect for the legislation, whatever the age of people
they are dealing with, because we know so much more now about the dangers of how
sunbeds are used. I think it is really important that the usage of them is much more
under control because, unfortunately, this is an industry where it has largely been
ignored. The more you ignore the regulations, the more you open people up to health
risks and the more you find that they are susceptible to getting melanomas from
sunbeds.
I too have to say that I am impressed wit h the overall cross -party support that was
shown in the Health Committee. It is certainly rewarding to New Zealanders when we
are able to work together to achieve great results. The Health Committee is definitely a
pleasurable place to go, and I give credi t to all the members of the team. I have to say
that it is also reflective of our chair, Simon O’Connor, who does a great job in chairing
4092 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 27 May 2015
the committee. Since the first Act in 1956, as I have said before, the knowledge and
scientific development have put f orward strong evidence in a lot of these areas. It was
great to see that evidence coming in, and having people talking to us.
I am very pleased with the outcomes that we are putting forward this evening in the
House. On balance, I know we have heard a bit  about whether we should widen the
scope of sunbeds, but I think the evidence of health harm gives sufficient justification
for intervention, particularly around those people who are under 18. Other than that, the
measures in this legislation largely provi de for better tools for public health. We have a
better opportunity for staff to deal with infectious diseases, especially when people do
not offer to seek voluntary treatment. So if somebody is not actually coming in and
presenting with a disease, and not  obviously offering voluntarily to behave in a best -
practice way around this, then this legislation gives the officials a chance to do
something about it. It places a duty on the medical practitioner who is in charge to
provide information to officials who  are in charge as to whether there are measures
needed to prevent the further spread of disease. I think this is such an important thing,
and the cooperation between the health officials and the public means a safer
environment for all New Zealanders.
I want to say that we did have quite a bit of discussion, and we did have some people
coming in to the select committee who were rather concerned about privacy issues
around that. But the bill has provisions in it that make sure that everybody’s privacy is
absolutely protected. However, there is always a balance and there is always a
judgment, and I think we are reaching that right judgment where there is a balance
between the person’s own privacy issues and protecting the public as a whole. And so
you do not get to the point where, actually, you are keeping someone’s privacy so quiet
that the rest of the public are exposed to a huge risk.
It is a pleasure to be here tonight supporting this second reading of the bill, to
improve the tracing of people and to in crease the range of infectious diseases that are
notifiable. I think it also provides a series of incremental options for the management of
individuals with significant diseases whose behaviours do put others at risk of
contracting a disease. There are a n umber of changes that will streamline legislation,
such as the inclusion of tuberculosis as a notifiable disease under the Act, and the
consequent repeal of the Tuberculosis Act 1948 —that is an Act that goes back quite a
way in time. It is my pleasure toni ght to commend this second reading of the bill to the
House. Thank you.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES -GALLOWAY
items.text: I must say, it is a
pleasure to hear that the Health Co mmittee is still operating with a constructive and
mostly bipartisan approach. As someone who was a member of the committee for 6
years, I must say that I miss that committee. I understand that under the chairmanship of
Simon O’Connor, it is doing well.

items.speaker: Sarah Dowie
items.text: I’m hurt. You’re on TPR—I’m hurt.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: Well, Sarah Dowie, we have got an interesting select
committee tomorrow, so we will cross that bridge when we get to it —more interesting
for you guys than it is for us, I must say. But it is good to hear that there is a convivial
mood at the select commi ttee, and it was good to hear that we can have a bipartisan
approach to some of these health issues, and how constructive it can be. I am pleased
that the member who was speaking previously, Barbara Kuriger, was enthusiastic about
the bipartisan approach —a new member who delivered a very good 10 -minute speech;
well done.
This bill does a number of important things —a number of important things that I
think, as some of my colleagues have pointed out, could have been introduced quite a
long time ago, if the l egislation that included these aspects and others had been
27 May 2015 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 4093
supported by the National Party back when the Labour Government introduced them.
So we could have been 7 years ahead of where we are right now, if we had had that
same bipartisan and constructive a pproach back when National was in Opposition. It is
a shame that we did not have that same bipartisan and constructive approach.
This bill does a number of things that I know the National Party has had some issue
with in the past. It increases the range o f infectious diseases that are notifiable; it
improves the management of individuals with infectious diseases whose behaviour puts
other people at risk of contracting a disease, by providing new management options,
including directions issued by the medica l officer of health, court orders, and urgent
health-risk orders and interventions; and it strengthens the legislative provisions for
contact tracing of people who may have an infectious disease or may be exposed to one.
All of those measures require a deg ree of, I suppose, a person having to divulge
information about themselves. It may be uncomfortable for people to divulge some of
that information, but it is really important for public health, for our community, and for
our collective health that those individuals are expected, and are now required under this
legislation, to offer up that information.
The New Zealand National Party has not always been a big fan of this approach. I go
back to the minority view expressed in the report back on the Public Heal th Bill, which
was the Labour bill that was introduced by Annette King that contained many of these
provisions as well as others. Under a paragraph entitled “Forced disclosure of health
information”, National had this to say: “ The bill, in requiring disclo sure of health
information, creates a provision for non -Government health care providers to
mandatorily supply information to the Ministry of Health, beyond what, if any, is
already voluntarily provided. This has potential to create significant costs for t hese non-
Government providers (such as private hospitals, general practices and Māori health
providers) and funders (such as health insurers) without reimbursement. For example,
the cost to private hospitals of employing specialist coding staff to supply s urgical data
by purchase unit or diagnostic related group to the ministry will not be insignificant.
The ministry advisers even acknowledged that it may take considerable time for
providers to collate requested information.  Providers and funders could be r equired to
provide confidential financial and business information in the name of ‘advancing
health knowledge, health education or health research’.”
It goes on. It goes on to talk about National’s concerns about people having to
divulge information and h ealth providers having to provide such information, the costs
that would be related to that, and the impact on people’s individual freedom to maintain
that information. That was one of the somewhat spurious reasons on which National
based its opposition. This is not new. We have seen the National Party do this a number
of times where it sees a political opportunity to make political attacks and to undermine
a Government, whether or not that actually is in the interest of advancing the well -being
or the health of New Zealanders.
The fact that 7 years on we are hearing from members about the wonderful bipartisan
approach that has occurred at the select committee and the fact that these are all
important measures to improve the public health I think absolutely  reveals the appalling
political games that the National Party played with health when it was in Opposition. It
is just true. Some newer members are looking over at me shaking their heads a little bit.
Well, this might be a history lesson for them. They mi ght not have been aware of this,
but actually time and time again in the 6½ years that I have been in Parliament we have
actually debated and passed, nearly unanimously in most cases, legislation that the
National Party in Opposition vehemently and loudly opposed because there was some
group out there that it was trying to appeal to, or even if there was not a group out there
4094 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 27 May 2015
that it was trying to appeal to, but it just saw an opportunity to undermine the Labour
Government. That was all it was about.

items.speaker: Brett Hudson
items.text: The unions elected your leader and you talk about people being
beholden to groups. What a joke!

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: Well, there you go. That is the level of debate. That is
what Brett Hudson thinks is an importan t contribution to make to a debate about public
health. He is wrong, of course. He obviously actually has not understood how the
Labour Party works, but what we are talking about here, Brett Hudson, is advancing the
public health and well -being of New Zeal anders and the fact that the National Party
plays politics—the fact that the National Party plays politics around these things. It is
great and it is fantastic that we are doing this and that the select committee in its
bipartisan and constructive approach  has actually come back expecting that even more
information will be devolved including sex, date of birth, National Health Index
number—all things that are going to be useful in terms of bringing under control
notifiable infectious diseases and advancing the public health and well -being of New
Zealand. I just come back to the fact that we could have done this 7 years ago —we
could have done this 7 years ago. But what does the National Party do with all this
stuff? It always plays politics.
I had a look, because I am not on the select committee any more, at the departmental
reports and I found that there were two departmental reports —one on infectious
diseases and one on the issue around sunbeds —both of which were nearly 100 pages
long. There were numerous submissions and there was obviously a lot of evidence to go
through. It would appear that for the most part the select committee in its bipartisan and
constructive approach has taken an evidence -based approach to these issues, including
the issues around th e link between sunbeds and melanoma. I noticed one of the reports
that the select committee received noted that there was a strikingly high rate of
university students who use suntan beds. Those would be university students, I assume,
who are over 18 and w ho are possibly in their early 20s who are using these beds. It is
concerning that these young people are perhaps using these beds in an unregulated
environment, not being fully aware of what the long -term impacts might be of using
those beds.
It is good to see that Parliament is working together to do things that are
constructive, that take a long-term view of health, and that are about maintaining health
and well -being to try to prevent disease further down the track, particularly around
melanoma. It is good to see that for the most part the Government seems to have
followed the evidence. There are some small differences of opinion between this side
and the other side of the House about how far it went in following the evidence, but for
the most part this side of the House is very pleased to see the continuing passage of this
legislation. We are just so disappointed that it has taken 7 long years for National to
finally see sense.

items.speaker: Dr SHANE  RETI
items.text: It is my privilege to speak to the
Health (Protection) Amendment Bill tonight. Just in brief reply to the previous member,
Iain Lees-Galloway, I would indicate that we are certainly interested in learning from
the past, but we a re more interested in working in the present, and that is certainly
where I would like to be tonight. I would also like to acknowledge my colleagues on the
Health Committee for the due diligence they have done in progressing this bill, and the
guidance of the chair, Simon O’Connor.
There are two themes to this bill, as has been commented on. There is the infectious
disease theme and the UVB tanning theme. I will talk to each of them.
I will talk first of all to the infectious disease theme, and there are s everal parts that
this bill actually talks to. First of all, it talks about modernisation, improving contact
27 May 2015 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 4095
tracing, and improving management options. As has been commented on, the previous
Act is an old Act, from 1956, and it is modernised in this new am endment. If we look at
some of the areas that are modernised, we had Toi te Ora suggest to us amending
“premises” to include “vehicles”, so the definition of “premises” now reads “… any
commercial premises, private premises, vehicle, ship, or aircraft”. That makes sense. An
“educational institution” was also clarified as “… any place where people gather for the
purpose of education or training ;”, and “an individual who has an infectious disease”
now includes “… an individual who is infected or colonised by,  or is a carrier of, an
organism capable of causing the disease, even if the individual does not exhibit any of
the symptoms of the disease.” We have modernised the Act with this bill.
The second part of the bill that I will talk to is around some of the n ew diseases that
have become notifiable. In fact, they are not new diseases, but they are now notifiable.
Very important diseases —HIV, gonorrhoea, syphilis —are now added to the schedule,
along with hepatitis A, hepatitis B, hepatitis not otherwise specified, leprosy, rabies, and
malaria. So these are really important diseases that we have now put on the correct
schedule. This bill also attends to contact tracing. I was  a sexually transmitted disease
officer in Northland for many years and contact tracing wa s very, very important to us.
It is nice to see these regulations tighten up and give us new and better tools for what
we are doing.
What we have done with contact tracing is significantly strengthened, with graduated
measures, a sliding scale, and a rang e of techniques we can bring to the task, ranging
from voluntary to non -voluntary contact tracing and also including self -managed
contact tracing. Significant powers have been given to the medical officers of health, for
example. To safeguard those potenti ally intrusive activities that they have, the bill
enunciates a number of principles that describe the balance between voluntariness, self -
management, and public risk. These principles include “Respect for individuals”,
“Voluntary compliance”, “Individual to be informed”, the “Principle of
proportionality”, “Least restrictive alternative”, “Measures to apply no longer than
necessary”, and that the “paramount consideration … is the protection of public health”.
I think these are some of the safeguards to the new powers we have given under the bill.
We have also looked, in the amendments to section 74, at notification of some of the
infectious diseases. This was the point that Kevin Hague made, which I think is
absolutely correct. There was a lot of discussio n around provision of identifying
information with the notification information. I would add here that the New Zealand
AIDS Foundation, when it presented to the select committee, was very comfortable with
the range of information we were looking to collect . That aside, we felt that we should
peel it back and that we did not need all of it. So where the initial list was name, date of
birth, sex, address, place of work, and National Health Index (NHI) number, we have
peeled that back to sex, date of birth, an d NHI number. Again, the New Zealand AIDS
Foundation and other stakeholders were very, very comfortable that that was
appropriate information to be collected —particularly NHI numbers, which can be
symmetrically identified to a person. The foundation felt t hat, considering the NHI is
stored appropriately and meets a lot of privacy constraints, it was comfortable with that.
Behaviour that is risky to public health is also covered under this bill. As I have
mentioned, medical officers of health are given increased powers of compulsion. There
are other safeguard measures. One of them is in regard to the Director -General of
Health. In many places in the bill it is stated: “If the Director -General so requires, the
medical officer of health must send him or her a copy of all or any of the directions
given … under this section”, which is another really good safeguard. There is anoth er
part to that: “If the disease that the individual is believed to have is not a notifiable
4096 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 27 May 2015
infectious disease, every direction given to the individual must have the prior approval
of the Director-General.” Again, that is another good safeguard.
I would like to talk briefly about chlamydia. I think this is a really important thing
that the Health Committee has had added to this bill. Chlamydia was commented on as
the most obvious sexually transmitted infection that was not on the infectious diseases
schedule and not on the notifiable diseases schedule. A 2014 report by the Institute of
Environmental Science and Research, looking at 2013 data, showed that across all the
district health boards there was an incidence rate of 633 cases of chlamydia per 100,000
people. That was less than what it had been in the previous year, so it was improving,
but it was still twice that of Australia and, in absolute numbers, it was 25,000 positive
tests. This committee raised the attention of officials to chlamydia and place d it on the
schedule. We have placed it on the infectious diseases schedule and its type is non -
notifiable—that is in the Health Act, schedule 1, Part 2, as amended by clause 10.
This is a big step. If we look across the bill and ask what parts of the bil l will touch
the largest number of people and impact on the largest number of people, I think this
clause is an unexpected benefit that we will look back on and say: “Ha! We really did
something good there. We really had an impact on vulnerable communities  with that
clause. I mean, we didn’t know at the time whether we were quite going to do that.” So
chlamydia now joins other infectious diseases that are non -notifiable in schedule 1, Part
2, which includes standard influenza, scabies, and impetigo contagio sa, which is school
sores. They may seem trivial but, let us remember, some of these can be really quite
significant. School sores can certainly destroy your kidney through a bizarre
autoimmune process. So, again, I just want to commend the committee and o fficials for
taking into account and including chlamydia in that schedule.
I would like to now turn to the second theme, which is around artificial UV tanning
services. As the member Jacqui Dean commented, it is actually quite common in
hospitals to find UV services. Particularly in the dermatology department you will find
UVB, which is used quite frequently, and UVA. UVA, particularly, is used in
“PUVA”—psolaren plus UVA. Again, she mentioned psoriasis, and 10 to 20 percent of
New Zealanders have psoriasi s. Probably those in this room tonight who have dry skin
on their elbows and knees will think it is just dry skin, but no, it is not; it is psoriasis. Of
those who have the unfortunate affliction of dandruff, 20 percent will actually have
psoriasis as well. So it is quite common. Therapeutically we would use—

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: Give me a script for that.

items.speaker: Dr SHANE RETI
items.text: I could. Actually, you do need a prescription for light therapy. It
just shows how controlled it needs to be.
Anyway, Part 5 of this bill talks to UV tanning services and fundamentally restricts
them to being used by those over 18. The question first would be: well, why restrict it at
all? There is very clear evidence of the nexus or the relationship between ultra violet
radiation and skin cancer. We generally break skin cancer into two types: melanomatous
and non-melanomatous. The melanomas are the brown moles that change in size, shape,
and colour, and, certainly, that can be very terminal. There is, in fact, a ve ry high
frequency in young people. It is one of the most common causes of cancer in young
people. The non -melanomatous are the scaly lesions on the back of your hands —the
basal cell carcinomas, squamous cell carcinomas, and solar keratosis moles—
Simon O’Connor: The full squamous cell.

items.speaker: Dr SHANE RETI
items.text: The full squamous cell, as you say. There is very clear evidence
from the people who presented to us of the relationship between UVB and
melanomatous and non -melanomatous skin c ancer. It is unequivocal; there is no
question on that.
27 May 2015 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 4097
Where there was some debate was around age. We looked at age and said, look, it
needs to be consistent with other legislation. It needs to be consistent with where we
think the age of autonomous consent and autonomous understanding sits, and consistent
with other legislation such as tobacco and alcohol legislation. If we are going to set an
age, as was correctly mentioned by someone, we need to consider how we are going to
monitor that. How are we going to check that the sunbed industry is indeed treating only
people over the age of 18? What is required there, and what you will see in Part 5, is
quite a detailed infringement platform, or infringement programme, if you like. We
wanted to be firm but we wanted to also be fair in what we were doing, so there are
escalating infringements to try to avoid the unnecessary criminal prosecution pathway,
which can be long and expensive. Having said that, the officials made it very clear that
if there were repeate d and deliberate infringements, they would head to criminal
prosecution.
It has also been commented, and I think it is interesting, that our prime intervention
here is on age. We could look at what the Auckland Council has done. It has actually
regulated the industry under by -law. I think there are some interesting things coming
out of that as well. There are actually other parts of the legislation that can be brought to
bear in this arena —there is legislation around electrical safety and various other
things—but I think, reassuringly, at the end of the day what we have said in the new
Part 5 is that we will review it in 3 years’ time. So let us learn the lessons from what
Auckland Council has done as a by-law. Let us see how this goes.
I think this is an e xcellent piece of legislation and I think it will give us much better
tools to do a better job. I commend it to the House. Thank you.
Bill read a second time.
GAMBLING AMENDMENT BILL (NO 3)
Second Reading

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I move, That the Gambling
Amendment Bill (No 3) be now read a second time . At the outset I would like to thank
the members of the Government Administrati on Committee for their efforts in
thoroughly considering this bill. It was referred to the committee in November of last
year and was reported back to the House on 11 May this year, a considerably faster
track than its predecessor. The select committee rec eived 126 written submissions on
the bill, as well as hearing oral submissions in Wellington and Auckland.
This bill makes a limited number of amendments to the Gambling Act 2003 but does
so in several key areas. The majority of these changes relate to ga ming machines, or
pokies, in bars and pubs. This form of gambling generates a significant amount of
money. For example, in the 2013 -14 financial year, New Zealanders spent around $700
million on over 13,000 pokie machines in commercial venues across the co untry. The
select committee’s report recommends a range of key amendments to the bill, which I
support. Many are quite specific, and traverse a wide variety of aspects of the Act. For
example, the committee’s report tidies up the important definition of “k ey person” in
the bill to prevent unintended consequences. The regulation -making powers under the
Act involving the way societies distribute funds to the community are also improved,
and this will resolve some gaps and fix some drafting issues.
One purpose of the Act is to limit opportunities for crime and dishonesty associated
with conducting gambling. People can be involved with conducting gambling either
through a society that is licensed to conduct the gambling or as venue personnel where
the gaming machines are located. Obviously, there are those who receive grant funding
as well. The Act looks to prevent conflicts of interest by prohibiting personal benefits
4098 Gambling Amendment Bill (No 3) 27 May 2015
being given or taken between those groups. The objective here is to ensure that personal
gain is not a prime motivator for people’s actions over and above community benefit.
This is a very difficult area, because it is hard to define exactly what the unwelcome
behaviour is. It is also a problem getting sufficient proof to successfully prosecute
offenders. So the committee has recommended a change of approach, considering that
the bill originally went too far in trying to clamp down on transactions between these
groups. Instead, it has recommended an amendment to the bill so that the behaviour at
issue is more effectively targeted.
That will prevent everyday transactions between, say, the society and venue staff
from triggering a potential conflict situation. For example, someone from a society
buying a meal at a bar where pokie machines happen to be located could well have been
caught by the provision in the bill as drafted. I think the committee has arrived at a
reasonable outcome. It has also introduced a longer limitation period for bringing
prosecution actions for conflict of interest offences, and that will more accurately reflect
the length of time it takes to uncover the behaviour and gather enough evidence to
mount a prosecution.
Let me touch on some other improvements to the bill that the committee has made. It
has recommended changes to give greater certainty in a few areas . One such change
concerns the ability of the secretary in screening licence applicants in terms of their
suitability to be involved in providing gambling. It is important that all relevant
information can be considered, to give a complete picture of a per son’s past behaviour.
Another change protects the ability of affected parties to seek a judicial review. The
Gambling Commission has been given the power to delay the effective date of its
decision so that a review can be sought. Another change of note con cerns licence
periods. The intention is to allow longer licences for highly compliant operators, and the
committee’s recommendations make it very clear that that will be a decision for the
Secretary for Internal Affairs to make, which will mean that there will no longer be
appeals and arguments about why everyone is not getting a longer licence.
I note that the committee’s report includes minority views on the most notable area
of change that the bill introduces. This is in the area of payments to venues t hat actually
host the machines. The committee has a couple of minority reports in that regard. New
regulations would need to be developed to replace the current system, which is agreed
by all parties to be very cumbersome and time -consuming. The minority r eports from
Labour and the Greens describe particular concerns about the favoured option, which is
a commission -based system. Their concerns, essentially, are that a commission -based
system could incentivise operators to maximise gambling in their venues. It was their
perception that venue operators could take advantage, therefore, of vulnerable patrons
rather than carrying out their duty to be responsible hosts. In response to those concerns
I note that the design of the system for the regulations is still  being developed. The aim
here is for a payment scheme to cover the cost of venues. It is not intended to provide
profits.
Of course, no system will be absolutely perfect, but I do believe a change is needed.
The current system requires a considerable amo unt of time and effort by the department
and the societies. If payments were simplified, the department could focus on other
areas like harm prevention, to ensure greater compliance by the sector. In short, I want
to give the House an assurance that the po tential concerns about a new payment system
are being taken seriously. Under the Gambling Act, when new regulations are being
proposed I am required to be satisfied that consultation has occurred with the people
likely to be substantially affected. There i s an onus on the department to ensure that all
groups are consulted before final proposals are put forward and that their views are
27 May 2015 Gambling Amendment Bill (No 3) 4099
considered. Once the new system is in place, class 4 operators will be expected to meet
their harm prevention responsibilities.
One of the purposes of the principal Act is to ensure that money from gambling
benefits the community. I believe that this sits at the very heart of what we try to
achieve in this country when it comes to the regulation of gambling. We are unique in
the world in the way we channel money from gambling back into community purposes.
It is a feature that I think we need to keep to the fore when we look at changes to our
gambling laws. Gambling is an established, legitimate form of entertainment. For the
most part it is harmless fun, but for a small few it is not fun but extremely destructive.
We need to do all we can to make gambling a safe pastime, and that is where the Act
balances the provision of gambling with the need for harm minimisation measures to be
put in place.
I am aware that some have advocated the introduction of pre -commitment
technology into our gaming machines. Although the Act already includes an ability to
do this through regulations, the evidence on pre -commitment is still unclear. The
overseas experience has been mixed. Much depends on the specific design and features
of such a system. In short, there are many unknowns. Although I accept that the use of
technology in this area has a lot of potential and could be a powerful way of
encouraging people to gamble in a way that is appropriate to their circumstances, and
there are advantages in such a system, I do not think we need to be rushing to impose
that new technology. It would create a significant cost at the expense of community
purposes. A reasonably strong, compelling case is needed for features that will work
best in the New Zealand context. I expect the Department of Internal Affairs to remain
active in monitoring research and developments in this space, including having
discussions with the Ministry of Health and the Associate Minister of Health,  who has
an interest in this issue, as well.
Finally, can I conclude by acknowledging all of those who took time to make
submissions to the select committee. It is a well-known fact that gambling issues always
prompt a range of strong views from across the community. I think the committee has
done a good job in working its way through those and presenting us with a workable
piece of legislation. As a consequence of the committee’s work, I th ink that the bill that
has now come back to the House responds to the specific concerns raised about pokie
operators. It does provide for better transparency in the sector and also some greater
controls. That, in turn, will help ensure that the very import ant objectives of the
Gambling Act are fulfilled. So I have great pleasure in commending the Gambling
Amendment Bill (No 3) to the House.

items.speaker: ADRIAN RURAWHE
items.text: Talofa lava. Malo Samoa.
Malo le soifua. It is a pleasure to speak on the Gambling Amendment Bill (No 3) in this
second reading. I want to acknowledge the 126 submitters who sent their submissions,
from problem gambling organisations to venues and societies to individuals. I want to
thank them all, because I think they contributed greatly to the amendments that have
been made to this bill, which I think have made this bill a lot better than it was at its first
reading.
The Labour Party will be supporting this b ill, but we do have some concerns. I want
to thank the Minister of Internal Affairs for addressing those very concerns that we have
in his speech, first up. There is the issue around commission payment. A number of
problem gambling organisations made submi ssions about their concerns about putting
in place a commission -based payment system. Their concerns, as the Minister said,
were around incentivising gambling so that venues would be better off with the more
money that went through those machines and, in s o doing, it would put their host
responsibilities at risk. We want to highlight that.
4100 Gambling Amendment Bill (No 3) 27 May 2015
I have heard what the Minister has said, and maybe there is room for a
Supplementary Order Paper to make sure that that happens. One of the models that
could be used in developing a commission payment system could be to place a cap on
the percentage or the total amount that any venue can gain from one particular machine.
I think that could address that issue, so I guess the challenge for this House in taking up
what the Minister has said is to make this bill even better than it is now. If we were to
put something in this bill as a Supplementary Order Paper —and I am sure that I am
bound to want to do that —it would be to make certain that the commission -based
system does not incentivise more gambling.
I have to point out that at the end of last year, in the Department of Internal Affairs
mystery shopper study, only one of the 102 venues was compliant. So that does not give
me a lot of encouragement about some of the venues a ctually being in a position at this
time to not take the incentive of a commission -based system. That is why it is really
important, I believe, that we think carefully about that and make sure that the
commission-based payment system does not incentivise gambling.
The other area that I want to pay particular attention to is harm minimisation
measures. I think that we have missed an opportunity here. I believe that at every single
opportunity when we are talking about gambling and the Gambling Amendment Bil l
(No 3) before us, we should have, and could have, taken stronger measures around
minimising the harm caused by gambling. The Minister mentioned —and it was also
raised in the minority reports —implementing a pre -commitment system. Other
countries have impl emented this very system, and I believe it is incumbent upon this
Parliament to actually make sure that we have every opportunity to implement systems
that do address the harm caused by gambling. Two of the submitters —I will not
mention them by name —on two  separate occasions spoke to the Government
Administration Committee about their experiences of the harm that they have suffered
through gambling. That was very passionate, it was very powerful, and what was very
clear to me was that a system that actually  worked around pre-commitment could have
prevented the experience that they had had to go through. So I want to thank those two
particular submitters, who told us in very raw detail about the effect that gambling had
had on their lives.
There are some good things in this bill, and that is why our party is supporting it. We
have already heard from the Minister about the suitability of key persons and the key
persons’ issues that are addressed in this bill. I want to focus on the benefits with
conditions attached. The inclusion of just one word altered the whole of clause 16 to the
satisfaction of the many, many submitters who submitted against this particular clause,
and that was the inclusion of the word “improper”. Just one word, and it changed the
whole nature of the clause. Feedback from those submitters indicated that the inclusion
of that word has addressed their issues, because their issues were about things like being
able to pay their staff because the clause had some unintended consequences that mea nt
that, as key persons, they would not be able to walk into the pub of another society’s
venue and order their dinner and a drink without breaking this law. So that is a proper
thing for them to be able to do. The intention of the clause was to eliminate improper
actions. So that was something that collectively, as a select committee, we were able to
address.
There were a number of submissions around the definition of a “relative”, and that
issue, also, was addressed. It was narrowed down to parents, son,  daughter, spouse, or
partner rather than the wider whānau. Some of us have got really big whānau, which
would have meant that we and the rest of our family would all be unable to carry out a
normal transaction if we were a key person. Also, we extended th e limitations from 2
years to 5 years because there were indications that cases had been advised through the
27 May 2015 Gambling Amendment Bill (No 3) 4101
proper authorities but they were out of time. Two years seemed to be too short, and so
that has now been extended to 5 years. Also, there are some specific clauses that the
New Zealand Racing Board needed to be addressed, and those amendments address
those issues to an extent that I understand that it is satisfied. I am not sure whether all its
members are happy, but they are certainly satisfied with  the amendments that have been
made.
So, finally, I just want to again thank the submitters and also acknowledge the
members of the Government Administration Committee for the work that has been
done. I also acknowledge the Minister again for acknowledgin g those key issues and
concerns we have with this bill. Nō reira, tēnā tātou.

items.speaker: SARAH DOWIE
items.text: Talofa lava. Greetings, Mr Deputy
Speaker, and thank you for allowing me to take this call on the Gambling Amendment
Bill (No 3). The fact that it is No. 3 suggests something. It is a series of technical bills
off the back of a parent Act, the Gambling Ac t 2003, which was reform legislation to
minimise harm in the industry of gambling.
This bill, I believe, is an example of the MMP environment at work. It is the
Government working with its coalition partners —in particular the Hon Peter Dunne,
who has shepherded this bill through the House, and the Māori Party. But I also want to
take this time to thank the Government Administration Committee. We often hear that it
is a high-powered select committee that hears some very important bills. I want to thank
the committee members for their collegial spirit in panel beating this bill into shape.
I think it is worth noting that even though this is an amendment bill and it is technical
in nature, gambling—and this is certainly something I have learnt from other subm itters
whom we heard in Wellington and Auckland —affects all New Zealanders, whether
directly or indirectly, at some point in their lives. That is why I think these bills should
not be taken for granted. They do affect us and they are important when we are
finessing this industry to minimise harm. This bill is, in particular, in respect of class 4
pokie machines, and they are pokies that are held off site from casinos. We are trying to
make the industry more transparent and, of course, at the end of the day,  a better
industry.
We heard from 126 submitters and, as I said before, we heard them in Wellington
and Auckland. Most of those submitters were in support of, had conditional support for,
or had a mixed view on the mooted draft bill. There were some submi tters not in
support of the bill because, as we heard from our counterparts, they believed that the bill
did not go far enough in respect of some of the harm minimisation measures. I think that
their intent is admirable and I certainly listened carefully t o what they were saying, but
at the end of the day I believe that that went beyond the ambit of what this bill was
considering. But it was certainly educational for me to hear those submissions, and I
take their wisdom on board.
In respect of what this bi ll is trying to achieve, in the first instance  it is trying to
achieve transparency around grant decision -making. This bill introduces new
requirements for publicising societies’ grants: the details as to what has been applied
for, what is received, the pu rpose, and what has been granted. It also provides that this
information is detailed and sent through to the Department of Internal Affairs, so as to
achieve a balance and check on that society and so that the public can scrutinise that
society and what it  is providing —the funds that it is sending back to the community
from where, essentially, they had been lost.
The bill also requires any real conflicts of interest between societies that collect the
money from gambling class 4 pokies and those grant recip ients to be published, again
adding to the transparency and the accountability in the community as to how those
funds have been applied. Regulations are to be developed later, and they will set out the
4102 Gambling Amendment Bill (No 3) 27 May 2015
detail as to how all of this will be achieved, so it may well be that general information is
published in a local newspaper, but then more detailed information is published online.
Regardless of the mix of that, the information will be readily available, and, hence, that
adds to the accountability.
The secon d theme of this bill is to increase transparency around the operations of
societies themselves. Under regulations, the publishing of financial statements and the
form in which they are published by societies will be mandated, highlighting the
efficiency of  the operation itself. So, again, we are running with the theme of
transparency and are trying to tidy up the industry and filter funds back into the
community in which they were lost.
