The third theme I want to touch on is simplifying compliance costs in venue
payments. We have heard from members opposite that they believe that a commission -
based system will incentivise gambling societies to increase the number of machines or
to be irresponsible hosts. They also oppose rewarding societies that perform well  with
longer licences at the discretion of the Department of Internal Affairs. On this side of
the House we do not believe that that view has foundation. There is no evidence to
suggest that moving to a commission -based system will incentivise gambling, an d the
design of any new payment system will be detailed in regulations. As we are advised,
the department will run a full consultative process in respect of that, and I think that that
consultative process is extremely important for the purpose of giving m ore thought to
what exactly the best cost recovery basis is to keep compliance costs down and, again,
to keep things simple. Furthermore, the grant of longer licences to societies that perform
well does not equate with an abuse because those licences will be at the discretion of the
regulator, which will take into account the suitability of the applicant and past
performance.
It would not be appropriate for me to end this speech without some examples of
some responsible class 4 operators that are performing well and that, of course, leads me
back to my own electorate, Invercargill, and the Invercargill Licensing Trust. It is
responsible for sponsoring our community in a fantastic way. It has allocated total
grants of $49.57 million—

items.speaker: Paul Foster-Bell
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: SARAH DOWIE
items.text: —total grants of $49.57 million—during the 2008 to 2013 period,
which is an average of $9.92 million per year. It has delivered some really big -ticket
items like our stadium, ILT Stadium Southland, and the velodrome, which is
responsible for some really fantastic projects. The stadium is integral, obviously, to our
community. The weather is not always great. Of course, I keep waxing on that our
people are so positive we do not need weather to keep us positiv e, but we can go
indoors and use our stadium and enjoy that. But the trust has also delivered electronic
whiteboards in schools. It has built learners’ pools for swimming, and even contributed
to tertiary scholarships. In saying that, it has granted more t han 170 scholarships to
individual Invercargill students, locally and abroad. Each student receives $2,000 for 3
years and the total paid in 2012 and 2013 was $374,000 -odd. This is an example of a
society working hard for the community. It can be done well  and I believe that these
measures in this bill will uplift the industry, make it more transparent, and minimise
harm, as the 2003 Act set out to do. So with that I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: I would like to begin by requesting an
extension of time for the member who has just resumed her seat, Sarah Dowie —maybe
for another 3 minutes. Seriously, can I begin my contribution by saying talofa lava,
malo le soifua, as part of my contribution to the celebration of the wonderful Samoan
language this week. The week to celebrate Samoan language immediately follows New
Zealand Sign Language Week, which we had last week. I am calling on the member
27 May 2015 Gambling Amendment Bill (No 3) 4103
Ron Mark to gi ve as much highlighting to the Samoan language as he did to New
Zealand Sign Language Week last week, but perhaps in a more gentle way. But the
publicity we got for that language was great.
This is a pretty momentous occasion tonight. I think that there have been few times
since 2008 that we have not had on the Order Paper a gambling bill of some description,
so I am delighted to be speaking to the Gambling Amendment Bill (No 3). The other
significance of this legislation, as other members have indicated —the Minister who
spoke, the member from Invercargill, and my colleague who is responsible for gambling
issues for Labour, Adrian Rurawhe —is that with a couple of policy points as
exceptions, this bill has been supported by the Government Administration Committee
and most of the submitters. The submitters came to our committee and said: “We
support this bill except for one area, and it does not go far enough in another.” That was
the basis of th e contribution of some really substantial submissions, and I have to say
also that there were some submissions that were very moving.
It is a huge difference to be debating a bill that has got agreement as opposed to that
shonky Skycity deal that Minister  Joyce brought to this House, where we saw Skycity
getting more pokies in return for a convention centre. In 2011, when Skycity booted out
all the competition, we were told would get a convention centre that could
accommodate up to 5,000 people. We will ha ve a convention centre that can take fewer
than 3,000. Is that an international convention centre? I do not think so.
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 10 p.m.

WEDNESDAY, 27 MAY 2015 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
POINTS OF ORDER 
Chamber, Lobbies, and Galleries—Audio System 
Hon PETER DUNNE (Leader —United Future) : I raise a point of order, Mr 
Speaker. I realise that both you and the Clerk are speaking pretty softly at the moment, 
but there may be some problem with the amplification system. It is a little hard to hear 
in this quadrant of the House. 
Mr SPEAKER : We will have someone look at the mikes immediately. In the 
meantime, if the mikes are not working, it would be helpful if members would keep 
their interjections to a minimum level. 
ORAL QUESTIONS  
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Social Development—Providers 
1. DARROCH BALL (NZ First)  to the Minister for Social Development : Does 
she agree with the Minister of Finance when he said of the delivery of social services, 
“There is no evidence at all that contracting out, as the member calls it, will reduce 
service provision.”? 
Hon ANNE TOLLEY (Minister for Social Development): Yes. 
Darroch Ball : In her Government’s statements indicating a  shift in social service 
provision to a voucher system, is the Minister aware that a 2009 evaluation on a 
voucher system in Australia, the Netherlands, and the USA found that quality and 
supply to rural and provincial communities were reduced significantly, aligning with the 
concerns in the Productivity Commission’s recent report; if so, how is she going to 
address this? 
Hon ANNE TOLLEY: I have made no such statement. 
Darroch Ball: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The question was— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! [Interruption] Order! I am going to ask the member to repeat 
the question. The question as I understood it was more whether the Minister was aware 
of something. It is difficult to hear; the mikes are not working. So I invite the member to 
ask his question again. 
Darroch Ball : In her Government’s statements indicating a shift in social service 
provision to a voucher system, is the Minister aware that a 2009 evaluation on a 
voucher system in Australia , the Netherlands, and the USA found that quality and 
supply to rural and provincial communities was reduced significantly, aligning with the 
concerns in the Productivity Commission’s recent report; if so, how is she going to 
address this? 
Hon ANNE TOLLEY: The Government has made no such statements.  
Darroch Ball: Is the Minister aware that under her Government’s current investment 
approach for the delivery of social services a regular flow of regional closures has 
included services to Veterans Affairs New Zealand and to youth services provided by 
the Salvation Army, which have shut down in Kaikohe, Matamata, Wairoa, 
Waipukurau, Cambridge, Ngāruawāhia, and Blenheim? 
Hon ANNE TOLLEY : This Government has made no decisions on an investment 
strategy. 
4022 Oral Questions  27 May 2015 
 
Darroch Ball: That is interesting. How can she justify letting Relationships Aotearoa 
close its doors on 7,000 clients —operating under her Government’s failing investment 
approach to social services—and now leaving a huge gap in domestic violence expertise 
and expertise on working with Māori whānau, with nothing to replace it? 
Hon ANNE TOLLEY: None of those assertions are correct. The Ministry of Social 
Development has worke d very hard with Relationships Aotearoa over a number of 
years. In fact, the figures I produced in this House last week showed that Ministry of 
Social Development funding had in fact increased by more than a Consumers Price 
Index adjustment. However, no Go vernment, whatever the colour —whatever the 
colour—can underwrite with taxpayers ’ money an organisation that is not financially 
viable. Unfortunately, Relationships Aotearoa is not solvent. Moreover, it was not 
delivering. It was not actually delivering the  services it was paid for. It made the 
decision to close. This Government is working with a number of service providers to 
make sure that those clients of Relationships Aotearoa are well looked after.  
Darroch Ball: Can she reassure New Zealanders in our regions that social service 
provision will not continue to decrease, with providers shutting down under her 
Government’s investment approach, or be under threat of decreased supply and quality 
by the new voucher system; and how will she replace the vital services already lost?  
Hon ANNE TOLLEY : What I can say from this Government is that we are 
absolutely determined to make sure that every dollar of taxpayers’ money that is 
invested in our communities actually gets some results. That is what we want. We want 
to change people’s lives for the better and we want to use that $313 million that the 
Ministry of Social Development alone spends in our communities supporting the social 
sector to make a difference in people’s lives.  
Housing, Auckland—Housing Developments on Crown Land 
2. ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he 
have confidence in the Ministe r for Building and Housing, given that the Minister is 
considering building houses in Auckland on the site of an electrical substation? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister) : Yes, and I can ass ure the member that no 
houses will be built on a substation. But I do agree with this comment supporting the 
Government’s policy to free up Crown -owned land for new housing: “it is a no brainer 
to develop vacant government land in Auckland.” That, of cours e, was from Phil 
Twyford after the Budget was so well received by Labour, I thought, on Thursday. I 
thank Labour for the support.  
Andrew Little : Did anyone in his Government bother to check with Transpower 
about why it has a buffer of land  around its substation and high -voltage power pylons 
before Nick Smith said he can jam some houses in there? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: I may be incorrect, but I do not actually think it was Dr Smith 
who raised that particular piece of land in ques tion—I think it was Mr Twyford. 
Actually, as we can see in this photograph, there is lots of land —and oh! What are 
those? They are houses. So I guess if you are building there— 
Hon Gerry Brownlee: Are they next door? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Yes, they are right next door. They are just there, you see? If 
you can build them there, I guess you can build them on the other side, I suppose. 
[Interruption]  
Mr SPEAKER: Order! It is hard enough to conduct question time today when the 
microphones are not working. I have called for silence to assist Andrew Little with his 
supplementary question.  
Andrew Little: Has he been advised that an explosion and fir e at the substation in 
question cut power to much of west Auckland, with one nearby resident saying: “there 
27 May 2015 Oral Questions  4023 
 
was a really loud arcing sound, and a second after that there was a huge explosion.”? Do 
Bill English’s reassuring words that “I presume it’s not al ways exploding.” relate to the 
substation or to Nick Smith’s portfolio? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I am sure Mr English is right. I am sure it is not always 
exploding. Otherwise all of the neighbours here in this photo would be concerned. But 
let u s just get something in perspective here. What the Minister has said is that he 
thinks—and that is the best advice I have had —there will be around about 430 hectares 
of land. Is that a shock? Well, no, because the Government actually owns 150,000 
hectares of Crown land in Auckland, and I am sure we will eke 430 out from all of that. 
Andrew Little: Can he categorically deny that the Māngere Lawn Cemetery is on 
any of the lists, including the initial list, of sites identified by the Government  as 
residential land that it could build houses on? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I do not have the list from the Minister, but I am happy to 
accept it is quite a good idea to build houses on Crown land. Why do I think that is a 
good idea? I know, bec ause in 2008 Helen Clark actually announced it. And, believe or 
not, the programme, Home Ownership on the Public Estate, was called “HOPE”. Back 
then Labour Party members had hope for housing in Auckland. Now they have hope 
that the Labour Party will just survive. [Interruption] 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! When I am on my feet members will be quiet. 
Andrew Little: How can anyone trust Nick Smith’s denials about his list when that 
Minister flatly denied any substations on his land on Monda y, only to discover a 
substation on his land on Tuesday? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: The member is just making it up. There is a thorough process 
that the Minister is going through to identify what is the best estimate from the Ministry 
of Business, Innovation and Employment of about 430 hectares out of 150,000. Here is 
a bit of logic for you. If it is such a hard idea to identify 430 hectares, answer this 
question: how on earth was Labour going to build 100,000 houses on Crown land? Oh, 
that is right. If it is Labour’s idea— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! The question has been answered.  
Andrew Little: Does he agree with Nick Smith’s assessment of his 500 hectares for 
affordable housing in Auckland that any house sold, no matter the p rice, “will be 
affordable to somebody”; if not, how on earth can he justify leaving him in charge of 
affordable housing? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : By definition, that is correct. [ Interruption] Well, it is just 
technically correct. But the aim of what we are going to do on this approximate 430 
hectares of land is to do what we did in Weymouth and other places. I go back to the 
point I was making earlier. If Labour believes it could build 100,000 houses on Crown 
land, surely it must be possible for National in Government to build a smaller subset 
than that. We cannot both be right or wrong in this particular instance. Either the land is 
there or not, and it is there. 
Andrew Little: Will he guarantee to every New Zealander that the hou ses built on 
the Crown land that he and his Minister are talking about will all be affordable houses 
for Aucklanders? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : The member has just defeated his own question because he 
said—by definition every house is affordable to somebody. 
Andrew Little: Given that his housing announcement can now be summarised as a 
speculator tax that will be lucky to catch a thousand speculators a year, requirements on 
foreign buyers that are so weak they are a joke, and the building of unaffordable houses 
among Auckland’s power plants and gravestones, when will he admit that he and his 
Government have no answers to Auckland’s housing crisis? 
4024 Oral Questions  27 May 2015 
 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I can see where the “live in hope” policy came from. Let us 
just get a few facts on the table. House prices doubled under Labour and went up faster 
in Auckland than they have under National. Secondly, if the member thinks it is soft, 
when it comes to foreigners, actually having to give us an Inland Rev enue Department 
number, to have a New Zealand bank account, and to actually have any profits withheld 
for tax, I would hate to think what he thinks difficult is. If you look at the activity 
happening in Auckland under a National -led Government and the poli cies that we have 
adopted, Aucklanders can see real progress. What they saw under Labour was no 
progress. 
Budget 2015—Economic Programme 
3. JACQUI DEAN (National —Waitaki) to the Minister of Finance : Ho w does 
Budget 2015 continue the Government’s plan to manage spending and start paying 
down debt? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associate Minister of Finance): on behalf of the Minister 
of Finance: Spending is firmly under control. Core Crown expenses have fallen from 
34.1 percent of GDP in 2008 -09 and are expected to drop to 30 percent next year. We 
have stuck to a $1 billion allowance in Budget 2015, but we have been able to spend 
$1.5 billion per year on new initiatives because we have identified around half a billion 
dollars of savings in reprioritisation each year. This spending restraint means that we 
have come from an $18.4 billion deficit 4 years ago to seeing steadily rising sur pluses 
into the future. In line with our long -term fiscal target, net debt is now expected to fall 
to 19.7 percent of GDP in 2020-21. 
Jacqui Dean : What initiatives are included in Budget 2015 to support more 
economic growth and jobs? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : Constrained Government spending is helping to keep 
interest rates lower for longer, and that makes it easier for businesses to invest and to 
hire more staff. As part of the Business Growth Agenda, Budget 2015 also invests in a 
range of initiatives that contribute to better infrastructure, more innovation, and lower 
costs for business. These include around half a billion dollars of further ACC levy 
reductions, on top of the $1.5 billion already in place, $86 million for targeted increases 
in university tuition rates, $100 million from the Future Investment Fund for Lincoln 
University to rebuild its science facilities; $80 million for research and development 
growth grants; and $210 million from the Future Investment Fund to invest  in the 
national rail network. 
Jacqui Dean: What are Treasury’s latest expectations for job and wage growth for 
New Zealand families? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : This Government is working very hard to support higher 
wages for Kiwi families. Treasury’s Budget forecasts show that there are 194,000 extra 
jobs in the economy since late 2010, and another 150,000 jobs are expected by 2019. 
Unemployment is expected to fall below 5 percent in 2016. Average annual wages have 
increased by $5,700 in the last 4 years and are forecast to rise to around $63,000 a year 
in 4 years’ time, and that is an increase of a further $7,000. If we take the 8 -year period 
as a whole, the average wage is expected to go up almost $13,000, or over 25 percent, 
over that period, compared with inflation of less than 14 percent over the same time. So 
the Business Growth Agenda is supporting a growing economy that is working for New 
Zealanders. 
Jacqui Dean: What other measures are being progressed to support further growth in 
the regions? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : Almost all of the initiatives announced in the Budget will 
support the regions, from increased health and education spending to higher welfare 
27 May 2015 Oral Questions  4025 
 
payments for families and reductions in ACC levies. In addition, Budget 2015 also 
provides up to $25 million to support the establishment of new privately led regional 
research institutes to undertake scientific research in the regions, $210 million to extend 
the roll-out of ultra -fast broadband into smaller regional towns, and an additional $150 
million from the telecommunications development levy, which will go into rural 
broadband and filling mobile black spots. The first tranche of the $212 million regional 
highway package will be $97 mill ion, and up to $52 million will be provided to replace 
the Waitangi wharf on the Chatham Islands.  
Rt Hon Winston Peters: If there is a plan to start paying down debt, what is the total 
debt attributable to the Crown, as opposed to core Crown debt? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: I do not have that figure in front of me for the member, but 
if he is happy to put it down in writing, then I am more than happy to give an answer to 
it. 
Local Government—Māori Representation 
4. MARAMA FOX (Co -Leader—Māori Party)  to the Minister of Local 
Government: What advice has she received through report back from officials in 
March this year about Māori participation in local governm ent processes, and what 
consideration, if any, has been given by her as a result of that advice? 
Hon PAULA BENNETT (Minister of Local Government): I have not yet received 
the advice that the member is referring to, because officials are taking more time to 
work on it than originally thought. What I would say to the member, though, is that I am 
very supportive of Māori representation within local councils, and I certainly s upport 
that and would like to see that increasing. For example, here in the House, over 20 
percent of the members of Parliament are Māori. However, I think it is quite interesting 
to point out that 72 percent of our Māori MPs are in general seats or are fr om the list, 
and, actually, 28 percent are from Māori seats. We can see the skew that is going 
towards people being selected and put forward in general seats, and that is what I would 
like to see happening on local councils. 
Marama Fox : Althou gh we celebrate the Te Arawa partnership proposal and the 
decision that was made in Rotorua, what is the Minister prepared to do to remove unfair 
provisions in current legislation that allow for the establishment of Māori wards on local 
councils to be over turned by referendum, given this discriminatory legislation applies 
only to Māori representation, as witnessed by the result in New Plymouth?

my time today in this call talking about some of the initiatives that this Government is 
taking as a result of the Budget this year in the areas my portfolio responsibil ities:

warrant on a lot of these unwelcome eco -invaders. Unless we can do that the 2 percent 
decline in kiwi numbers on our mainland will continue to grow at an alarming rate, and 
in our grandchildren’s time there will be no more kiwi on the mai nland. My aim in life 
is to reverse that decline, and I intend to spend that $11.2 million on reversing that 
decline so that there is a 2 percent increase in kiwi numbers. This is a tall order.  
In addition to pest and predator control, we are going to be working with a group that 
has been around in New Zealand doing great work saving kiwis, encouraging breeding 
programmes, for more than 20 years, and I am referring to Kiwis for Kiwi. I am going 
to be joining forces with them and encouraging them to make as  an umbrella movement 
a sort of a bringing together of all of the groups that have been working independently 
to save our kiwi. Kiwis for Kiwi will effectively deliver to the community programmes 
to allocate the money, and to really pull together the progr ammes in conjunction with 
the Department of Conservation, and I think that is the way ahead.  
We have had some successes in the past year or so with helping our native birds 
come back from the brink of extinction. Battle for our Birds has been enormously 
successful. It is in fact the largest ever predator programme in New Zealand’s history, 
and it covered some 600,000 hectares of land. We were aiming to save about 12 of our

and I am very pleased to be able to report that the 1080 aerial drops, which were at the

heart of that particular programme, have been very successful. We have done some

Next week is Arbor Day, and I intend to be in the electorate of my colleague and 
friend Scott Simpson. In Coromandel their beaches are not quite as good as ours on the 
North Shore but, certainly, they have some remarkable natural attributes, so I am going 
to be talking with him about some of the kauri dieback measures. We have spent, as 
many of you are well aware, more than $21.5 million. That was allocated in the la st 
Budget; we have not yet spent it. I felt that the case for kauri dieback and the need to 
fight it in the last Budget was so urgent that we have brought forward the time when we 
can start spending that money, and we have a designated team now who will be  
focusing on kauri dieback, and I will be making further announcements on this in the 
Coromandel next week. But, really, when you look at the level of groundwork that 
needs to be done, it is extensive. The key thing about kauri dieback is that it spreads 
through foot traffic. It spreads through soil particles being caught up on the hooves or 
paws of animals, as well as on human beings’ boots, and then the spores of the soil -
borne pathogen are transferred from places —including by pigs, goats, and a number of  
other creatures.  
So we are being very careful to ensure that what we can do in terms of 
mechanisms—advancing education, really. A lot of people do not really understand how 
it is spread, so we are putting up different signage in different languages. We are putting 
up more than 500 extra hygiene stations, which will enable people to clean their boots. 
We will also be ensuring that boardwalks are built. So that money is going to be well -
spent in the next few years. We are set to begin this month with a deta iled data analysis, 
including the mapping of tracks and the cost estimates for the upgrades. We also need to 
prioritise the tracks that need to be either closed or contained in some way. Track 
closures are not something we do readily and easily but sometim es it is the only way to 
stop the spread of the disease, particularly in the winter months, because when there is 
mud it sticks to boots and so forth and is more readily spread. So our boardwalk 
specifications are based on field trials of drainage specific ations to ensure the natural 
flow of water has been improved, and those are the sorts of things we have been 
planning to do and are now rolling out.  
We cannot, of course, do any of this alone. No one Government department, even if 
it is as good as the Dep artment of Conservation, can do all of this by itself, so we need 
partnerships and collaboration. I am pleased to be able to say that regional councils 
collectively are aiming to commit more than $700,000 per year towards the research

ALASTAIR SCOTT (National —Wairarapa): Talofa lava, Mr Speaker. Over the 
last week or so Opposition members have criticised us for our projected surplus 
forecasts. They say that they are not big enough. Well, the question is:  what would they 
do differently? We know that a surplus comes from two parts: the income side and the 
expenditure side. We know that the revenue side has taken a hit because of lower dairy 
payouts and the lower interest -rate environment that we find oursel ves in —all these 
things affect the revenue side and are out of our control. So to increase our surplus, we 
have to look at the cost side: the expense side. We have to spend less. So the question to 
the Opposition members is: what would they have done? What  would they have cut to 
get a larger surplus today, tomorrow, and in the future? 
Would they have cancelled free GP visits for under -13-year-olds? I do not think so. I 
do not think they could. Would they have cancelled the increase in paid parental leave 
that we put in place? Would they have cancelled the $11 million of funding available 
for the kiwi breeding programme, I ask the Minister of Conservation? Would they have 
cut the funding for kauri dieback? Would they have reduced expenditure in health, 
which would have seen waiting lists grow, cancer treatment patients go back to 
Australia, and queues for elective surgery? These are the consequences of cutting 
expenditure, which is the only thing you can do if you want to increase your surpluses. 
Would they ha ve cut the rheumatic fever investment that this Government has made? 
Would they have taken away the $359 million that we are investing in schoolteachers, 
to encourage and incentivise teachers to do better for our kids? Maybe they would claw 
back the $790 m illion that we have just announced for the most needy —that is, the 
children in beneficiary households. 
These are the sorts of things that you have to do if the surplus is the only thing that 
you are concerned about. But we are not because we know that it i s much more 
important to continue the spending and the investment in those things that I have just 
mentioned. You know where Labour is going to get the money from? It is going to go 
for the superannuitants. It is going for the superannuitants. There are tw o or three things 
that it could do. It could raise the age of entitlement, which we have said we would not 
do. Maybe it could means test superannuation, which we have said we would not do. Or 
maybe it can simply reduce the amount, which we have said we would not do. 
This Budget focuses on those who are in need the most: the children of beneficiary 
families. This Budget is a good Budget. This Budget is fiscally responsible. This Budget 
has cut the kick -start programme, which is a programme that is not about focusing on 
the most needy. We know that the $1,000 per person was going only to middle and 
higher-income families. It was not targeted at beneficiaries and it was not targeted at 
lower-income families, which is why we are cutting that back. There are 2.5 million 
people involved in that programme. It is working. I support this Budget. Thank you.

DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First): New Zealand has developed a housing crisis since 
the National Government took office in 2008. It has developed it since then. It has been 
like the frog in the saucepan, waiting for the heat to increase without noticing it until the 
pot boils over. The crisis during that time has become chronic and this Government has 
done little or nothing about it. In fact, this Government has had a worse record in 
meeting housing demand than any other Government in living history. In the last 6 
years house prices have gone through the roof in Auckland, and nobody over there 
could deny it. Houses are now unaffordable to most homebuyers, and very little is being 
done to help. We have had some action taken on access to KiwiSaver, at the price, 
though, of compromising retirement savings. Too many people do not have access to 
enough money in a KiwiSaver account to make any difference. The causes of the crisis 
have not been addressed. Few Kiwis have left for Australia, that is true, and that has led 
4046 Budget Debate 27 May 2015 
 
to an increase in demand, but so has relatively uncontrolled immigration —56,000 in the 
last year. That has led to a very significant increase in demand for housing, and the 
Government has done nothing at all about that. According to the Bank of New Zealand, 
11 percent of homes are sold to foreign buyers in Auckland —11 percent —and the 
Government has done virtually nothing about that.  
Even this Government cannot deny the problem now. It is belatedly bolstering tax 
rules on residential property, which is something that should have  been done years and 
year ago. There is no need at all for a capital gains tax if income tax is broad enough. 
No action has been taken on that either. The Government is not doing enough about 
foreign buyers. Requiring overseas buyers to have a New Zealand tax number is not 
nearly enough. Determined buyers from overseas will not be deterred by that at all. The 
brightline test for all buyers selling within 2 years is much too easily avoided and will 
have little effect. Two years is too short. Although special  housing areas and accords 
with councils will help, the real issue has been the Government’s unwillingness to 
invest directly in housing itself. New Zealand First’s policy is for the Government to 
buy and develop land for housing, and to use existing Crown  land for the same purpose, 
and for the Government to sell directly smaller sections, thereby making modest homes 
more available to more people, with easy repayments over 25 years at a low interest 
rate.  
The Government has taken a leaf out of New Zealand First’s book with its use of 
Crown land, but only 400 hectares of it —a very small portion. It is only 400 hectares 
and only as a last -minute effort in the Budget to try to look a little bit better. It is very 
cosmetic. Even that land is ill -defined. We do not really know exactly what land the 
Government has got in mind, and not all of it, of course, will be suitable. Only $52 
million has been allowed for in the Budget to develop that land, and that seems very 
light. There is also very little information about how all that will work. The Government 
should take another leaf out of New Zealand First’s policy, which requires a permanent 
special agency to buy and develop land for residential housing.  
The Government has had an even worse record in social housing.  The average rental 
is now $379 a week. Since 2008 the increase under National has been $65 a week or 20 
percent, and 11.7 percent above the Consumers Price Index. That is huge. People cannot 
avoid that. In Auckland people typically have to pay 50 percent of their take -home 
income in rent, and that is crippling. In Christchurch people often have to pay 
something like $1,000 a week or more for an ordinary three -bedroom house. It is a very 
significant problem in the major cities. The Government’s social housi ng measures will 
not help to increase rental housing stock. Those measures are designed to minimise the 
role of the State and to emasculate Housing New Zealand. This Government is actually 
abdicating its responsibility for social housing by contracting it out to non-governmental 
organisations and private providers. Government members say there will be flexible 
purchasing, as described in the Government’s recent legislation, allowing what they call 
tailored agreements, dictated in detail by Ministers, who wi ll be biased, of course. That 
is to try to give certainty to providers so that they can go out and borrow money and 
build homes. But are they really capable of doing this job? We really will not know 
until it happens —until the worst happens, perhaps. But H ousing New Zealand, of 
course, could do all that, and used to do all that much faster and much better. So what is 
the point of this exercise of farming it out to non-governmental organisations?  
The whole thrust of the Government’s housing programme is to suppress demand for 
State rentals, to do little for first -home buyers, and it simply does not adequately 
address the housing crisis at all.

Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM (Green): Mr Assistant Speaker, a split call? 
The ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Hon Trevor Mallard): A 5-minute call. 
Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM: Yes. As a number of my colleagues have already noted, 
the 2015 Budget statement said virtually nothing about the biggest economic issue 
facing this country—that is, climate change. The Budget revealed new policy, of course, 
on a variety of household issues. They are important issues, especially to those directly 
affected, but they are not the overarching macroeconomic issues that will at the global 
level—and, therefore, at the national level —overwhelm e verybody if they are not 
properly addressed.  
The Minister of Finance is tinkering at the margin with his seventh Budget. It is like 
the captain of a ship transferring his passengers into a dingy with an outboard motor. 
Both are heading into the hurricane ahead. The captain is saying: “Not to worry, we 
have just enough freeboard to stay afloat.” He is saying this even as the sea is getting 
bigger. That hurricane is climate change —literally hurricanes, storms, and floods that 
are already occurring.  
Why is e xtreme weather relevant to New Zealand’s Budget? It is because the stress 
on the planet’s resources through global population increase and burgeoning economic 
activity per person is unsustainable. We are incurring today a global ecological 
overshoot of 50 percent. Although New Zealand is rare in having a national ecological 
surplus, we are negatively affected, including our fiscal outlook, by the unsustainable 
and worsening global economy. That is the reason the Minister is failing, even though 
he is widely seen as a successful economic steward.  
The most important global meeting to date occurs in December. It is the 21 st annual 
United Nations Climate Change Conference in Paris. It is the equivalent of the failed 
conference in Copenhagen in 2009, but it is m ore important because we have lost 6 
critical years, yet there is not a word on this in the Budget.  
The world has lost ground. No longer are the negotiators engaged in global planning. 
Top-down is out; bottom -up is in. Binding commitments are out; volunta ry 
contributions are in. We going to tame dangerous climate change, you understand, 
through voluntary contributions by 194 competing States jealous of their national 
sovereignty. God help us, for we know not what we do.  
That voluntary contribution is labe lled in the latest jargon “INDC”, or intended 
nationally determined contribution. It is “nationally determined”, not “globally 
determined”; it is “intended”, not “committed”, and the jargon is sanitised to the point 
of stupefaction. Global warming above 4 degrees, which is labelled by international 
organisations as catastrophic, is described by this Government as having “substantial 
environmental, economic and human impacts”. God help us.  
New Zealand is lumbering its way towards its intended nationally det ermined 
contribution. It has held public consultations throughout the country. The Minister for 
Climate Change Issues is conspicuously absent. He does not care; his mind has moved 
on. He will, none the less, announce the intended nationally determined cont ribution 
within a few months. It will be insufficient —probably between 10 and 20 percent. He 
will pepper it with conditions and irrelevancies. He will imply that he is in possession of 
complex and arcane knowledge that accords superior insight.  
The Green Party has already said that the intended nationally determined 
contribution must be 40 -plus percent. That would bring New Zealand’s net emissions 
down from 67 megatonnes today to 40 megatonnes in 2030. That is consistent with the 
Green Party policy of achieving climate neutrality by 2050. Is getting to 40 megatonnes 
4052 Budget Debate 27 May 2015 
 
feasible? Yes, it is. As far as can be determined, we could do at least that, and we are 
talking about domestic abatement alone. In fact, it is possible that we could go further. 
What might be N ew Zealand’s maximum abatement potential, assuming all policy 
signals are optimal and there is sufficient political will? The experts will differ, but the 
range could be anything from 40 megatonnes down to perhaps 20. So let us have the 
debate over what ca n be done —a genuine public debate, not a trite, ministerial 
sermon—and let us then have a genuine, cross-party political debate.  
My final point is that that is simply our domestic abatement. If we are talking about 
doing our fair share in the global effor t to ensure a 2 degrees Celsius outcome, New 
Zealand’s national responsibility target goes far, far beyond that.

HEALTH (PROTECTION) AMENDMENT BILL 
Second Reading 
Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN (Minister of Health) : I move, That the Health 
(Protection) Amendment Bill be now read a second time . I would like to thank the 
Health Committee for its work on this bill. The committee received 71 submissions and 
heard 22 oral submissions. 
Of course, good health is hugely important to New Zealanders. I think when you 
look at it, it would be the No. 1 priority for people across the nation. That is why  I am 
very pleased that this bill supports the Government’s unwavering commitment to good 
public health, as reflected in the recent Budget whereby health received over $400 
million of new funding. Of course, there were a number of excellent new initiatives  
there that are supporting working families in New Zealand in terms of their health. But 
it was a health Budget for all New Zealanders. 
Anyway, this particular bill will amend the Health Act 1956. Back in October 2013 
the Government decided to improve the range of measures in the Health Act in two 
specific areas: measures to protect the public from the risk of the spread of some 
infectious diseases and, in the case of people under 18 years of age, measures to protect 
them from the harm associated with artif icial UV tanning. The bill will protect people 
from these preventable harms, and it will do so through measures that are proportionate 
to the risks that are faced. 
Unfortunately, New Zealand has very high levels of sexually transmitted diseases. 
This impacts heavily on individuals, families, relationships, and communities. Sexually 
transmitted infections have a variety of complications including chronic pain, infertility, 
neonatal morbidity, and genital -tract cancer. The bill adds new provisions for the 
surveillance and management of infectious diseases. These measures will improve the 
availability of information on certain conditions, provide for more effective 
management of behaviours that put others at risk of infection, and strengthen legislative 
provisions for contact tracing. The bill strengthens the principles applying to medical 
officers of health and the courts in exercising disease management powers. People 
exercising powers will be required to take into account any known special 
4074 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 27 May 2015 
 
circumstances or vu lnerabilities of the individual. These might be due to youth, 
disability, incapacity, or other circumstances. 
The bill also requires that measures are proportionate to the public health risk that 
they pose. The principles also encourage individuals to take  responsibility for their own 
health. Currently, sexually transmitted infectious diseases, with the exception of AIDS, 
are not notifiable by medical practitioners and laboratories in New Zealand. The bill 
makes HIV, gonorrhoea, and syphilis notifiable on a  non-identified basis, along with 
AIDS. The notifying information needs to be sufficient to enable different kinds of 
public health interventions while complying with privacy safeguards. Submitters said 
that clause 5 and clause 6 went too far in restrictin g effective monitoring of serious 
sexually transmitted infections in favour of privacy. This is because the list of 
identifying information that should not be disclosed with disease notifications included 
sex, date of birth, and National Health Index numbe r. The reported -back bill requires 
notification of these matters, while protecting the individual’s identity from being 
disclosed in the first instance. 
Submitters were also concerned about potentially coercive actions by officers, such 
as contacting a you ng person’s employer or school and asking for details about friends 
and associates. Reluctance to disclose information or to be diagnosed or treated could 
arise from fear of the consequences as a result. However, that information may be 
absolutely vital in  identifying those who may be at risk, and to prevent the further 
spread of disease. The bill says that information requested and provided under new Part 
3A will not be used or disclosed for any purpose other than the management of 
infectious diseases. Con tact tracing is a valuable public health tool in preventing and 
managing infectious disease outbreaks, particularly diseases with a rapid onset such as 
meningococcal disease and gonorrhoea. New Subpart 5 extends contact tracing powers 
to contacts of people suspected of having an infectious disease, and that is an important 
change. That will allow for speedy follow-up, diagnosis, treatment, and containment. 
It is important that contact tracers are trained, and are suitably qualified health or 
community work practitioners, and the bill has been changed to require that. It clarifies 
the interface between appointed formal contact tracers and informal contact tracers. The 
latter might be general practitioners, sexual health clinic staff, or organisations like the  
New Zealand AIDS Foundation. The bill will not regulate their largely voluntary 
contact tracing practices unless they are nominees of district health board employees or 
a medical officer of health. 
The committee was clear that existing venereal disease le gislation is badly in need of 
an update. The current definition of “venereal disease” is not fit for modern conditions. 
For example, it does not include HIV, AIDS, or chlamydia. Other outdated provisions 
the bill will repeal include section 79 of the Healt h Act. That authorises a medical 
officer of health to detain and isolate people likely to cause the spread of infectious 
disease. New Part 3A effectively replaces section 79 with graduated powers of 
increasing robustness when an individual is not complying  with management aimed at 
preventing the spread of further infection. 
Part 2 of the bill prohibits the commercial provision of artificial ultraviolet light or 
UV tanning services for people under the age of 18. The Health Committee reported 
back that it is satisfied that the bill will protect the vulnerable under -18 age group while 
allowing adults to make informed decisions. That is comparable to other legislation, 
such as legislation on the sale and use of alcohol, which recognises that 18 is an age 
where people are capable of making their own choices. 
Clause 8 and clause 13 include several new provisions. These provide an 
infringement process to deal with breaches of the ban on providing artificial UV tanning 
services to people under the age of 18. This process would deal efficiently with offences 
27 May 2015 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 4075 
 
and prevent expensive and time -consuming criminal prosecutions. Voluntary standards 
and guidelines on the operation of UV tanning beds already exist. However, surveys 
have found consistently that there is variable  compliance with those voluntary steps 
designed to minimise harm, despite considerable effort to educate operators and to 
encourage compliance. I have therefore asked health officials to look into whether the 
licensing of premises and operators and the int roduction of mandatory standards are 
appropriate. 
This bill is going to improve the protections we have for the health of New 
Zealanders. It is an important part of our legislative framework for managing and 
reducing health risks. I commend this bill to the House.

the range of measures available to protect the public from the harm associated with
