clearly set out the aim of the bill and, just briefly, it is to increase the range of infectious 
diseases that are notifiable to the medical officer of health, without identifying the 
information of the patient or the diseased person. As the Minister said, this includes 
HIV, gonorrhoea, and syphilis. It also improves the management of persons with 
infectious diseases b y providing new management options, including directions issued 
by the medical officer of health, court orders, urgent health risk orders, and 
interventions. It strengthens legislative provisions for contact tracing of people who 
may have an infectious dis ease, and this bill introduces a ban on the provision of 
commercial artificial UV tanning services to people under 18 years of age. 
I just do want to correct the Minister —maybe he had not been informed —it was not 
a unanimous decision of the Health Committe e that we would only ban commercial UV 
tanning services for people under 18. In fact, there is a minority report provided from 
Labour, the Greens, and New Zealand First, and I will get to that in a moment. I do 
want to say, however, that I am really please d at the way the Health Committee is 
working under the chairmanship of Mr Simon O’Connor. I thought that we had a very 
good chair in Dr Paul Hutchison, and we worked very well together. I have to say that 
Mr O’Connor is shaping up to be a very good and open chair. 
The work that was done on this bill, I think, is commendable, because when you look 
at the number of amendments that have been made, they were made —with the 
exception of UV tanning services—through listening to the submissions that came from 
the p ublic. Also, I think a very good contribution was made by Kevin Hague, who, 
because of his background and the work that he had done in many different spheres but, 
particularly, working for the AIDS Foundation, was very helpful in helping us make 
some of these amendments. 
4076 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 27 May 2015 
 
I do not want to go through all the amendments we made. Anyone reading the bill 
would see that the select committee improved the bill by the amendments we made. But 
I do want to look at the amendment relating to privacy and identifications of persons. 
We have recommended that the changes here will ensure that the information collected 
by the new Part 3A, “Management of infectious diseases”, is to be used or disclosed  
only under the provision of the Health Act. This is to encourage individual s to provide 
private information without fear of inappropriate disclosure. I think it is really important 
that the fear that something about a person could somehow be made public is 
recognised. I think that we have amended that so we make that a lot stronger. Also, with 
regard to identifying information, it does allow the sex, date of birth, and the National 
Health Index number of a person with a notifiable disease to be disclosed. That will 
assist medical officers of health with disease surveillance. 
The only other point I want to mention is in the whole area of appeals. I want to pay 
credit to Kevin Hague for raising this issue and getting an amendment up, which would 
never have happened in the way it did if we had the previous Minister of Health, Tony 
Ryall. Although Dr Coleman is not here to hear this little bit of praise I may give him —
and this will be a very rare occasion —Dr Coleman was sent the suggested amendment 
that was made within the committee as we were deliberating. It was an amendment 
made by K evin Hague that enabled a person to be able to make an appeal to the High 
Court about a District Court’s decision on an order, part of an order, a variation of an 
order, or an extension of an order. It gave a proper appeal process, which was not in the 
original bill. When we came to an agreement on it, it was sent to the Minister of Health, 
and the Minister of Health responded within a very short time and accepted the 
amendment. I say sincerely that I do not believe that we would have got the same 
response having been through a number of bills under the previous Minister. 
However, I do want to express my real disappointment —and I actually even think 
that most members on the committee share this disappointment —that we could not get 
the Government to agree to ban commercial UV tanning services in New Zealand. You 
see, we are a Health Committee, and we do like to base our decisions on good evidence. 
That is what we must do. We must look at the evidence, and we must then say: “What is 
the best we can do for the p ublic health of New Zealand?”. The Minister said: “These 
changes we’re making are proportionate to risk.” Well, that does not apply, I have to 
say, to the banning of UV tanning services, which applies only to those under 18. 
I would like to say why. The Wo rld Health Organization classified sunbeds as a 
carcinogenic in 2009. It estimates that sunbed use before the age of 35 —not 18, but 
before the age of 35 —increases the risk of melanoma by 75 percent. Can I repeat that: 
sunbed use before the age of 35 increa ses the risk of melanoma by 75 percent. Skin 
cancer is one of the most common forms of cancer affecting New Zealanders. Each year 
over 2,000 new melanoma cases are identified, and on average 325 New Zealanders die 
from melanoma every year. 
Sunbed operators  at the Health Committee —and we had  only one submission, I 
think, that we heard; only one came along to support it —claimed that artificial UV 
tanning beds are an important source of vitamin D. Well, the Ministry of Health, the 
National Institute of Water a nd Atmospheric Research, the World Health Organization, 
senior dermatologists, and the Commerce Commission argued that short -wave UVB 
rays, which are rays that reach the outer layer of your skin, from commercial use, pose a 
cancer risk that far outweighs a ny minor vitamin D benefits. The overwhelming 
majority of submitters were opposed to the commercial use of these sunbed services. 
In fact, Australia, which does not often beat us in terms of public health in many 
health measures, has banned them. It can se e that they are of no benefit. We are now 
going to rely on some sort of code. Unfortunately, there was very recently, on 8 May, an 
27 May 2015 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 4077 
 
undercover surveillance of tanning salons undertaken by Consumer New Zealand, and it 
uncovered that more than 40 percent of t he 60 sunbed operators it visited failed to 
implement safety checks, such as checking the customer’s age, asking them to sign a 
consent form, and providing information on the dangers of UV exposure. One operator 
allowed a 14-year-old to use a sunbed. 
We do not believe this bill has gone far enough. This was the opportunity for us to 
ban the commercial use. We cannot stop what people do in their own homes; that is up 
to them. But there is absolutely no benefit from the commercial use of sunbeds. There is 
high risk presented to New Zealanders. I just feel that many members on the committee 
felt the same way as we did but were unable to do anything about it. So although we 
support the bill, we want to strongly stress that during the Committee stage we will be 
introducing a Supplementary Order Paper to ban the commercial use of sunbeds. 
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—Tāmaki): I am very pleased to take a call on this 
Health (Protection) Amendment Bill, which is on its second reading here. Can I thank 
the Hon Annette King for her generous words. I think such generosity is probably 
costing me thousands of votes in my electorate a t the moment —people who are going: 
“Oh, what’s he doing?”. But, actually, in all seriousness I do want to acknowledge all 
the members of the Health Committee, and in particular Annette King, Kevin Hague 
from the Green Party, and Barbara Stewart from the Ne w Zealand First Party, for the 
cooperative nature in which the committee is working —Louisa Wall, as well, as a 
Labour member, and then my fellow National Party members, Jacqui Dean, Barbara 
Kuriger, Scott Simpson, and Dr Shane Reti. It is a fine committee and I think it is one 
that is working together because we understand that there is always politics in all things, 
but health is one of those matters where we try to work together. 
I think we have heard in the speeches tonight, two so far, that by and large  there is a 
lot of agreement, but also —and it hints at the political nature or the difference of 
views—that you do not agree on everything. I am very pleased to see that members of 
the House from all the parties are supporting this, as I understand it. Thi s bill is in two 
parts. The substance of the bill is around contact tracing, and the second part of the bill, 
not as substantial but of course as important, is around sunbeds. 
As the Minister pointed out, we had 71 submissions. I thought that was actually a 
really good number in light of the nature of this bill. In fact, I thought there was a very 
high quality of submitters who came before us. I cannot remember the exact breakdown 
of how many came to talk to us around the contact tracing side of things vers us the UV 
tanning, but I am sure other members will echo —well, I hope they will—that it was the 
quality of the submissions and the quality of the oral presentations. These were people 
who are experts in their field. That is not to take away from the indivi duals who might 
come and choose to share their experiences. But I thought there were very high -level 
submissions to us. Twenty-two people were heard. It kept the committee busy, but I can 
say for myself, and I am sure for the others, that, actually, it was  incredibly fascinating 
as we would talk through the different issues. 
The first part of this Health (Protection) Amendment Bill is around contact tracing. 
For those in the House, and particularly for those at home, this is about how we work 
out whom a person with an infectious disease has been in contact with. The intention of 
this bill is to enable health authorities to better manage infectious disease outbreaks or 
to limit them when they arise. So we are talking infections, and I hope my father, 
listening at home, is not going to blush. We are talking about things like syphilis, 
gonorrhoea, tuberculosis, HIV, and the like—so some serious diseases that are out there 
in the community, or potentially so. With those I note that tuberculosis is currently 
under another Act. One of the elements of this bill is to actually take it from being a 
4078 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 27 May 2015 
 
distinct Act of Parliament, the Tuberculosis Act, and integrate it into this Health 
(Protection) Amendment Bill. 
These are serious infectious diseases and when they arise we , as a society, need to 
move swiftly and promptly to limit their effect. One only needs to think of the measles 
outbreak. That is not —I had better be clear —one of the infectious diseases noted at the 
highest end of this bill. There are good reasons for tha t, but I think of the outbreak —I 
think it was in Christchurch —and just how swiftly these diseases can spread and 
therefore, consequently, the State, the health authorities if you will, need to move 
swiftly to manage them. 
So we have introduced these extra diseases to be traced. A big part of that is: who are 
the people whom those with an infection have been in contact with? Up to now the 
provisions have not been sufficient enough or proportionate enough. To put it really 
simply, if someone chose not to actu ally enable contact tracing to help with certain 
diseases, it would not happen. So we are strengthening the ability of health agents to 
encourage and then enforce the information required so that we can make those contacts 
and better understand the spread of disease. One of the debates, of course, is around 
privacy, and that was discussed at length. There was some concern from some 
submitters, particularly around the use of the National Health Index number —that it 
could lead to the identification of particu lar people and consequently discourage them 
from coming forward. 
We heard from a good number of submitters who work within the epidemiological 
field, who said that the need for this data is absolutely paramount. Having data such as 
the sex, date of birth, and the National Health Index number are very, very important. 
One thing the committee did in a few of the changes it looked to bring about was to list 
principles, which we are hoping will be clear not only to the public but to the courts if 
they need to get involved. The first principle above all others is that the intention of this 
bill is to protect public health, not just the person with the infectious disease but all of 
us. That is the paramount principle. 
But we, as a committee, thought it was also really important to stress that the respect 
and dignity of the individual must always be noted and upheld, and, thirdly —although 
not in a priority order in this case —that a proportionate response is followed. So, 
depending on the nature of the infection, t heir proximity to people, for example, the 
length of the infection and so forth —what is the proportionate response? Because, as 
indicated implicitly by Annette King in her speech, there is the ability to bring about 
court orders to force an individual to r elease the information required. Again, we would 
want that to be a proportionate response depending on the infection. 
I want to briefly touch on the question of acute hepatitis C. This was something that 
members on the committee will know about. We spent a n enormous amount of time 
considering whether acute hepatitis C should actually be brought into the same level as 
gonorrhoea, syphilis, HIV, and the like. We took a lot of advice and decided it did not 
require at this stage to be at that top level, but I think it is really important for the House 
to understand, and those submitters, that it does remain on the schedule. It is still part of 
the Act. One has to think of this as a graduated bill, a graduated response. Although it is 
not at the top level, it is in there. It is a formidable disease and, fortunately, one that 
does not occur as frequently as some others, but when it does it needs a lot of treatment. 
I am very pleased to see, actually, that there are a number of very good pharmacological 
options available now for people there. 
Briefly, I want to acknowledge, as the Hon Annette King did, Kevin Hague’s 
contribution around appeals. It is really important, and certainly for me, that you always 
have consistency in legislation. The ability of a person to be  able to reach through the 
respective courts to have their appeal heard around these matters is consistent, so 
27 May 2015 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 4079 
 
reaching the High Court makes a lot of sense. I think it is important though that the 
orders remain in place. The committee did debate this a bit , that if someone is going to 
start going through the legal appeal process, it is not going to stop the ability of the 
health organisations to engage. When it comes to infectious diseases we need to move 
promptly. 
I want to turn to the sunbeds, the UV tann ing beds. The science is very clear on this. 
It is unambiguous, and I am more than happy to stand on the Government side and say 
this, with the legislation as it is, with a graduated response to UV tanning beds. This bill 
seeks to say that under -18s should not use them and that there should be regulation for 
those who do. Auckland Council, amongst others, has actually quite a good system in 
place already and it was really good that it came in and talked us through how it 
regulates sunbeds in Auckland. I think it is a model to follow. I want to be clear that it is 
not the model; there are a few we can look at. But we are looking at a regulatory 
approach. It is sort of that graduated approach, or one step at a time.  
Again, the science is very clear. As many m embers know, I worked at Southern 
Cross before coming into Parliament, so although I am not a doctor, I involve myself 
with a lot of things medical and particularly in the dermatological and plastics field. 
Look, there is no doubt about the issue of skin c ancers in this country and the place that 
sunbeds can play in that. I think I heard from one of the experts, one of the doctors I 
used to contract with, that something like 7 minutes a day of sunlight is all that we need, 
so where is the need for sunbeds in that case? 
I think we have come to a proportional response in this regard. We understand the 
science; we understand the information put to us by a number of medical experts in the 
likes of the Cancer Society. On this side of the House I think we are sayi ng that we 
understand that, and we understand the excessive risk for those under 18, but at this 
point we feel that an outright ban is probably not the best way forward. We will 
introduce a graduated approach to that. We will see that regulations are put in place. 
As any responsible group would do —in this case, the Government, the ministry, or 
the Minister —we will continue to engage with the information. So I think we have 
landed in a good place and, if I might say as I conclude, I think it was good to put a bit 
of light on to this bill. 
LOUISA WALL (Labour —Manurewa): Kia ora. Lau Afioga le Fofoga Fetalai. 
Kia ora. I am a proud member of the Health Committee and I want to echo my 
colleague Annette King’s kōrero earlier about how this committee is working. It is a 
very productive committee. I think that a lot of the discussions that we have are 
incredibly important, because we are talking about a health system that we want to help 
design and to ensur e meets the health needs of all New Zealanders. Essentially, the 
Health (Protection) Amendment Bill covers two areas. I am going to touch a lot on one 
of those areas, but, briefly, the first area is about protecting the public from the risk of 
the spread o f some infectious diseases. I think that what we did in the committee was 
have quite an interesting discussion about what some of those diseases should be. 
Obviously, the bill wanted to introduce tuberculosis to the schedule, but there was much 
debate about whether or not hepatitis C should be added. Obviously, because of that, we 
had discussions about other diseases that we think should be monitored, because the 
spread is actually causing an adverse effect, particularly in some communities. The 
second area that the bill covered was really about protection from the harm associated 
with artificial UV tanning.  
I am going to spend the majority of my contribution talking about the ban on solaria 
or UV tanning machines, because I think the evidence was actually incredibly 
compelling that 18 is, in fact, not the right age to have set if we were going to protect 
the largest number of New Zealanders. I want to agree with my colleague Annette King 
4080 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 27 May 2015 
 
when she said that the World Health Organization is categoric in terms  of UV tanning 
machines causing cancer. From the evidence that the World Health Organization has 
gathered, in fact, 35 years should be the age that we ban the use of UV sunbeds, if we 
were going to set an age. That is part of the discussion that I think is  still ongoing. 
Essentially, we have set it at 18 years because once you are over 18, you are an adult 
and the State ceases to care about you. This is even though we have got overwhelming 
evidence that the use of these devices is harmful to you, and in spi te of 2,000 more New 
Zealanders getting diagnosed with melanoma every year, and over 326 of us dying 
because we get melanoma. So, in spite of all the evidence, we set the age at 18 because 
up to the age of 18 you are a child and, as the State, we will prot ect you. But, if you are 
over the age of 18, you are on your own and you make your own decisions. So, if you 
are not as informed, or if you practise UV sunbed use because you think it makes you 
look attractive and you want to be browner, or whatever it mig ht be, we say that that is 
your choice.  
What we in the Opposition say is that it actually should not be your choice because, 
at the end of the day, there are alternatives. If you want to get brown, you can spray 
stuff on you these days, right? So if you a re doing it for cosmetic reasons, there are 
actually alternatives that are not going to kill you. What we said was that, actually, 
given that there is an existing by -law—Auckland Council has one that already bans 
under-18-year-olds from using UV tanning ma chines—the effectiveness of this piece of 
legislation is essentially going to benefit only 25 percent of the sunbeds that are out 
there. Auckland Council made that decision, and the other interesting submission from 
my perspective was from Palmerston North  City Council. It made a decision as a 
council. It made a decision because it had some evidence from a dermatologist, a 
woman called Louise Reiche—I hope I am pronouncing her name correctly—that in the 
MidCentral District Health Board region, the rate of m elanoma is 51.55 per 100,000 
people. The national average is 39.12.  
So, as a council, it got actively involved in this piece of legislation because it was 
relevant to the council, and also there was a case of a young 16 -year-old, Jessie Anitoni, 
who got c ancer. There was a lot of publicity, I guess, in that community about the 
effects of UV tanning machines, so it was very clear that it wanted central government 
to ban them. Rather than having every local council in the country going through a 
process of b anning these machines, it wanted us to take responsibility as central 
government and enact a piece of legislation that was going to benefit the community —
the public good. This is because, when you look at who actually benefits from using UV 
sunbeds, there are some cohorts of New Zealanders who do, such as those who suffer 
from seasonal depression and are actually prescribed to go and have some UV sunbed 
treatments, and also people with psoriasis. So, actually, there is a medical rationale for 
using UV sunbeds that we agree with. In fact, it would have been exempted in terms of 
a ban because it was to be used in a medical procedure. Those beds are actually in 
hospitals and they are available to people who need them.  
So I think that the decision that the comm ittee made to set the age at 18 is really not 
in the interests of New Zealanders. It is not in the interests of the 326 people who die 
from melanoma every year and the over 2,000 New Zealanders who get diagnosed with 
melanoma every year. If we had been bra ve—and I do not even think that we would 
have been brave. In fact, Australia and Brazil have already banned UV sunbeds because 
they realise that it is bad for the community and for the citizens of their countries. Are 
their rates higher than ours? Actually, they are not. We have higher rates than Australia. 
We have higher rates than Brazil. So this really was, I think, one of the critical decisions 
that the committee made —the decision not to ban them —because we think that that 
would have somehow sent the message that we were being nanny State, we were telling 
27 May 2015 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 4081 
 
people how to live their lives, and we were not allowing them to be adults and make 
decisions for themselves. Well, actually, no. Our responsibility as legislators is to 
protect the people of New Zealan d, and when we have evidence, which is 
overwhelming, that says that the effects of UV sunbed usage is so detrimental and that 
there is nothing to be gained from it, then I think it is incumbent on us to act. I have not 
given up hope. I want to acknowledge that my colleague Annette King has got an 
amendment that wants a progressive system over a period of time that will mean that in 
5 years there will be no more UV sunbeds. So we are not going to take them away 
immediately, but we want to phase them out prog ressively, and let those people find the 
spray-cans if they are doing it because they want to look lovely. They can go to the 
chemist and buy those and look all brown, and people will think that they have been in 
the sun. They do not need to sit under those sunbeds and actually harm themselves.  
The only other thing I wanted to cover was that I was really interested in the 
discussion about what is ionising and what is non -ionising. What I want to highlight in 
my take -away from the ionising/non -ionising deba te is that I understand that non -
ionising is actually low frequency —it is not as intense. But what I also got from the 
discussion we had with the experts was that it is about the compound effect. It is about 
the compound effect, so how much is too much? If  you go and have these sunbeds once 
a week, once a fortnight, once a month —actually, what is the frequency, when the 
compound use of these things actually has the same effect as ionising radiation? That 
was not clear. I am clear about what is ionising and non-ionising because associated 
with UV radiation are cell phone towers, Wi -Fi, power lines, and all those things. They 
are in our environment. I understand that. We live with those. But what we did not get 
to do was to consider that if this is non -ionising with a compound effect, then actually 
maybe we should limit the frequency. So are we going to say: “OK, you are over 18. 
You can make up your own mind, but actually you can use these things only once a 
fortnight. If you use them more than that, the compo und effect is like using ionised 
radiation.”? So that is my contribution to this debate. I look forward to an ongoing 
discussion, because I am hopeful that the Government is going to support Annette 
King’s amendment. Nā reira, tēnā koutou katoa. Talofa lava. 
SCOTT SIMPSON (National —Coromandel): It is a pleasure to stand and take a 
call on the second reading of the Health (Protection) Amendment Bill. Just following 
from the last speaker, Lo uisa Wall, I think that for many on the Health Committee the 
biggest education was actually not about the terms ionising and non -ionising; it was 
actually to separate them from iodising. At one stage we had someone who was 
convinced that the word was “iodi sed”, as in salt, and, of course, it is a completely 
different thing.  
I would like to join with other speakers tonight in congratulating the work of the total 
committee, actually. When we see a select committee working at its collegial best to 
ensure good  outcomes for legislation, I think that that is when we see Parliament 
working at its best. I am delighted to report to the House that under the chairmanship of 
my colleague Simon O’Connor the committee is functioning very well, very collegially, 
and we are getting good results. I think members will have seen something of the tone 
of the committee reflected in the speeches that we have heard tonight, and I am sure that 
will continue to be the case as this debate continues.  
Notwithstanding the minority report of the Labour Party, New Zealand First, and the 
Green Party, I am very pleased to learn that I think all those parties are going to support 
the progress of this bill through the House. The point of difference between 
Government members and Opposition me mbers around the committee stems, as Louisa 
Wall has said, from the extension or the potential extension of the commercial UV 
tanning clinics, and as the committee chair, Simon O’Connor, made clear during his 
4082 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 27 May 2015 
 
contribution—and the Minister—that is at this stage a step too far. I am personally quite 
relaxed about that at this stage, but I would like to reserve my personal view on how 
that might unfold over the years to come. I think that in many of these matters relating 
to health, science, and education we f ind that it is a learning process. Technology and 
information change, and we find ourselves in a position to be flexible and nimble of 
foot in terms of the legislative response.  
This bill seeks to amend the Health Act of 1956, and the fact that we are ame nding 
that Act gives some context to the change that has occurred in both medical science and 
in human knowledge over the period of time since the principal Act was passed by this 
House. So it is very appropriate, given the changes in both medicine and als o in society, 
that we update legislation to accommodate changed circumstances.  
Back in 1956 I doubt that there could have conceivably been a situation like one that 
may exist today where people, for reasons that were probably almost criminally 
motivated, would use the fact that they had some kind of communicable disease, some 
kind of infectious disease, to actually wreak harm upon other human beings. I think that 
would be something that the legislators back in 1956 would have found difficult to 
comprehend.  
Regrettably, we have had cases in our recent history where, for instance —and this is 
very rare, I know, but it is important that as a legislature we accommodate the rare 
situations—people infected with AIDS or HIV have gone about actually infecting others 
in a way that is, as I say, criminally negligent and culpable if not anything to do with 
medical responsibility.  
So we need to update our legislation to ensure that as a society we have an 
opportunity to protect the greater good of the wider community from what are 
essentially rogue individuals. This amendment bill essentially does that. It creates a 
progressive stage of restrictions, management, if you like —controls might be another 
word we might like to use —in terms of managing people who have a defined range of 
infectious diseases. Some of those diseases are quite damaging, and they are highly 
infectious, and I think we have an obligation, an absolute obligation, as legislators to put 
the protection of the wider community first.  
There are times when we have to think about the potential impact on the rights of 
individuals versus the rights of the greater, wider comm unity. This bill, I think, seeks to 
achieve that through a number of means. One of the, I guess, constitutional issues that 
those who are interested in matters relating to civil rights and personal human rights 
might have been concerned about —and it was ra ised in the select committee —was the 
question of how far these additional management provisions would go in terms of 
inhibiting the rights of individuals who may be infected with a particular disease.  
So the framework that the committee and this legislati on seek to adopt uses a 
principle of risk management and proportionality based on the risk associated with the 
individual versus the risk to the wider community. I think the bill places as few 
restrictions as are possible while at the same time maintaining  that greater good concept 
and principle that is important to protecting the wider public health objectives of the 
original statute and, of course, this amending piece of legislation.  
The measures provide, actually, better tools for public health staff to deal with people 
who, for one reason or another, do not voluntarily seek treatment or do not voluntarily 
modify their behaviour once they have been diagnosed with a communicable and 
notifiable disease. So that behaviour, I think, is one that we need to be  able to balance 
carefully against the individual’s rights.  
So where consent is not given —and I stress that this is a very small minority of 
potential cases —the current legislation simply does not allow for an appropriate 
response. For instance, the curre nt legislation does not allow for the detention of an 
27 May 2015 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 4083 
 
infected person. The provisions in the bill cover the rights, duties, offences, and 
penalties, and a range of restrictive powers and procedures for directions and court 
orders, and it also creates a reg ime for urgent orders for people whose consistent and 
persistent behaviour may place others at risk. I think that is an appropriate, moderate 
response given the state of society and science today.  
Powers at the lesser end of that regime —for example, the power to give directions—
are able to be exercised by a medical officer of health, and I think that, again, provides 
an appropriate response to the lesser communicable and infectious diseases. Directions 
are the community-level measures, and they may include , for instance, directing people 
to seek testing or treatment, or counselling, or they may involve the direction of people 
not to attend public places for a specified period of time. There would be some who 
would argue that the restriction on the movement of an individual may be a step too far. 
I am not one of those people. I think that this is a balance that is about right. If people 
choose not to take their responsibilities to their wider community seriously, then I think 
we as a society have an obligation to enforce those responsibilities for them.  
The lack of such intermediate powers has been identified as a weakness in the 1956 
legislation, so this amending bill we are considering here tonight provides a more 
restrictive power—for example, detention in some cases. But that can be exercised only 
following a public health order made by a District Court. The select committee 
considered appeals and the process all around that sort of thing, and I think we have 
landed in a pretty good spot.  
I have addressed most of my comments this evening in the second reading to matters 
relating to civil rights and the ability of the State and us as a legislature to enforce 
powers on individuals in cases when that is required and, I think, balanced and 
necessary. This is, I think, a very good piece of legislation. It updates some now quite 
old legislation that was well intentioned in 1956 but that is in serious need of an update. 
This bill does that and I thoroughly commend it to the House. Once again I thank the 
select committee for the collegial and congenial way it has conducted its affairs. Thank 
you. 
KEVIN HAGUE (Green) : Talofa lava, Mr Assistant Speaker. I want to begin by

As others have noted, this bill has two parts, and both of those parts go to the 
limitation of individual liberty. Part 1 limits individual liberty for the sake of the public 
good and, therefore, seeks to strike the balance on that issue. Part 2 deals with  another 
situation, the restraint of individual liberty, which is where the State intervenes to curtail 
the liberty of an individual to take action that would cause harm to themselves. These 
are two of the kinds of situations that this House grapples with from time to time.  
Picking up on one of Scott Simpson’s comments in the most recent contribution, Part 
1, as he said, seeks to amend the Health Act of 1956. I am reminded that a couple of 
years ago in this House we passed the marriage equality Act, which was overhauling a 
piece of legislation from 1955. That legislation had fossilised in law some attitudes and 
mores from our society at that time. I have worked with Nikki Kaye, in fact, to draft a 
bill to completely overhaul adoption law because the Adoption Act 1955 fossilises some

mores and attitudes about children that pertained to that time but are no longer relevant 
in ours. In 1956 the Health Act was written to deal with some particular issues—chiefly, 
tuberculosis, in fact —and it applied attitudes tow ards the restraint of liberty that 
prevailed at that time but no longer seem as relevant.  
Perhaps unusually in this House, I have had some experience of applying the 1956 
Health Act. I used to be the executive director of the New Zealand AIDS Foundation. I 
dealt with a situation —in fact, a couple of situations —in a New Zealand city of a 
person who had HIV and who had persisted, despite all efforts to change his behaviour, 
in having unsafe sex with multiple sexual partners, and I was faced with the dilemma of 
what on earth I should do about it. Doing nothing would mean that a number of people 
would be needlessly exposed to the risk of HIV infection—something I certainly did not 
want on my conscience —so I looked to the law. What did the law allow me to do? 
What did the Privacy Act permit me to do? What did the Health Act permit me to do? I 
was astonished that, essentially, the only path that the Health Act made available was 
for me to notify the medical officer of health, who then would seek a court order to 
detain this man indefinitely. That was the only option that the law provided.  
So I am relieved that I have played an active part in some of the work that went into 
drafting the Public Health Bill, which sits at No. 30 on the Order Paper —it would be

the risks that they are trying to mitigate. I am very pleased to see these measures  
progress through the House.  
I did have some concerns —which I expressed in the first reading debate, and 
members of the select committee will know that I raised them repeatedly during our

I want to just briefly note my approval that we are adding chlamydia to the list of

I come to Part 2, which is the part of the bill concerned with sunbeds. As the

Kevin Hague mentioned in his speech tonight —and he gave some very thoughtful 
contributions on this in the select committee —the issue of the need for contact tracing 
whilst at the same time protecting the privacy of some vulnerable populations. This was 
a point that was also considered very closely by the committee. On the one hand, there 
is the need to stop the spread of some pretty infectious diseases such as gonorrhoea and 
hepatitis in some populations. STDs are not great diseases to have, and they can hang 
around for many years and can cause all sorts of problems later in life —all sorts of 
health issues. They are not diseases to be taken lightly. But, as Kevin Hague poi nted out 
to the committee—and this was also backed up by submissions —the provisions around 
contact tracing need to be very carefully applied so that the rights of individuals are not 
4088 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 27 May 2015 
 
necessarily impinged, and so that the rules around contact tracing and th e provision of 
information are commensurate with the potential risk that is posed by the disease. 
In this bill, contact tracing is designed not to be a mallet, but rather to be a process 
that has gradual interventions. The first stage of that is to attempt  to gain voluntary 
consent from somebody who has presented at a hospital or a GP’s surgery and is found 
to have what is now going to be a notifiable disease. If that consent is not gained 
voluntarily, then the bill introduces a duty on a person who may hav e an infectious 
disease or who might have been exposed to an infectious disease to provide the 
prescribed contact information. That contact information could well be, clearly, people 
whom they have had contact with —names, addresses; that sort of thing —obviously so 
that the medical officers can trace those people and can confine the outbreak, or 
potential outbreak. 
The practice of seeking voluntary consent for contact tracing will be the preferred 
method and the first option for managing the risk of infectio n. The provisions in the bill 
increase the range of infectious diseases that are notifiable, thereby improving the 
surveillance of infectious diseases that are of concern, including their long -term impact 
on health. The more quality information that is hel d about these things, the more likely 
it is that any potential outbreak or spread of an infectious disease or STD can be 
contained. There are measures being introduced in the bill to protect the identity of 
individuals and to allay concerns that people mig ht not seek treatment if they believe 
that their identity will be made public. The issue that Kevin Hague brought very clearly 
to the committee is that we do not want populations of people hiding away for fear of 
being publicly exposed as having a certain notifiable disease or STD. 
The approach taken in the bill, and I congratulate the Minister on this approach, is to 
use the principles of risk management and proportionality. Rather than, as I said, using a 
mallet to strike a walnut, the principles of risk management and proportionality are 
brought into play in this bill. This is a good bill, which is being well supported around 
the House. We do have a point of difference, of course, around tanning services —of 
course we do—but otherwise I am pleased to see t hat the bill is enjoying good support 
and good debate. I commend it to the House.

4090 Health (Protection) Amendment Bill 27 May 2015 
 
The bill gives effect to the Government’s decision in October 2013 to improve the 
range of measures available to protect the public from the harm associated with some 
infectious diseases and with artificial UV tannin g. The aim of the bill is to increase the 
range of infectious diseases that are notifiable to medical officers of health without 
identifying the information of patients or diseased persons. This will include HIV 
infection, gonorrhoea infection, acquired im mune deficiency syndrome —AIDS—and 
syphilis. It also aims to improve and manage persons with infectious diseases by 
providing new management options, including directions issued by a medical officer of 
health, court orders, urgent health risk orders, and in terventions. It also aims to 
strengthen legislative provisions for the contact tracing of people who may have an 
infectious disease or who may have been exposed to one. It also aims to introduce a ban 
on the provision of commercial artificial UV tanning se rvices to people under 18 years 
old.

Opposition members, has been around the full banning of commercial UV operations —
i.e., tanning beds. Of course, Labour will be intro ducing an amendment for the House’s 
consideration when we come to the Committee of the whole House, which is around 
why we propose an outright ban.

committee. I was not a member on that committee, but I do acknowledge the way in

actually tap on—

GAMBLING AMENDMENT BILL (NO 3) 
Second Reading 
Hon PETER DUNNE (Minister of Internal Affairs) : I move, That the Gambling 
Amendment Bill (No 3) be now read a second time . At the outset I would like to thank 
the members of the Government Administrati on Committee for their efforts in 
thoroughly considering this bill. It was referred to the committee in November of last 
year and was reported back to the House on 11 May this year, a considerably faster 
track than its predecessor. The select committee rec eived 126 written submissions on 
the bill, as well as hearing oral submissions in Wellington and Auckland.  
This bill makes a limited number of amendments to the Gambling Act 2003 but does 
so in several key areas. The majority of these changes relate to ga ming machines, or 
pokies, in bars and pubs. This form of gambling generates a significant amount of 
money. For example, in the 2013 -14 financial year, New Zealanders spent around $700 
million on over 13,000 pokie machines in commercial venues across the co untry. The 
select committee’s report recommends a range of key amendments to the bill, which I 
support. Many are quite specific, and traverse a wide variety of aspects of the Act. For 
example, the committee’s report tidies up the important definition of “k ey person” in 
the bill to prevent unintended consequences. The regulation -making powers under the 
Act involving the way societies distribute funds to the community are also improved, 
and this will resolve some gaps and fix some drafting issues.  
One purpose of the Act is to limit opportunities for crime and dishonesty associated 
with conducting gambling. People can be involved with conducting gambling either 
through a society that is licensed to conduct the gambling or as venue personnel where 
the gaming machines are located. Obviously, there are those who receive grant funding 
as well. The Act looks to prevent conflicts of interest by prohibiting personal benefits 
4098 Gambling Amendment Bill (No 3) 27 May 2015 
 
being given or taken between those groups. The objective here is to ensure that personal 
gain is not a prime motivator for people’s actions over and above community benefit. 
This is a very difficult area, because it is hard to define exactly what the unwelcome 
behaviour is. It is also a problem getting sufficient proof to successfully prosecute 
offenders. So the committee has recommended a change of approach, considering that 
the bill originally went too far in trying to clamp down on transactions between these 
groups. Instead, it has recommended an amendment to the bill so that the behaviour at 
issue is more effectively targeted.  
That will prevent everyday transactions between, say, the society and venue staff 
from triggering a potential conflict situation. For example, someone from a society 
buying a meal at a bar where pokie machines happen to be located could well have been 
caught by the provision in the bill as drafted. I think the committee has arrived at a 
reasonable outcome. It has also introduced a longer limitation period for bringing 
prosecution actions for conflict of interest offences, and that will more accurately reflect 
the length of time it takes to uncover the behaviour and gather enough evidence to 
mount a prosecution.  
Let me touch on some other improvements to the bill that the committee has made. It 
has recommended changes to give greater certainty in a few areas . One such change 
concerns the ability of the secretary in screening licence applicants in terms of their 
suitability to be involved in providing gambling. It is important that all relevant 
information can be considered, to give a complete picture of a per son’s past behaviour. 
Another change protects the ability of affected parties to seek a judicial review. The 
Gambling Commission has been given the power to delay the effective date of its 
decision so that a review can be sought. Another change of note con cerns licence 
periods. The intention is to allow longer licences for highly compliant operators, and the 
committee’s recommendations make it very clear that that will be a decision for the 
Secretary for Internal Affairs to make, which will mean that there will no longer be 
appeals and arguments about why everyone is not getting a longer licence.  
I note that the committee’s report includes minority views on the most notable area 
of change that the bill introduces. This is in the area of payments to venues t hat actually 
host the machines. The committee has a couple of minority reports in that regard. New 
regulations would need to be developed to replace the current system, which is agreed 
by all parties to be very cumbersome and time -consuming. The minority r eports from 
Labour and the Greens describe particular concerns about the favoured option, which is 
a commission -based system. Their concerns, essentially, are that a commission -based 
system could incentivise operators to maximise gambling in their venues. It was their 
perception that venue operators could take advantage, therefore, of vulnerable patrons 
rather than carrying out their duty to be responsible hosts. In response to those concerns 
I note that the design of the system for the regulations is still  being developed. The aim 
here is for a payment scheme to cover the cost of venues. It is not intended to provide 
profits.  
Of course, no system will be absolutely perfect, but I do believe a change is needed. 
The current system requires a considerable amo unt of time and effort by the department 
and the societies. If payments were simplified, the department could focus on other 
areas like harm prevention, to ensure greater compliance by the sector. In short, I want 
to give the House an assurance that the po tential concerns about a new payment system 
are being taken seriously. Under the Gambling Act, when new regulations are being 
proposed I am required to be satisfied that consultation has occurred with the people 
likely to be substantially affected. There i s an onus on the department to ensure that all 
groups are consulted before final proposals are put forward and that their views are 
27 May 2015 Gambling Amendment Bill (No 3) 4099 
 
considered. Once the new system is in place, class 4 operators will be expected to meet 
their harm prevention responsibilities.  
One of the purposes of the principal Act is to ensure that money from gambling 
benefits the community. I believe that this sits at the very heart of what we try to 
achieve in this country when it comes to the regulation of gambling. We are unique in 
the world in the way we channel money from gambling back into community purposes. 
It is a feature that I think we need to keep to the fore when we look at changes to our 
gambling laws. Gambling is an established, legitimate form of entertainment. For the 
most part it is harmless fun, but for a small few it is not fun but extremely destructive. 
We need to do all we can to make gambling a safe pastime, and that is where the Act 
balances the provision of gambling with the need for harm minimisation measures to be 
put in place.  
I am aware that some have advocated the introduction of pre -commitment 
technology into our gaming machines. Although the Act already includes an ability to 
do this through regulations, the evidence on pre -commitment is still unclear. The 
overseas experience has been mixed. Much depends on the specific design and features 
of such a system. In short, there are many unknowns. Although I accept that the use of 
technology in this area has a lot of potential and could be a powerful way of 
encouraging people to gamble in a way that is appropriate to their circumstances, and 
there are advantages in such a system, I do not think we need to be rushing to impose 
that new technology. It would create a significant cost at the expense of community 
purposes. A reasonably strong, compelling case is needed for features that will work 
best in the New Zealand context. I expect the Department of Internal Affairs to remain 
active in monitoring research and developments in this space, including having 
discussions with the Ministry of Health and the Associate Minister of Health,  who has 
an interest in this issue, as well.  
Finally, can I conclude by acknowledging all of those who took time to make 
submissions to the select committee. It is a well-known fact that gambling issues always 
prompt a range of strong views from across the community. I think the committee has 
done a good job in working its way through those and presenting us with a workable 
piece of legislation. As a consequence of the committee’s work, I th ink that the bill that 
has now come back to the House responds to the specific concerns raised about pokie 
operators. It does provide for better transparency in the sector and also some greater 
controls. That, in turn, will help ensure that the very import ant objectives of the 
Gambling Act are fulfilled. So I have great pleasure in commending the Gambling 
Amendment Bill (No 3) to the House.

me a lot of encouragement about some of the venues a ctually being in a position at this 
time to not take the incentive of a commission -based system. That is why it is really 
important, I believe, that we think carefully about that and make sure that the 
commission-based payment system does not incentivise gambling.  
The other area that I want to pay particular attention to is harm minimisation 
measures. I think that we have missed an opportunity here. I believe that at every single 
opportunity when we are talking about gambling and the Gambling Amendment Bil l 
(No 3) before us, we should have, and could have, taken stronger measures around 
minimising the harm caused by gambling. The Minister mentioned —and it was also 
raised in the minority reports —implementing a pre -commitment system. Other 
countries have impl emented this very system, and I believe it is incumbent upon this 
Parliament to actually make sure that we have every opportunity to implement systems 
that do address the harm caused by gambling. Two of the submitters —I will not 
mention them by name —on two  separate occasions spoke to the Government 
Administration Committee about their experiences of the harm that they have suffered 
through gambling. That was very passionate, it was very powerful, and what was very 
clear to me was that a system that actually  worked around pre-commitment could have 
prevented the experience that they had had to go through. So I want to thank those two 
particular submitters, who told us in very raw detail about the effect that gambling had 
had on their lives.  
There are some good things in this bill, and that is why our party is supporting it. We 
have already heard from the Minister about the suitability of key persons and the key 
persons’ issues that are addressed in this bill. I want to focus on the benefits with 
conditions attached. The inclusion of just one word altered the whole of clause 16 to the 
satisfaction of the many, many submitters who submitted against this particular clause, 
and that was the inclusion of the word “improper”. Just one word, and it changed the 
whole nature of the clause. Feedback from those submitters indicated that the inclusion 
of that word has addressed their issues, because their issues were about things like being 
able to pay their staff because the clause had some unintended consequences that mea nt 
that, as key persons, they would not be able to walk into the pub of another society’s 
venue and order their dinner and a drink without breaking this law. So that is a proper 
thing for them to be able to do. The intention of the clause was to eliminate improper 
actions. So that was something that collectively, as a select committee, we were able to 
address.  
There were a number of submissions around the definition of a “relative”, and that 
issue, also, was addressed. It was narrowed down to parents, son,  daughter, spouse, or 
partner rather than the wider whānau. Some of us have got really big whānau, which 
would have meant that we and the rest of our family would all be unable to carry out a 
normal transaction if we were a key person. Also, we extended th e limitations from 2 
years to 5 years because there were indications that cases had been advised through the 
27 May 2015 Gambling Amendment Bill (No 3) 4101 
 
proper authorities but they were out of time. Two years seemed to be too short, and so 
that has now been extended to 5 years. Also, there are some specific clauses that the 
New Zealand Racing Board needed to be addressed, and those amendments address 
those issues to an extent that I understand that it is satisfied. I am not sure whether all its 
members are happy, but they are certainly satisfied with  the amendments that have been 
made.  
So, finally, I just want to again thank the submitters and also acknowledge the 
members of the Government Administration Committee for the work that has been 
done. I also acknowledge the Minister again for acknowledgin g those key issues and 
concerns we have with this bill. Nō reira, tēnā tātou. 
SARAH DOWIE (National —Invercargill): Talofa lava. Greetings, Mr Deputy 
Speaker, and thank you for allowing me to take this call on the Gambling Amendment 
Bill (No 3). The fact that it is No. 3 suggests something. It is a series of technical bills 
off the back of a parent Act, the Gambling Ac t 2003, which was reform legislation to 
minimise harm in the industry of gambling.  
This bill, I believe, is an example of the MMP environment at work. It is the 
Government working with its coalition partners —in particular the Hon Peter Dunne, 
who has shepherded this bill through the House, and the Māori Party. But I also want to 
take this time to thank the Government Administration Committee. We often hear that it 
is a high-powered select committee that hears some very important bills. I want to thank 
the committee members for their collegial spirit in panel beating this bill into shape.  
I think it is worth noting that even though this is an amendment bill and it is technical 
in nature, gambling—and this is certainly something I have learnt from other subm itters 
whom we heard in Wellington and Auckland —affects all New Zealanders, whether 
directly or indirectly, at some point in their lives. That is why I think these bills should 
not be taken for granted. They do affect us and they are important when we are 
finessing this industry to minimise harm. This bill is, in particular, in respect of class 4 
pokie machines, and they are pokies that are held off site from casinos. We are trying to 
make the industry more transparent and, of course, at the end of the day,  a better 
industry.  
We heard from 126 submitters and, as I said before, we heard them in Wellington 
and Auckland. Most of those submitters were in support of, had conditional support for, 
or had a mixed view on the mooted draft bill. There were some submi tters not in 
support of the bill because, as we heard from our counterparts, they believed that the bill 
did not go far enough in respect of some of the harm minimisation measures. I think that 
their intent is admirable and I certainly listened carefully t o what they were saying, but 
at the end of the day I believe that that went beyond the ambit of what this bill was 
considering. But it was certainly educational for me to hear those submissions, and I 
take their wisdom on board.  
In respect of what this bi ll is trying to achieve, in the first instance  it is trying to 
achieve transparency around grant decision -making. This bill introduces new 
requirements for publicising societies’ grants: the details as to what has been applied 
for, what is received, the pu rpose, and what has been granted. It also provides that this 
information is detailed and sent through to the Department of Internal Affairs, so as to 
achieve a balance and check on that society and so that the public can scrutinise that 
society and what it  is providing —the funds that it is sending back to the community 
from where, essentially, they had been lost.  
The bill also requires any real conflicts of interest between societies that collect the 
money from gambling class 4 pokies and those grant recip ients to be published, again 
adding to the transparency and the accountability in the community as to how those 
funds have been applied. Regulations are to be developed later, and they will set out the 
4102 Gambling Amendment Bill (No 3) 27 May 2015 
 
detail as to how all of this will be achieved, so it may well be that general information is 
published in a local newspaper, but then more detailed information is published online. 
Regardless of the mix of that, the information will be readily available, and, hence, that 
adds to the accountability.  
The secon d theme of this bill is to increase transparency around the operations of 
societies themselves. Under regulations, the publishing of financial statements and the 
form in which they are published by societies will be mandated, highlighting the 
efficiency of  the operation itself. So, again, we are running with the theme of 
transparency and are trying to tidy up the industry and filter funds back into the 
community in which they were lost.  
The third theme I want to touch on is simplifying compliance costs in venue 
payments. We have heard from members opposite that they believe that a commission -
based system will incentivise gambling societies to increase the number of machines or 
to be irresponsible hosts. They also oppose rewarding societies that perform well  with 
longer licences at the discretion of the Department of Internal Affairs. On this side of 
the House we do not believe that that view has foundation. There is no evidence to 
suggest that moving to a commission -based system will incentivise gambling, an d the 
design of any new payment system will be detailed in regulations. As we are advised, 
the department will run a full consultative process in respect of that, and I think that that 
consultative process is extremely important for the purpose of giving m ore thought to 
what exactly the best cost recovery basis is to keep compliance costs down and, again, 
to keep things simple. Furthermore, the grant of longer licences to societies that perform 
well does not equate with an abuse because those licences will be at the discretion of the 
regulator, which will take into account the suitability of the applicant and past 
performance.  
It would not be appropriate for me to end this speech without some examples of 
some responsible class 4 operators that are performing well and that, of course, leads me 
back to my own electorate, Invercargill, and the Invercargill Licensing Trust. It is 
responsible for sponsoring our community in a fantastic way. It has allocated total 
grants of $49.57 million— 
Paul Foster-Bell: How much? 
SARAH DOWIE: —total grants of $49.57 million—during the 2008 to 2013 period, 
which is an average of $9.92 million per year. It has delivered some really big -ticket 
items like our stadium, ILT Stadium Southland, and the velodrome, which is 
responsible for some really fantastic projects. The stadium is integral, obviously, to our 
community. The weather is not always great. Of course, I keep waxing on that our 
people are so positive we do not need weather to keep us positiv e, but we can go 
indoors and use our stadium and enjoy that. But the trust has also delivered electronic 
whiteboards in schools. It has built learners’ pools for swimming, and even contributed 
to tertiary scholarships. In saying that, it has granted more t han 170 scholarships to 
individual Invercargill students, locally and abroad. Each student receives $2,000 for 3 
years and the total paid in 2012 and 2013 was $374,000 -odd. This is an example of a 
society working hard for the community. It can be done well  and I believe that these 
measures in this bill will uplift the industry, make it more transparent, and minimise 
harm, as the 2003 Act set out to do. So with that I commend this bill to the House. 
Hon RUTH DYSON (Labour —Port Hills): I would like to begin by requesting an 
extension of time for the member who has just resumed her seat, Sarah Dowie —maybe 
for another 3 minutes. Seriously, can I begin my contribution by saying talofa lava, 
malo le soifua, as part of my contribution to the celebration of the wonderful Samoan 
language this week. The week to celebrate Samoan language immediately follows New 
Zealand Sign Language Week, which we had last week. I am calling on the member

Ron Mark to gi ve as much highlighting to the Samoan language as he did to New 
Zealand Sign Language Week last week, but perhaps in a more gentle way. But the 
publicity we got for that language was great.  
This is a pretty momentous occasion tonight. I think that there have been few times 
since 2008 that we have not had on the Order Paper a gambling bill of some description, 
so I am delighted to be speaking to the Gambling Amendment Bill (No 3). The other 
significance of this legislation, as other members have indicated —the Minister who 
spoke, the member from Invercargill, and my colleague who is responsible for gambling 
issues for Labour, Adrian Rurawhe —is that with a couple of policy points as 
exceptions, this bill has been supported by the Government Administration Committee 
and most of the submitters. The submitters came to our committee and said: “We 
support this bill except for one area, and it does not go far enough in another.” That was 
the basis of th e contribution of some really substantial submissions, and I have to say 
also that there were some submissions that were very moving.  
It is a huge difference to be debating a bill that has got agreement as opposed to that 
shonky Skycity deal that Minister  Joyce brought to this House, where we saw Skycity 
getting more pokies in return for a convention centre. In 2011, when Skycity booted out 
all the competition, we were told would get a convention centre that could 
accommodate up to 5,000 people. We will ha ve a convention centre that can take fewer 
than 3,000. Is that an international convention centre? I do not think so.
